  32. 优西比乌，《教会史》(H. E.)，VIII.1。↩︎

  33. 阿瑟·詹姆斯·梅森 (Arthur James Mason)的《戴克里先的逼迫》(Persecution of Diocletian)一书，就是这样开篇的。↩︎

  34. 马克西米安 (Maximian，别号赫库利乌斯〔Herculius〕)统治意大利和非洲；伽列里乌斯 (Galerius，阿尔门塔里乌斯〔Armentarius〕)统治多瑙河沿岸地区，后来又统治东方；君士坦提乌斯(Constantius，克洛鲁斯〔Chlorus〕)统治高卢、西班牙和不列颠；戴克里先则将亚细亚、埃及和色雷斯 (Thrace)留归自己，驻居尼科米底亚。伽列里乌斯和君士坦提乌斯休弃原配之后，前者娶了戴克里先的女儿（不幸的瓦莱里娅〔Valeria〕），后者娶了马克西米安名义上的女儿（狄奥多拉〔Theodora〕）。被休弃的海伦娜(Helena) 之子君士坦丁 (Constantine)，娶马克西米安的女儿法乌斯塔 (Fausta)为继室（父子二人娶了两姐妹）。他于306年7月25日被擢升为凯撒。见吉本(Gibbon)，第XIII、XIV章。↩︎

  35. 拉克坦提乌（《逼迫者之死》，De Morte.Persec.，第9章）称他为“一头野兽”，其中怀有“天生的野蛮，以及罗马血统所无的凶残”。他最终死于一种可怕的疾病，拉克坦提乌对此有详细记述（第33章）。↩︎

  36. 拉克坦提乌指控伽列里乌斯纵火，说他如同第二个尼禄，为要惩罚无辜的基督徒，竟使皇宫陷入危险。当时住在宫廷的君士坦丁，后来在一个庄严的场合，将这场火灾归因于雷击（《致圣徒的演说》，Orat.ad Sanct.，第25章）；但火灾一再发生，却加强了拉克坦提乌的怀疑。↩︎

  37. 吉本在第XVI章暗示，这可能是一场政治阴谋。他谈到尼科米底亚皇宫的火灾时说：“嫌疑自然落到了基督徒身上；有人提出一种颇有几分可能的说法，认为这些亡命的狂热者，受当前的苦难激怒，又担忧迫在眉睫的灾祸，便与他们忠实的弟兄——宫中的宦官——结成阴谋，图谋杀害两位皇帝；他们憎恨这两位皇帝，视他们为上帝教会不共戴天的仇敌。”布克哈特(Burkhardt)在论君士坦丁的著作中，第332页及后，再次提出吉本的猜测，却没有任何证据。鲍尔斥之为牵强附会，极不可信（《教会史》，Kirchengesch.，I.452，注）。梅森（第97页及下页）驳斥了此说。↩︎

  38. 见拉克坦提乌 (Lactantius)，《逼迫者之死》(De MortePersec.)，第18、19、32章；吉本(Gibbon)，第XIV、V章（史密斯版，第II卷，第16页）。马克西明 (Maximin)原名达扎 (Daza)。不可将他与马克西米安 (Maximian)混淆（后者年纪较大，比他早死三年）。他是个粗野、无知而迷信的暴君，残酷不亚于伽列里乌斯，荒淫之不可思议更有过之（见拉克坦提乌，前引书，第37章及后）。313年，他被李锡尼(Licinius) 击败后，服毒而死。↩︎

  39. 关于马克西明的这道敕令，见优西比乌(Eusebius)，《巴勒斯坦殉道者》(Mart. Pal.)，IX.2；博兰德派文献(Boll.) 中的《殉道者行传》，5月8日，第291页，及10月19日，第428页；梅森(Mason)，前引书，第284页及后。↩︎

  40. 莱特福特 (Lightfoot)在其博学的“优西比乌”条目中为他辩护，见史密斯与韦斯 (Smith and Wace)编《基督教传记辞典》(Dict. of Christ. Biogr.)，II.311。↩︎

  41. 若将第一道宽容敕令之后（311—313年）马克西明和李锡尼所施行的地方性逼迫也计算在内，则为十年。↩︎

  42. 例如：“Nomine Christianorum deleto; superstitioneChristiana ubique deleta, et cultu Deorumpropagato.”（基督徒之名已被抹去；基督教的迷信已处处铲除，诸神的崇拜得以推广。）铭文全文见巴罗尼乌斯(Baronius)（ad.ann.，304年，第8、9条）；然而，这些铭文与宽容敕令承认逼迫失败的说法相矛盾，连加姆斯(Gams) 也承认它们毫无价值（《西班牙教会史》，K. Gesch. v.Spanien，I.387）。↩︎

  43. 详情见各部《殉道录》及《圣徒传》，亦见巴罗尼乌斯(Baronius) 的《编年史》(Annal.)。这位历史学家对“insigne etperpetuum miraculum sanguinis S.Januarii”（圣雅努阿里乌斯之血那显著而长存的神迹）深信不疑，以致认为不必举出任何见证人，因为“totaItalia, et totus Christianus orbis testis estlocupletissimus!”（整个意大利以及整个基督教世界，都是最充分的见证！）Adann.，305年，第6条。↩︎

  44. 德布罗意先生 (M. deBroglie)（《教会与帝国》，L’Église etl’Empire，I.182）对这份宣言的描述十分贴切：“Singulier document,moitié insolent, moitié suppliant, qui commence par insulter chrétienset finit par leur demander de prier leur maÎ tre pourlui.”（这是一份奇特的文告，半是傲慢，半是哀求；开头辱骂基督徒，结尾却请求他们向自己的主为他祈祷。）梅森(Mason)（前引书，第299页）说：“这位垂死的皇帝毫无悔意；除了承认自己无能为力，别无认罪。他假装自己不是逼迫者，而是改革者，想以此蒙骗那发怒的基督，胜过他的智慧。他带着咒骂，把宽容敕令掷在教会脸上，却又迷信地盼望借此免受惩罚。”↩︎

  45. 通常的说法是（凯姆〔Keim〕，前引书；吉泽勒〔Gieseler〕；鲍尔〔Baur〕，第I卷，第454页及后，亦如此说），君士坦丁(Constantine) 和李锡尼 (Licinius)颁布过两道宽容敕令，一道在312年，另一道于313年在米兰颁布，因为后一道提及先前的一道敕令。但这里所指似乎是随伽列里乌斯311年敕令一同发给官员、如今已经佚失的指示；君士坦丁也是该敕令的联署者。312年并没有敕令。见察恩(Zahn)，尤其见梅森 (Mason)（第328页及下页）；亦见乌尔霍恩(Uhlhorn)（《冲突》等，Conflict, etc.，英译本，第497页）。↩︎

  46. “Ut daremus et Christianis et omnibus liberampotestatem sequendi religionem, quam quiscunquevoluisset.”（使基督徒以及所有人，都有自由的权利，信奉各自所愿信奉的宗教。）见优西比乌(Eusebius)，H.，X.5；拉克坦提乌(Lactantius)，《逼迫者之死》(De Mort. Pers.)，第48章。梅森(Mason)（第327页）论《米兰敕令》说：“这是第一次宣告这样一种学说：如今人们视之为文明的标志与原则、稳固自由的基础、现代政治的特征。它以有力而鲜明的语句，阐明了完全的良心自由，以及不受束缚的宗教选择。”↩︎

  47. 关于君士坦丁及其与教会的关系，更详尽的叙述见下一卷。↩︎

  48. 参较匿名的《致丢格那妥书》(Ep. ad Diognetum)第6、7章末尾的类似段落，以及殉道者游斯丁 (Justin M.)的《与犹太人特利丰对话》(Dial. c. Tryph. Jud.)，第110章。↩︎

  49. 《论逼迫中的逃避》(De fuga inpersec.)，第13章：“Massaliter totae ecclesiae tributum sibiirrogaverunt.”（整个教会集体给自己摊派贡金。）↩︎

  50. Ὁμολογηταί*，confessores（认信者）；《马太福音》10:32；《提摩太前书》6:12。↩︎

  51. Μάρτυρες*（见证人、殉道者）；《使徒行传》22:20；《希伯来书》12:1；《彼得前书》5:1；《启示录》17:6。↩︎

  52. 参较《马太福音》10:23；24:15—20；《腓立比书》1:20—25；《提摩太后书》4:6—8。↩︎

  53. 在阿尔瓦公爵 (Duke of Alva)统治下，荷兰殉道者的人数，据格劳秀斯 (Grotius)说，超过100,000人；据罗马天主教历史学家P. 萨尔皮 (P. Sarpi)说，则为50,000人。莫特利 (Motley) 在其《荷兰共和国兴起史》(Historyof the Rim of the Dutch Republic)第II卷第504页中，论到阿尔瓦的恐怖统治时说：“那些城市陷于火海与饥荒，遭到洗劫和摧毁，其间所行的暴虐几乎令人难以置信；未出生的婴儿从活着的母亲腹中被撕扯出来；成千上万的妇女和儿童遭到强暴；整城居民被士兵烧死、砍碎，残酷之人恣意挖空心思所能想出的各种手段，无不施用。”巴克尔(Buckle) 和弗里德兰德 (Friedländer)（III.586）断言，在托尔克马达(Torquemada)掌权的十八年间，西班牙宗教裁判所按最低估计也惩处了105,000人，其中8,800人被烧死。在安达卢西亚(Andalusia)，仅一年内就有2,000名犹太人被处死，17,000人受惩处。↩︎

  54. Ὀλίγοι κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ σφόδραεὐαρίθμητοι τεθνήκασι.*.《驳塞尔苏斯》(Adv. Cels.)，III.8。撒狄的米利都 (Melito ofSardis) 那篇由优西比乌 (Eusebius)保存的著名《护教辞》残篇（IV.26），提供了更早的见证；但它所说的，只是马可·奥勒留(Marcus Aurelius) 以前施行逼迫的皇帝为数不多。↩︎

  55. 《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.)，IV，第33章，§9：Ecclesia omni in loco ob eam, quam habet erga Deum dilectionem,multitudinem martyrum in omni tempore praemittit adPatrem.（教会因着对上帝的爱，在各处、在一切时候，都将大批殉道者先行送到父那里。）↩︎

  56. 《坡旅甲殉道记》(MartyriumPolycarpi)，第17章；参较优西比乌 (Eusebius)，《教会史》(H.E.)，IV.15。↩︎

  57. Ἡμέρα γενέθλιος,γενέθλια*，natales, natalitiamartyrum（殉道者的诞辰、诞辰纪念日）。↩︎

  58. Lavacrumsanguinis（血的洗濯），βάπτισμα διὰπυρός*（火的洗礼）；参较《马太福音》20:22；《路加福音》12:50；《马可福音》10:39。↩︎

  59. 不过，值得注意的是，士每拿 (Smyrna)会众在《坡旅甲殉道记》(Martyrium Polycarpi)中记述的一些惊人现象，在优西比乌 (Eusebius)的叙述（IV.15）中并未出现，可能是后来插入的。↩︎

entry.title: 《基督教会史》·第二卷·第一章 基督教的传播
entry.content:
Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The ChristianChurch

第一章 基督教的传播

目录

§ 3. 文献

§ 4. 阻碍与助力

§ 5. 基督教成功的原因

§ 6. 传播的途径

§ 7. 基督教在罗马帝国的分布范围

§ 8. 亚洲的基督教

§ 9. 埃及的基督教

§ 10. 北非的基督教

§ 11. 欧洲的基督教

§ 3. 文献

I. 史料

没有统计资料或确切的记述，只有散见于下列文献中的零星线索：

普林尼 (Pliny，107年)：《书信》(Ep.) x.96及下篇（致图拉真的信）。伊格那丢(Ignatius，约110年)：《致马格尼西亚人书》(AdMagnes.)，第10章。《致丢格那妥书》(Ep. adDiogn.，约120年)，第6章。

殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr，约140年)：《对话录》(Dial.)117；《护教辞》(Apol.) I. 53。

爱任纽 (Irenaeus，约170年)：《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.) I.10；III. 3、4；v. 20等。

德尔图良 (Tertullian，约200年)：《护教辞》(Apol.) I.21、37、41、42；《致异教徒》(Ad Nat.) I.7；《致斯卡普拉》(Ad Scap.)，第2、5章；《驳犹太人》(Adv.Jud.) 7、12、13。

奥利金 (Origen，卒于254年)：《驳塞尔苏斯》(Contr. Cels.) I.7、27；II. 13、46；III. 10、30；《论原理》(DePrinc.)，第IV卷，第1章，§ 2；《马太福音注释》(Com. inMatth.)，第857页，德拉吕 (Delarue) 编。

优西比乌 (Eusebius，卒于340年)：《教会史》(Hist. Eccl) III.1；v. 1；vii. 1；viii. 1，另参第ix、x卷。鲁菲努斯(RUFINUS)：《教会史》(Hist. Eccles.) ix. 6。

奥古斯丁 (Augustin，卒于430年)：《上帝之城》(De CivitateDei)。M. 多兹 (M. Dods)英译，爱丁堡，1871年；新版（收入沙弗的《尼西亚及后尼西亚教父文库》），纽约，1887年。

II. 著作

米歇尔·勒基安 (Mich. LeQuien，一位博学的多明我会士，卒于1733年)：《基督教东方》(OriensChristianus)。巴黎，1740年。3卷，对开本。这是一部完备的东方教会地理著作，按君士坦丁堡、亚历山大、安提阿和耶路撒冷四大牧首辖区编排。

莫斯海姆 (Mosheim)：《历史评注》(Historical Commentaries)等（默多克〔Murdock〕编），I. 第259–290页。

吉本 (Gibbon)：《罗马帝国衰亡史》(The Decline and Fall of theRoman Empire)，第xv章。

A. 伯尼奥 (A. Beugnot)：《西方异教消亡史》(Histoire de ladestruction du paganisme enOccident)。巴黎，1835年，2卷。获铭文与美文学学院 (Académie desinscriptions et belles-letters) 奖。

艾蒂安·沙斯泰尔 (EtienneChastel)：《东罗马帝国异教消亡史》(Histoire de la destruction dupaganisme dans I’ empire d’ Orient)。巴黎，1850年。该学院(Académie) 的获奖论文。

尼安德 (Neander)：《基督教宗教与教会史》(History of the ChristianRelig. and Church)（托里〔Torrey〕译），I. 第68–79页。

维尔奇 (Wiltsch)：《教会地理与统计手册》(Handbuch der kirchl.Geographie u. Statistik)。柏林，1846年。I. 第32页及后。

Chs. 梅里韦尔 (Chs. Merivale)：《罗马帝国的归信》(Conversion ofthe RomanEmpire)（1864年度波义耳讲座），纽约，1865年重印。另参其《帝国统治下的罗马人史》(Historyof the Romans under the Empire)，记述自尤利乌斯·凯撒 (JuliusCaesar) 至马可·奥勒留 (Marcus Aurelius) 的历史，伦敦及纽约，7卷。

爱德华·A. 弗里曼 (Edward A. Freeman)：《欧洲历史地理》(TheHistorical Geography ofEurope)。伦敦及纽约，1881年。2卷（第I卷，第II、III章，第18–71页）。

参弗里德兰德 (Friedländer)：《罗马风俗史》(Sittengesch.Roms)，III. 第517页及后；以及勒南(Renan)：《马可·奥勒留》(Marc-Aurèle)，巴黎，1882年，第xxv章，第447–464页（“基督教的统计与地理扩展”〔Statistiqueet extension géographique du Christianisme〕）。

V. 舒尔策 (V. Schultze)：《希腊罗马异教衰亡史》(Geschichte desUntergangs des griech-römischen.Heidenthums)。耶拿，1887年。

§ 4. 阻碍与助力

在最初三个世纪中，基督教被置于最不利的环境之下，为要使它彰显自身的道德力量，并且单凭属灵的兵器战胜世界。直到君士坦丁(Constantine)统治之时，它在罗马帝国内甚至不具有合法地位；起初被当作犹太教的一个派别而受到漠视，后来又被视为叛逆性的新事物，遭到诽谤、禁止和逼迫，信奉它的人要受到没收财产和处死的刑罚。此外，它不像后来的伊斯兰教那样，对人心败坏的倾向稍有迁就，反而与犹太人和异教徒的流行观念相对立，坚持要求人悔改归信、舍弃自我与世界，毫不宽贷；以致照德尔图良所说，因贪恋享乐而不肯加入这个新教派的人，比因贪生而不肯加入的人还多。基督教的犹太渊源，以及大多数信奉者的贫穷与卑微，也尤其触犯了希腊人和罗马人的骄傲。塞尔苏斯(Celsus)夸大了这个事实，无视许多例外，讥讽地说，传讲这种“非理性信仰”的，都是“织工、鞋匠和漂洗工，这些最没有学问的人”，而他们尤其懂得怎样把它推荐给“妇女和儿童”。

然而，尽管有这些异乎寻常的困难，基督教仍不断发展，为其神圣的起源及其适合人类更深层需要的特性提供了鲜明的证据；当时的爱任纽、游斯丁、德尔图良及其他教父，也确实以此作为论据。不仅如此，这些阻碍本身，在上帝护理的手中，反成了促进发展的工具。逼迫导致殉道，而殉道不仅令人恐惧，也具有吸引力，激发了最高尚、最无私的志向。每一位真正的殉道者，都是基督教真实与圣洁的活见证。德尔图良能够向异教徒高呼：“你们精心设计的一切残酷手段，都不能有所成就；它们不过是吸引人归入这个教派的诱饵。你们越是残害我们，我们的人数就越增加。基督徒的血就是他们的种子。”基督徒在道德上的认真，与当时普遍的腐败形成强烈对照；它虽使轻浮纵欲的人退避，却必然给心灵最深邃、最高尚的人留下极深的印象。贫穷和受压迫者对福音的偏爱，证明了福音安慰与救赎的能力。不过，从一开始，上层社会和有教养的阶层中，也有人受到这个新宗教的吸引，人数虽不多，却包括尼哥底母、亚利马太的约瑟、使徒保罗、方伯士求·保罗、雅典的丢尼修、哥林多的以拉都，以及一些皇室成员。在图密善(Domitian) 的逼迫中受难的，包括他自己的近亲弗拉维娅·多米提拉 (FlaviaDomitilla) 及其丈夫弗拉维乌斯·克莱门斯 (FlaviusClemens)。在卡利斯图斯地下墓窟 (Catacomb of Callistus)最古老、以圣卢基娜 (St. Lucina) 命名的部分，葬有显赫的庞波尼乌斯氏族(gens Pomponia)的成员，或许还有弗拉维王朝家族的成员。元老和骑士阶层也产生了若干公开或隐蔽的归信者。普林尼哀叹，小亚细亚各个阶层的人（omnisordinis）都转而归向基督徒。德尔图良断言，迦太基 (Carthage)有十分之一的人信奉基督教，其中包括元老、出身最高贵的妇女，以及阿非利加方伯的至亲。从第二世纪中叶起，众多教父，如殉道者游斯丁、爱任纽、希波吕托斯(Hippolytus)、革利免 (Clement)、奥利金、德尔图良、居普良(Cyprian)，在才智与修养上，超过了或至少不逊于同时代最杰出的异教徒。

这种进展也不限于某些特定地区，而是同样遍及帝国各处。德尔图良在《护教辞》中说：“我们不过是昨日才出现的一个群体，却已遍布你们的一切地方——城市、岛屿、堡垒、市镇、集会，甚至你们的军营、部族、团体、宫廷、元老院、广场！我们只把神庙留给你们。你们的军队，我们数得清；而我们仅在一个行省中的人数，就比他们更多。”这一切事实，都揭露了塞尔苏斯那种可憎指控的不公；一位近代怀疑论者又重述了这一指控，说这个新教派几乎全由民众中的渣滓组成——农民和工匠、男孩和妇女、乞丐和奴隶。

§ 5. 基督教成功的原因

基督教迅速传播并最终得胜，其首要的积极原因，在于它作为普世救恩之宗教所具有的绝对内在价值，也在于其兼具神人二性的创立者那完美的教训和榜样；他向每一颗相信的心证明，自己是救人脱离罪恶的救主，是永生的赐予者。基督教适合人类一切阶层、境况和关系，适合一切民族和种族、一切文化程度，适合每一个渴望从罪中得赎、渴望圣洁生活的灵魂。它的价值，显明在其教义的真理及自证之力中；显明在其训诫的纯洁与崇高中；显明在它使人心灵和生活重生、成圣的果效中；显明在妇女及其所主持的家庭生活地位的提升中；显明在穷苦患难者处境的改善中；也显明在信仰告白者的信心、弟兄之爱、善行以及得胜的死亡中。

除了这些内在的道德与属灵见证，又有强有力的外在证据证明基督教的神圣起源，就是旧约的预言与预表，在新约中如此鲜明地得到应验；最后还有神迹的见证。按照夸德拉图斯(Quadratus)、殉道者游斯丁、爱任纽、德尔图良、奥利金及其他人的明确记述，在这一时期，神迹仍不时伴随着传教士的宣讲，使异教徒归信。

特别有利的外在环境，是罗马帝国的广大疆域、秩序与统一，以及希腊语言和文化的普及。

除了这些积极原因，犹太教与异教世界毫无希望的处境，也从反面给基督教带来了有力的优势。自耶路撒冷毁灭这一可怕的审判之后，犹太教便在咒诅之下漂泊不安，不再有自己的国家。异教在外表上仍占统治地位，内里却已腐烂，正走向不可避免的衰亡。民间宗教与公共道德，受到怀疑主义和唯物主义哲学的侵蚀；希腊的学术与艺术丧失了创造力；罗马帝国仅靠刀剑的力量和现世利益来维系；社会的道德纽带已经断裂；无边的贪婪和各样罪恶，从王座到陋室，横行于罗马及各行省，连塞涅卡(Seneca) 和塔西佗 (Tacitus) 这样的人也承认这一点。像安敦宁·庇护(Antoninus Pius)和马可·奥勒留这样有德行的皇帝，只是例外而非常例，也无法阻止道德的日趋败坏。古典时代在其最辉煌的岁月所产生的一切，没有一样能够医治这个时代的致命创伤，甚至不能给予暂时的缓解。在渐浓的黑夜中，唯一的希望之星，就是耶稣那年轻、清新、无畏的宗教；它不惧死亡，信心坚强，爱火炽烈，注定要日益获得一切有思想者的认同，被视为现今与未来唯一有生命的宗教。当世界不断受到战争、革命和公共灾难的震荡，当种种哲学体系和王朝兴起又消逝之时，这个新宗教尽管遭遇外部可怕的反对和内部的危险，却以真理不可抗拒的力量，默默而稳步地前进，逐渐渗入人类的骨髓与血脉。

伟大的奥古斯丁说：“基督向这个衰老、败坏世界中的人显现，使他们在周围万物日渐凋零之际，能够借着他得到崭新、青春的生命。”

附注

吉本在他那著名的第十五章中，把基督教在罗马帝国内的迅速发展归因于五点：早期基督徒的热忱，对来世赏罚的信仰，神迹的能力，基督徒严谨（纯洁）的道德，以及紧密的教会组织。然而，这些原因本身，都是吉本所忽略的一个原因所产生的结果，即基督教的神圣真理，以及基督教训与榜样的完美。参约翰·亨利·纽曼博士(Dr. John Henry Newman)《赞同的文法》(Grammar ofAssent)，第445页及下页；乔治·P. 费舍尔博士 (Dr. George P.Fisher)《基督教的开端》(The Beginnings ofChristianity)，第543页及后。费舍尔说：“〔早期基督徒的〕‘热忱’，是对一个人的热忱，也是对与他不可分的事业的热忱；对来世生命的信仰，源于对那位曾死而复活、升入高天者的信心；早期门徒也自觉地把行神迹的能力与同一源头联系起来；道德的洁净，以及作为早期基督徒教会团契之基础的弟兄合一，同样是他们与基督的关系、以及他们共同爱他的结果。基督教在罗马世界的胜利，就是基督的胜利；他被举起来，为要吸引万人来归向他。”

莱基 (Lecky)（《欧洲道德史》Hist. of Europ. Morals，I.412）比吉本探究得更深，将早期基督教的成功归因于其内在的卓越，以及它对古罗马帝国时代需求的非凡适应性。他说：“基督教正是在这场运动中取得了优势；我们不难发现它获胜的原因。在这样的环境中，从来没有别的宗教兼具如此众多而各不相同的力量和吸引力。它不像犹太教，不受地域纽带的束缚，同样适合每一个民族、每一个阶层。它不像斯多葛主义(Stoicism)，而是以最强烈的方式诉诸人的情感，并提供一种富有同情之心的敬拜所具有的一切魅力。它不像埃及宗教，而是将其独特的教训与一种纯洁高尚的伦理体系结合起来，并证明自己能够在行动中将其实现。在社会与民族大规模融合的运动中，它宣告全人类普遍的弟兄关系。在哲学与文明使人心日渐柔和的影响下，它教导爱的至高神圣性。对于奴隶而言——他们在罗马宗教生活中从未发挥过如此重大的影响——它是受苦者和受压迫者的宗教。对于哲学家而言，它既是后期斯多葛派最高伦理的回响，也是柏拉图(Plato)学派最优良教训的扩展。对于一个渴求奇事的世界，它提供了一部充满奇迹的历史，其中的奇事比阿波罗尼乌斯(Apollonius) 的还要奇异；犹太人和迦勒底人 (Chaldean)的赶鬼者几乎无法与它的赶鬼者匹敌，而神迹不断发生的传说则在其信徒中流传。对于一个深感政治秩序正在瓦解、热切而焦虑地窥探未来的世界，它以震撼人心的力量宣告世界即将毁灭——它的一切朋友将得荣耀，它的一切仇敌将受永刑。对于一个已经厌倦凝视加图(Cato) 所体现、卢坎 (Lucan)所歌颂的那种冷峻而不动情感的伟大形象的世界，它呈现了一个怜悯与爱的理想——这个理想注定在此后许多世纪里，把世上一切最伟大、最高尚者吸引到它周围——一位能够在朋友坟前流泪、能够体恤我们软弱的教师。最后，对于一个被敌对的信条和相冲突的哲学搅扰得纷乱不安的世界，它传授自己的教义，不是将其作为人的思辨，而是作为神的启示；这启示的确证，与其说凭借理性，不如说凭借信心。‘人心里相信，就可以称义；’‘人若立志遵着我父的旨意行，就必晓得这教训或是出于上帝；’‘你们若不信，就不能明白；’‘天生属于基督的心；’‘心造就神学家’——这些话最能表达基督教起初对世界所产生的作用。它与一切伟大的宗教一样，更关切情感的方式，而非思想的方式。它成功的主要原因，是其教训与人类属灵本性的契合。正因为它忠实于那个时代的道德情操，忠实地体现了当时人们所趋向的至高完善典范，契合了他们的宗教需求、目标和情感，使人的整个属灵生命都能在其影响下舒展畅游，它才如此深深地扎根于人心之中。”

梅里韦尔 (Merivale)（《罗马帝国的归信》Convers. of the Rom.Emp.，序言）将罗马帝国的归信主要归于四个原因：1）所记载的预言显然应验，以及神迹为基督教真理提供的外在证据；2）基督教满足了人所承认的对救赎者与成圣者的需要，由此提供的内在证据；3）早期信徒在生与死中所彰显的良善与圣洁；4）基督教在君士坦丁(Constantine)治下所取得的现世成功，这成功“如同一场席卷一切的革命，使广大人类转向那在基督耶稣里启示出来、如旭日般升起的真理”。

勒南 (Renan)在其《马可·奥勒留》(Marc-Aurèle，巴黎，1882年)第31章，第561–588页，讨论了基督教获胜的原因。他主要将其归因于世界所需要的“新的生活规范”和“道德改革”，而这些是哲学或任何既有宗教都不能给予的。犹太人确实远远超越了当时的败坏。“Glorieéternelle et unique, qui doit faire oublier bien des folies et desviolence! Les Juifs sont les révolutionnaires du 1er et du2e siècle de notreère.”（“这是永恒而独一无二的荣耀，足以使人忘却许多愚妄和暴行！犹太人是公元第一、第二世纪的革命者。”）他们将基督教给予了世界。“Lespopulations se précipitèrent, par une sorte du mouvement instinctif,dans une secte qui satisfaisait leur aspirations les plus intimes etouvrait des ésperancesinfinies.”（“民众出于一种本能的冲动，蜂拥进入一个满足他们内心最深切渴望、为他们开启无限希望的教派。”）勒南十分看重不朽的信仰以及向每一个罪人提供完全赦免的应许，认为这些是基督教吸引人的因素；但他与吉本一样，忽略了基督教作为救恩宗教的真正力量。正是这种力量，说明了它不仅在古罗马帝国，而且在每一个扎下根来的国家和民族中取得成功的原因。

§ 6. 传播的途径

一个值得注意的事实是：使徒时期之后，直到中世纪开始，才再有伟大宣教士的名字见诸记载；那时，各民族的归信是由少数人促成或开创的，如爱尔兰(Ireland) 的圣帕特里克 (St. Patrick)、苏格兰 (Scotland) 的圣哥伦巴 (St.Columba)、英格兰 (England) 的圣奥古斯丁 (St.Augustine)、德国的圣卜尼法斯 (St. Boniface)、斯堪的纳维亚 (Scandinavia)的圣安斯加尔 (St. Ansgar)，以及斯拉夫 (Slavonic) 各族中的圣西里尔 (St.Cyril) 和美多迪乌斯 (Methodius)。尼西亚会议前时期 (ante-Niceneage)，没有差会，没有宣教机构，也没有有组织的宣教活动；然而，自圣约翰去世以后不到300年，当时代表文明世界的罗马帝国，其全体人口在名义上都已基督教化。

要理解这个惊人的事实，我们必须记住，使徒们亲自奠定的根基既坚固又深厚。他们从耶路撒冷直到罗马撒下的种子，经他们的鲜血滋润，长成了丰盛的庄稼。我们主的话又在更大的范围内应验了：“那人撒种，这人收割。我差你们去收你们所没有劳苦的；别人劳苦，你们享受他们所劳苦的”（《约翰福音》4:38）。

基督教一经建立，便成了自身最好的宣教士。它从内部自然生长。它仅凭自身的存在就吸引了人。它是照在黑暗中、照亮黑暗的光。虽然没有终身专门从事这项工作的职业宣教士，但每一个会众群体都是一个差会，每一位基督徒都是一位宣教士，受基督之爱的激励，热切地使同胞归信。耶路撒冷和安提阿(Antioch) 的教会，以及司提反 (Stephen)殉道后那些“分散各处，往各处去传道”的弟兄，已经树立了榜样。1殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr)的归信，是由于他“在海边散步”时遇见的一位可敬老人。德尔图良 (Tertullian)说，每一个基督徒工人“既寻见上帝，又将他显明出来，尽管柏拉图断言，发现创造主并不容易，即使寻见了，要使众人认识他也很困难”。塞尔苏斯(Celsus)嘲讽地说，漂布工、毛织工和皮革工人，以及乡野无知之辈，是传播基督教最热心的人，最先把它带给妇女和儿童。妇女和奴隶将它带进家庭；福音传给穷人，又借着穷人传扬，使他们富足，这正是福音的荣耀。奥利金(Origen)告诉我们，城市教会派遣宣教士前往乡村。人睡觉的时候，种子仍在生长，结出果实来，先发苗，后长穗，再后穗上结成饱满的子粒。每一个基督徒都向邻舍述说自己归信的故事，工人向工友述说，奴隶向同为奴隶的人述说，仆人向男女主人述说，正如水手讲述自己从海难中获救的故事一样。

福音主要通过活生生的讲道和个人交往而传播；圣经也在相当大的程度上发挥了作用，它很早就流传开来，并译成多种语言，包括拉丁文（北非和意大利的译本）、叙利亚文（库里顿译本〔Curetonian〕和别西大译本〔Peshito〕），以及埃及文（采用孟斐斯〔Memphitic〕、底比斯〔Thebaic〕和巴什穆尔〔Bashmuric〕三种方言）。从大马士革(Damascus) 到不列颠(Britain)，罗马帝国各地之间的往来相当便利而安全。为商业和罗马军团修筑的大道，也供和平的使者通行，为十字架无声的征服效力。商业本身在当时与现今一样，是一种强有力的媒介，将福音和基督教文明的种子带到罗马帝国最偏远的地方。

在这一时期，基督教传入各国的具体方式和确切时间，大多不能确定；我们所知道的，除了它确已传入这一事实之外，并无多少。毫无疑问，使徒及其亲传门徒所做的工作，远比《新约》告诉我们的多。但另一方面，中世纪的传统将许多国家教会和地方教会的起源追溯到使徒，而这些教会不可能在第二或第三世纪以前就已兴起。甚至亚利马太的约瑟(Joseph of Arimathaea)、尼哥底母 (Nicodemus)、亚略巴古的丢尼修(Dionysius the Areopagite)、拉撒路 (Lazarus)、马大 (Martha) 和马利亚(Mary)，也都被传说变成了前往异国的宣教士。

§ 7. 基督教在罗马帝国的分布范围

殉道者游斯丁约在第二世纪中叶说：“无论希腊人、蛮族，还是任何其他种族，无论他们以何种名称或风俗区别于人，无论他们对技艺或农业多么无知，无论住在帐棚里，还是乘着有篷的车辆四处漂泊——没有一个民族不奉被钉十字架的耶稣之名，向万有之父、万物的创造主献上祈祷和感谢。”半个世纪以后，德尔图良以挑战的口吻对异教徒说：“我们不过是昨日才出现的，却已遍满你们的城市、岛屿、军营、宫殿、元老院和广场；我们留给你们的，只有你们的庙宇。”2这些话，以及爱任纽 (Irenaeus)和阿诺比乌斯 (Arnobius)的类似说法，显然都是修辞上的夸张。奥利金的陈述较为谨慎而适度。不过，可以合理地断言，约在第三世纪末，帝国的每一个行省、每一座城市都已知道基督的名，这名既受尊崇，也遭逼迫。马克西米安(Maximian)在一道敕令中说，“几乎所有人”都已放弃祖先的崇拜，转而归附这个新教派。

由于缺乏统计资料，基督徒的人数只能凭推测。在第三世纪末、第四世纪初，他们的人数极可能接近罗马臣民的十分之一或十二分之一，即约一千万人。

然而，基督徒是一个紧密团结的群体，朝气蓬勃，充满活力与希望，人数日增；异教徒则大多是一盘散沙，人数日减。这一事实使教会实际蕴藏的未来力量大为增强。

基督教在罗马帝国境外的亚洲各地区和欧洲西北部蛮族中的传播，起初自然远离历史的主流，尚不足以立即产生重大影响。但它为那些地区的文明发展及其日后在世界上的地位预备了道路。

附注

吉本 (Gibbon) 和弗里德兰德 (Friedländer，III. 531) 估计，君士坦丁(Constantine)即位时（306年），基督徒约占其臣民的二十分之一，这一估计可能过低；马特(Matter) 和罗伯逊 (Robertson)估计为五分之一，则又过高。一些较早的作者受早期护教士夸张言辞的误导，甚至认为帝国境内的基督徒人数即使不超过异教崇拜者，也至少与之相等。若果真如此，单凭通常的审慎考虑，也早在君士坦丁以前就该采取宽容政策了。莫斯海姆(Mosheim) 在其《历史评注》等著作（Hist. Commentaries,etc.，默多克〔Murdock〕译本，第I卷，第274页及后）中，详论第二世纪基督徒的人数，却未得出确定结论。沙斯泰尔(Chastel)估计，君士坦丁时代基督徒在西方占人口的1/15，在东方占1/10，平均为1/12（《异教毁灭史》〔Hist.de la destruct. du paganisme,〕，第36页）。据屈梭多模 (Chrysostom)所说，他那个时代（380年）安提阿 (Antioch)的基督徒人口约有十万，即全城人口的一半。

§ 8. 亚洲的基督教

亚洲是基督教的摇篮，正如它也是人类与文明的摇篮。使徒们亲自将这新宗教传遍巴勒斯坦(Palestine)、叙利亚 (Syria) 和小亚细亚 (Asia Minor)。据小普林尼 (Pliny)所说，在图拉真 (Trajan)治下，小亚细亚诸神的庙宇几乎无人问津，献祭用的牲畜也几乎找不到买主。第二世纪，基督教传入美索不达米亚(Mesopotamia) 的埃德萨 (Edessa)，并深入波斯 (Persia)、米底亚(Media)、巴克特里亚 (Bactria) 和帕提亚 (Parthia)的一些地区；第三世纪，又传入亚美尼亚 (Armenia) 和阿拉伯(Arabia)。诚然，保罗本人曾在阿拉伯度过三年，但可能是在退隐默想中，为他的使徒职事作准备。有一个传说说，使徒多马和巴多罗买曾将福音传到印度。但更为可信的说法是，亚历山大(Alexandria) 的基督教教师潘代乌斯 (Pantaeus)约于190年前往该国，而到第四世纪，那里已有教会。

权力中心由罗马迁往君士坦丁堡(Constantinople)，以及君士坦丁一世治下东罗马帝国的建立，使小亚细亚，尤其是君士坦丁堡，在此后数世纪的教会史上占据了举足轻重的地位。从325年至787年的七次大公会议，全都在该城或其附近举行；有关三位一体和基督位格的教义争论，也主要在小亚细亚、叙利亚和埃及展开。

在上帝奥秘的护理之下，这些圣经与早期教会之地已被麦加 (Mecca)的先知征服，圣经被《古兰经》取代，希腊教会也沦于受奴役与停滞的境地；但东方因基督教不朽的精神而获得新生的日子，已不遥远。献身的传教士宣讲纯正的福音，过圣洁的生活，他们所进行的和平十字军东征，将重新征服圣地，并解决东方问题。

§ 9. 埃及的基督教

在非洲，基督教最先在埃及站稳脚跟，时间可能早至使徒时期。这片有法老、金字塔与狮身人面像、神庙与陵墓、象形文字与木乃伊、圣牛与鳄鱼、专制与奴役的土地，自族长时代起，便与神圣历史紧密交织，甚至以“为奴之家”的名称嵌入十诫之中。这里曾是约瑟及其弟兄的家，也是以色列的摇篮。早在公元前二百多年，犹太人的圣经便在埃及译成希腊文；这部连基督和使徒们也使用的希腊文译本，将希伯来思想传遍罗马世界，并孕育了新约特有的语言风格。亚历山大城聚居着众多犹太人，既是东方的文学中心，也是商业中心，还是连接东西方的纽带。最宏大的藏书汇集于此；犹太思想在这里与希腊思想密切接触，摩西的宗教也在这里与柏拉图(Plato) 和亚里士多德 (Aristotle)的哲学相遇。当基督在耶路撒冷和加利利教导人时，斐洛 (Philo)正在这里著书；他的著作注定要通过亚历山大学派的教父，对基督教释经产生重大影响。

据古老传统，传福音的马可奠定了亚历山大教会的根基。旧开罗(Cairo)，即埃及的巴比伦，其科普特人 (Copts)声称，彼得是在这里写下第一封书信的（《彼得前书》5:13）；但他所指的必是幼发拉底河畔的巴比伦，或是奥秘意义上的巴比伦——罗马。优西比乌(Eusebius) 列举亚历山大最早的几位主教为安尼亚诺斯(Annianos，公元62—85年)、阿比利奥斯 (Abilios，至98年) 和克尔东(Kerdon，至110年)。这一主教座自然逐渐获得了都主教及牧首的地位与尊荣。早在第二世纪，亚历山大便已有一所兴盛的神学院，革利免(Clement) 和俄利根 (Origen)在那里任教，成为圣经学术与基督教哲学的先驱。福音从下埃及传到中埃及、上埃及及邻近各省，或许在第四世纪已远达努比亚(Nubia)、埃塞俄比亚 (Ethiopia) 和阿比西尼亚(Abyssinia)。235年在亚历山大举行的一次会议上，有来自尼罗河之地各处的二十位主教出席。

第四世纪，埃及给教会带来了阿里乌派 (Arian) 异端、亚他那修(Athanasius) 的正统信仰，以及圣安东尼 (St. Antony) 和圣帕科米乌斯 (St.Pachomius) 的修道敬虔；这种敬虔以不可抗拒之势传遍了基督教世界。

埃及的神学文献主要用希腊文写成。早期希腊文圣经抄本大多抄写于亚历山大，其中可能也包括价值无可估量的《西奈抄本》(SinaiticMSS.) 和《梵蒂冈抄本》(VaticanMSS.)。但早在第二世纪，圣经就已用三种不同的方言译成本地语言。这些译本的残存部分，对于确定希腊文新约最早的文本，具有相当重要的分量。

信奉基督教的埃及人是法老时代埃及人的后裔，但已大量混有黑人和阿拉伯人的血统。基督教从未完全深入这个民族，而在哈里发欧麦尔(Omar)治下穆罕默德教徒征服埃及时（640年），几乎被一扫而空。欧麦尔焚毁了亚历山大宏伟的图书馆，借口是：书中的内容若与《古兰经》一致，便属无用；若不一致，便是有害，理当毁灭。自那时起，埃及几乎从教会史中消失，至今仍在新主人的统治下呻吟，依然是一个为奴之家。人民绝大多数是穆斯林，但科普特人——在五百五十万人中约占五十万——仍延续着祖先名义上的基督教，并成为西方较为活跃的各教会的传教工场。

§ 10. 北非的基督教

伯蒂格 (Böttiger)：《迦太基人史》(Geschichte derCarthager)。柏林，1827年。

莫弗斯 (Movers)：《腓尼基人》(DiePhönizier)。1840—56年，4卷。（一部权威著作。）

Th. 蒙森 (Th. Mommsen)：《罗马史》(Röm.Geschichte)，第I卷，第489页及后。（第III编，第1—7章，第5版。）

N. 戴维斯 (N. Davis)：《迦太基及其遗迹》(Carthage and herRemains)。伦敦及纽约，1861年。

R. 博斯沃思·史密斯 (R. BosworthSmith)：《迦太基与迦太基人》(Carthage and theCarthaginians)。伦敦，第2版，1879年。同一作者：《罗马与迦太基》(Romeand Carthage)。纽约，1880年。

奥托·梅尔策 (Otto Meltzer)：《迦太基人史》(Geschichte derKarthager)。柏林，第I卷，1879年。

这些书论述的是古代迦太基人的世俗历史，但有助于理解当地的处境与历史背景。

朱利叶斯·劳埃德 (Julius Lloyd)：《北非教会》(The North AfricanChurch.)。伦敦，1880年。叙述下迄穆斯林的征服。

北非各省的居民出自闪族(Semitic)，其语言与希伯来语相近，但在罗马统治下，其习俗、法律和语言都已拉丁化。因此，该地区的教会属于拉丁基督教，并在其早期历史中发挥着主导作用。

腓尼基人 (Phoenicians)是迦南人的余裔，堪称古代历史中的英国人。他们经营着世界的贸易；与此同时，以色列人为世界预备了宗教，希腊人为世界预备了文明。这三个居于小国的小民族，所完成的事业，比亚述、巴比伦和波斯这些庞大帝国，甚至比罗马所完成的，还更为重要。腓尼基人占据着叙利亚海岸黎巴嫩山与大海之间的一条狭长地带，他们的商船从推罗和西顿驶向旧世界各地，远自印度，直到波罗的海；他们比瓦斯科·达·伽马(Vasco de Gama) 早两千年绕过好望角，并从马拉巴尔 (Malabar)运回檀香木，从阿拉伯运回香料，从努比亚运回鸵鸟羽毛，从西班牙运回白银，从尼日尔(Niger) 运回黄金，从厄尔巴岛 (Elba)运回铁，从英格兰运回锡，从波罗的海运回琥珀。他们为所罗门供应黎巴嫩的香柏木，帮助他建造宫殿与圣殿。早在公元前八百多年，他们就在非洲最北部海岸建立了殖民地迦太基(Carthage)。3凭借这一有利位置，他们取得了对北非海岸从赫拉克勒斯之柱 (pillars ofHercules) 至大叙尔提斯湾 (Great Syrtes)，以及西班牙南部、撒丁岛(Sardinia)、西西里岛 (Sicily)和整个地中海的控制权。由此，迦太基与仅隔三日航程的罗马之间，竞争势不可免；由此发生了三次布匿战争(Punic wars)，尽管汉尼拔 (Hannibal)具有卓越的军事天才，战争最终仍以这座北非都城的彻底毁灭告终（公元前146年）。4 “Delenda estCarthago,”（迦太基必须毁灭），这就是老加图 (Cato)狭隘而残酷的政策。但在奥古斯都 (Augustus) 治下，尤利乌斯·凯撒 (JuliusCaesar)更为明智的计划得到实施，一座新迦太基在旧城废墟上兴起，成为富庶繁荣的城市，起初信奉异教，后来信奉基督教，直到被野蛮的汪达尔人(Vandals)攻占（公元439年），最终又被与其最初创建者同族的穆罕默德教阿拉伯人毁灭（647年）。自那时起，“一种悲凉而孤寂的沉默”再次笼罩着它的废墟。5

基督教在第二世纪，或许早在第一世纪末，就已传到由资深执政官治理的阿非利加行省(proconsularAfrica)，具体何时、如何传入，我们并不知道。这里与意大利之间往来不断。基督教迅速传遍毛里塔尼亚(Mauritania) 和努米底亚 (Numidia) 的沃野与灼热的沙地。居普良 (Cyprian)在258年能够召集八十七位主教举行会议，而在308年，造成分裂的多纳徒派(Donatists)在迦太基召开了一次有二百七十位主教参加的会议。当然，那时的教区都很小。

最古老的拉丁文圣经译本被误称为“意大利译本”(Itala)，是哲罗姆“武加大译本”(Vulgata)的基础；它很可能是在非洲为非洲人译成的，而不是在罗马为罗马人译成的，因为当时罗马的基督徒通用希腊语。拉丁神学也不是诞生于罗马，而是诞生于迦太基。德尔图良是其创始者。米努基乌斯·费利克斯(Minutius Felix)、阿尔诺比乌斯 (Arnobius)和居普良，见证了第三世纪非洲基督教与神学的活跃和兴盛。第五世纪的第一个四分之一世纪中，它在诸教父中最伟大的圣奥古斯丁(St. Augustin)崇高的智慧与火热的心灵里，臻于最高的完善；但在他去世（430年）后不久，它先被汪达尔人的野蛮势力埋没，到第七世纪，又被穆罕默德教徒的征服所掩埋。然而，他的著作在整个黑暗时代引领着拉丁教会的基督教思想，激励了宗教改革者，直到今日仍是一股充满生命力的力量。

§ 11. 欧洲的基督教

“帝国的进程一路向西。”

这一历史规律，也是基督教的规律。使徒教会的行程，是从耶路撒冷走向罗马。自此以后，宣教的进程便不断向西，越走越远。

对于整个西方，罗马教会远比其他教会重要。据优西比乌所说，第三世纪中叶，罗马教会有一位主教、四十六位长老、七位执事和同样数目的副执事、四十二位辅祭员，以及共五十位读经员、驱魔员和守门员；此外还有一千五百名寡妇和穷人由教会照管。由此我们或可估计，其信徒人数约有五六万，即全城人口的二十分之一左右；该城人口固然无法确切判定，但在安敦尼诸帝(Antonines) 统治时期，必已超过一百万。6基督徒埋葬死者的地下墓窟规模极其庞大，也证实了基督教在罗马的力量。

教会从罗马传播到意大利的各个城市。据我们所知，第一次罗马教省会议由特勒斯福鲁斯(Telesphorus，142–154年)主持，共有十二位主教参加。第三世纪中叶（255年），罗马的哥尼流(Cornelius) 召开了一次有六十位主教参加的会议。

177年的逼迫表明，第二世纪时，教会已经在高卢 (Gaul)南部建立。基督教大概是从东方传到这里的；因为里昂 (Lyons) 和维埃纳(Vienne)的教会与小亚细亚的教会关系密切，曾将有关逼迫的报告送交他们，而里昂主教爱任纽(Irenaeus) 又是士每拿的坡旅甲 (Polycarp) 的门徒。据图尔的贵格利 (Gregoryof Tours)记载，第三世纪中叶，有七位宣教士从罗马被差往高卢。其中的狄奥尼修斯(Dionysius) 建立了巴黎的第一所教会，在蒙马特 (Montmartre)殉道，后来成为法国的主保圣徒。后来的民间迷信把他与亚略巴古的丢尼修混为一人，后者是在雅典因保罗传道而归信的。

西班牙大概也在第二世纪接触了基督教，不过直到第三世纪中叶，我们才看到当地教会和主教的明确踪迹。306年的埃尔维拉会议(Council of Elvira)有十九位主教参加。使徒保罗曾计划前往西班牙宣教；按照罗马的革利免(Clement of Rome)的记载，他也曾在那里传道——如果我们把革利免所说保罗将福音传到的“西方的极处”理解为西班牙的话。7然而，现存记载中并没有他在西班牙工作的踪迹。传说全然不顾年代次序，将该国基督教的起源归于大雅各(James theElder)；他于44年在耶路撒冷被处死，据说葬于著名的朝圣地坎波斯特拉(Campostella)，其遗骨直到第八世纪末叶、阿方索二世 (Alphonse II)在位时才首次被发现.1。8

爱任纽谈到福音传到日耳曼人 (Germans)和其他蛮族中间，说他们“不用纸墨，却借着圣灵将救恩写在心里”；他所指的只能是日耳曼境内属于罗马帝国的地区（Germaniacisrhenana，莱茵河此岸的日耳曼）。

据德尔图良 (Tertullian) 所说，不列颠 (Britain)也在第二世纪末叶归服于十字架的权能之下。早在奥古斯丁 (Augustine)率领的罗马宣教团使盎格鲁—撒克逊人 (Anglo-Saxons) 归信以前，凯尔特教会(Celtic church)就已在英格兰、爱尔兰和苏格兰独立于罗马而存在；此后仍延续了一段时期，并将支派扩展到日耳曼、法国和低地诸国(LowCountries)，但最终先后并入罗马教会。它起初大概源自高卢，后来也从意大利获得传承。传说则将其起源追溯至圣保罗及其他使徒时期的奠基者。可敬的比德(Bede，†735年) 说，不列颠王卢修斯 (Lucius，约167年)曾请求罗马主教埃留特鲁斯 (Eleutherus) 差派宣教士。314年在高卢的阿尔勒(Arles，Arelate) 召开的会议上，有三位不列颠主教出席，分别来自埃博拉库姆(Eboracum，即约克，York)、伦迪努姆(Londinum，即伦敦，London)，以及伦迪嫩西乌姆殖民城 (ColoniaLondinensium，即林肯，Lincoln，或更可能是科尔切斯特，Colchester)。

北欧和西欧蛮族的归信，直到第五、第六世纪才真正开始；我们将在中世纪史中加以考察。

CHAPTER I. SPREAD OFCHRISTIANITY.

§ 3. Literature.

I. Sources.

No statistics or accurate statements, but only scattered hints in

Pliny (107): Ep. x. 96 sq. (the letter to Trajan). Ignatius(about 110): Ad Magnes. c. 10. Ep. ad Diogn. (about120) c. 6.

Irenaeus (about 170): Adv. Haer. I. 10; III. 3, 4; v. 20,etc.

Tertullian (about 200): Apol. I. 21, 37, 41, 42; Ad Nat. I.7; Ad Scap. c. 2, 5; Adv. Jud. 7, 12, 13.

Origen (d. 254): Contr. Cels. I, 7, 27; II. 13, 46; III. 10,30; De Princ. l. IV. c. 1, § 2; Com. in Matth. p. 857,ed. Delarue.

Eusebius (d. 340): Hist. Eccl III. 1; v. 1; vii, 1; viii. 1,also books ix. and x. RUFINUS: Hist. Eccles. ix. 6.

Mosheim: Historical Commentaries, etc. (ed. Murdock) I.259–290.

Gibbon: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. Chap.xv.

A. Beugnot: Histoire de la destruction du paganisme enOccident. Paris 1835, 2 vols. Crowned by the Académie desinscriptions et belles-letters.

Chs. Merivale: Conversion of the Roman Empire (BoyleLectures for 1864), republ. N. York 1865. Comp. also his History ofthe Romans under the Empire, which goes from Julius Caesar toMarcus Aurelius, Lond. & N. York, 7 vols.

Edward A. Freeman: The Historical Geography of Europe. Lond.& N. York 1881. 2 vols. (vol. I. chs. II. & III. pp. 18–71.)

Comp. Friedländer, Sittengesch. Roms. III. 517 sqq.; andRenan: Marc-Aurèle. Paris 1882, ch. xxv. pp. 447–464(Statistique et extension géographique du Christianisme).

§ 4. Hindrances and Helps.

For the first three centuries Christianity was placed in the mostunfavorable circumstances, that it might display its moral power, andgain its victory over the world by spiritual weapons alone. Until thereign of Constantine it had not even a legal existence in the Romanempire, but was first ignored as a Jewish sect, then slandered,proscribed, and persecuted, as a treasonable innovation, and theadoption of it made punishable with confiscation and death. Besides, itoffered not the slightest favor, as Mohammedanism afterwards did, to thecorrupt inclinations of the heart, but against the current ideas of Jewsand heathen it so presented its inexorable demand of repentance andconversion, renunciation of self and the world, that more, according toTertullian, were kept out of the new sect by love of pleasure than bylove of life. The Jewish origin of Christianity also, and the povertyand obscurity of a majority of its professors particularly offended thepride of the Greeks, and Romans. Celsus, exaggerating this fact, andignoring the many exceptions, scoffingly remarked, that "weavers,cobblers, and fullers, the most illiterate persons" preached the"irrational faith," and knew how to commend it especially "to women andchildren."

But in spite of these extraordinary difficulties Christianity made aprogress which furnished striking evidence of its divine origin andadaptation to the deeper wants of man, and was employed as such byIrenaeus, Justin, Tertullian, and other fathers of that day. Nay, thevery hindrances became, in the hands of Providence, means of promotion.Persecution led to martyrdom, and martyrdom had not terrors alone, butalso attractions, and stimulated the noblest and most unselfish form ofambition. Every genuine martyr was a living proof of the truth andholiness of the Christian religion. Tertullian could exclaim to theheathen: "All your ingenious cruelties can accomplish nothing; they areonly a lure to this sect. Our number increases the more you destroy us.The blood of the Christians is their seed." The moral earnestness of theChristians contrasted powerfully with the prevailing corruption of theage, and while it repelled the frivolous and voluptuous, it could notfail to impress most strongly the deepest and noblest minds. Thepredilection of the poor and oppressed for the gospel attested itscomforting and redeeming power. But others also, though not many, fromthe higher and educated classes, were from the first attracted to thenew religion; such men as Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathaea, the apostlePaul, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, Dionysius of Athens, Erastus ofCorinth, and some members of the imperial household. Among the sufferersin Domitian’s persecution were his own near kinswoman Flavia Domitillaand her husband Flavius Clemens. In the oldest part of the Catacomb ofCallistus, which is named after St. Lucina, members of the illustriousgens Pomponia, and perhaps also of the Flavian house, areinterred. The senatorial and equestrian orders furnished severalconverts open or concealed. Pliny laments, that in Asia Minor men ofevery rank (omnis ordinis) go over to the Christians.Tertullian asserts that the tenth part of Carthage, and among themsenators and ladies of the noblest descent and the nearest relatives ofthe proconsul of Africa professed Christianity. The numerous churchfathers from the middle of the second century, a Justin Martyr,Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Clement, Origen, Tertullian, Cyprian, excelled, orat least equalled in talent and culture, their most eminent heathencontemporaries.

Nor was this progress confined to any particular localities. Itextended alike over all parts of the empire. "We are a people ofyesterday," says Tertullian in his Apology, "and yet we have filledevery place belonging to you—cities, islands, castles, towns,assemblies, your very camp, your tribes, companies, palace, senate,forum! We leave you your temples only. We can count your armies; ournumbers in a single province will be greater." All these facts exposethe injustice of the odious charge of Celsus, repeated by a modernsceptic, that the new sect was almost entirely composed of the dregs ofthe populace—of peasants and mechanics, of boys and women, of beggarsand slaves.

§ 5. Causes of theSuccess of Christianity.

The chief positive cause of the rapid spread and ultimate triumph ofChristianity is to be found in its own absolute intrinsic worth, as theuniversal religion of salvation, and in the perfect teaching and exampleof its divine-human Founder, who proves himself to every believing hearta Saviour from sin and a giver of eternal life. Christianity is adaptedto all classes, conditions, and relations among men, to allnationalities and races, to all grades of culture, to every soul thatlongs for redemption from sin, and for holiness of life. Its value couldbe seen in the truth and self-evidencing power of its doctrines; in thepurity and sublimity of its precepts; in its regenerating andsanctifying effects on heart and life; in the elevation of woman and ofhome life over which she presides; in the amelioration of the conditionof the poor and suffering; in the faith, the brotherly love, thebeneficence, and the triumphant death of its confessors.

To this internal moral and spiritual testimony were added thepowerful outward proof of its divine origin in the prophecies and typesof the Old Testament, so strikingly fulfilled in the New; and finally,the testimony of the miracles, which, according to the expressstatements of Quadratus, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen,and others, continued in this period to accompany the preaching ofmissionaries from time to time, for the conversion of the heathen.

Particularly favorable outward circumstances were the extent, order,and unity of the Roman empire, and the prevalence of the Greek languageand culture.

In addition to these positive causes, Christianity had a powerfulnegative advantage in the hopeless condition of the Jewish and heathenworld. Since the fearful judgment of the destruction of Jerusalem,Judaism wandered restless and accursed, without national existence.Heathenism outwardly held sway, but was inwardly rotten and in processof inevitable decay. The popular religion and public morality wereundermined by a sceptical and materialistic philosophy; Grecian scienceand art had lost their creative energy; the Roman empire rested only onthe power of the sword and of temporal interests; the moral bonds ofsociety were sundered; unbounded avarice and vice of every kind, even bythe confession of a Seneca and a Tacitus, reigned in Rome and in theprovinces, from the throne to the hovel. Virtuous emperors, likeAntoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, were the exception, not the rule,and could not prevent the progress of moral decay. Nothing, that classicantiquity in its fairest days had produced, could heal the fatal woundsof the age, or even give transient relief. The only star of hope in thegathering night was the young, the fresh, the dauntless religion ofJesus, fearless of death, strong in faith, glowing with love, anddestined to commend itself more and more to all reflecting minds as theonly living religion of the present and the future. While the world wascontinually agitated by wars, and revolutions, and public calamities,while systems of philosophy, and dynasties were rising and passing away,the new religion, in spite of fearful opposition from without and dangerfrom within, was silently and steadily progressing with the irresistibleforce of truth, and worked itself gradually into the very bone and bloodof the race.

"Christ appeared," says the great Augustin, "to the men of thedecrepit, decaying world, that while all around them was withering away,they might through Him receive new, youthful life."

Notes.

Gibbon, in his famous fifteenth chapter, traces the rapid progress ofChristianity in the Roman empire to five causes: the zeal of the earlyChristians, the belief in future rewards and punishment, the power ofmiracles, the austere (pure) morals of the Christian, and the compactchurch organization. But these causes are themselves the effects of acause which Gibbon ignores, namely, the divine truth of Christianity,the perfection of Christ’s teaching and Christ’s example. See thestrictures of Dr. John Henry Newman, Grammar of Assent, 445sq., and Dr. George P. Fisher, The Beginnings of Christianity,p. 543 sqq. "The zeal" [of the early Christians], says Fisher, "was zealfor a person, and for a cause identified with Him; the belief in thefuture life sprang out of faith in Him who had died and risen again, andascended to Heaven; the miraculous powers of the early disciples wereconsciously connected with the same source; the purification of morals,and the fraternal unity, which lay at the basis of ecclesiasticalassociation among the early Christians, were likewise the fruit of theirrelation to Christ, and their common love to Him. The victory ofChristianity in the Roman world was the victory of Christ, who waslifted up that He might draw all men unto Him."

Lecky (Hist. of Europ. Morals, I. 412) goes deeper thanGibbon, and accounts for the success of early Christianity by itsintrinsic excellency and remarkable adaptation to the wants of the timesin the old Roman empire. "In the midst of this movement," he says,"Christianity gained its ascendancy, and we can be at no loss todiscover the cause of its triumph. No other religion, under suchcircumstances, had ever combined so many distinct elements of power andattraction. Unlike the Jewish religion, it was bound by no local ties,and was equally adapted for every nation and for every class. UnlikeStoicism, it appealed in the strongest manner to the affections, andoffered all the charm of a sympathetic worship. Unlike the Egyptianreligion, it united with its distinctive teaching a pure and noblesystem of ethics, and proved itself capable of realizing it in action.It proclaimed, amid a vast movement of social and national amalgamation,the universal brotherhood of mankind. Amid the softening influence ofphilosophy and civilization, it taught the supreme sanctity of love. Tothe slave, who had never before exercised so large an influence overRoman religious life, it was the religion of the suffering and theoppressed. To the philosopher it was at once the echo of the highestethics of the later Stoics, and the expansion of the best teaching ofthe school of Plato. To a world thirsting for prodigy, it offered ahistory replete with wonders more strange than those of Apollonius;while the Jew and the Chaldean could scarcely rival its exorcists, andthe legends of continual miracles circulated among its followers. To aworld deeply conscious of political dissolution, and prying eagerly andanxiously into the future, it proclaimed with a thrilling power theimmediate destruction of the globe—the glory of all its friends, and thedamnation of all its foes. To a world that had grown very weary gazingon the cold passionless grandeur which Cato realized, and which Lucansung, it presented an ideal of compassion and of love—an ideal destinedfor centuries to draw around it all that was greatest, as well as allthat was noblest upon earth—a Teacher who could weep by the sepulchre ofHis friend, who was touched with the feeling of our infirmities. To aworld, in fine, distracted by hostile creeds and colliding philosophies,it taught its doctrines, not as a human speculation, but as a Divinerevelation, authenticated much less by reason than by faith. ’With theheart man believeth unto righteousness;’ ’He that doeth the will of myFather will know the doctrine, whether it be of God;’ ’Unless youbelieve you cannot understand;’ ’A heart naturally Christian;’ ’Theheart makes the theologian,’ are the phrases which best express thefirst action of Christianity upon the world. Like all great religions,it was more concerned with modes of feeling than with modes of thought.The chief cause of its success was the congruity of its teaching withthe spiritual nature of mankind. It was because it was true of the moralsentiments of the age, because it represented faithfully the supremetype of excellence to which men were then tending, because itcorresponded with their religious wants, aims, and emotions, because thewhole spiritual being could then expand and expatiate under itsinfluence that it planted its roots so deeply in the hearts of men."

Merivale (Convers. of the Rom. Emp., Preface) traces theconversion of the Roman empire chiefly to four causes: 1) the externalevidence of the apparent fulfilment of recorded prophecy and miracles tothe truth of Christianity; 2) the internal evidence of satisfying theacknowledged need of a redeemer and sanctifier; 3) the goodness andholiness manifested in the lives and deaths of the primitive believers;4) the temporal success of Christianity under Constantine, which "turnedthe mass of mankind, as with a sweeping revolution, to the rising sun ofrevealed truth in Christ Jesus."

Renan discusses the reasons for the victory of Christianity in the31st chapter of his Marc-Aurèle (Paris 1882), pp.561–588. He attributes it chiefly "to the new discipline of life," and"the moral reform," which the world required, which neither philosophynor any of the established religions could give. The Jews indeed rosehigh above the corruptions of the times. "Glorie éternelle etunique, qui doit faire oublier bien des folies et des violence! LesJuifs sont les révolutionnaires du 1er et du 2e sièclede notre ère." They gave to the world Christianity. "Lespopulations se précipitèrent, par une sorte du mouvement instinctif,dans une secte qui satisfaisait leur aspirations les plus intimes etouvrait des ésperances infinies." Renan makes much account of thebelief in immortality and the offer of complete pardon to every sinner,as allurements to Christianity; and, like Gibbon, he ignores its realpower as a religion of salvation. This accounts for its success not onlyin the old Roman empire, but in every country and nation where it hasfound a home.

§ 6. Means of Propagation.

It is a remarkable fact that after the days of the Apostles no namesof great missionaries are mentioned till the opening of the middle ages,when the conversion of nations was effected or introduced by a fewindividuals as St. Patrick in Ireland, St. Columba in Scotland, St.Augustine in England, St. Boniface in Germany, St. Ansgar inScandinavia, St. Cyril and Methodius among the Slavonic races. Therewere no missionary societies, no missionary institutions, no organizedefforts in the ante-Nicene age; and yet in less than 300 years from thedeath of St. John the whole population of the Roman empire which thenrepresented the civilized world was nominally Christianized.

To understand this astonishing fact, we must remember that thefoundation was laid strong and deep by the apostles themselves. The seedscattered by them from Jerusalem to Rome, and fertilized by their blood,sprung up as a bountiful harvest. The word of our Lord was againfulfilled on a larger scale: "One soweth, and another reapeth. I sentyou to reap that whereon ye have not labored: others have labored, andye are entered into their labor" (John 4:38).

Christianity once established was its own best missionary. It grewnaturally from within. It attracted people by its very presence. It wasa light shining in darkness and illuminating the darkness. And whilethere were no professional missionaries devoting their whole life tothis specific work, every congregation was a missionary society, andevery Christian believer a missionary, inflamed by the love of Christ toconvert his fellow-men. The example had been set by Jerusalem andAntioch, and by those brethren who, after the martyrdom of Stephen,"were scattered abroad and went about preaching the Word."(1) JustinMartyr was converted by a venerable old man whom he met "walking on theshore of the sea." Every Christian laborer, says Tertullian, "both findsout God and manifests him, though Plato affirms that it is not easy todiscover the Creator, and difficult when he is found to make him knownto all." Celsus scoffingly remarks that fuller, and workers in wool andleather, rustic and ignorant persons, were the most zealous propagatorsof Christianity, and brought it first to women and children. Women andslaves introduced it into the home-circle, it is the glory of the gospelthat it is preached to the poor and by the poor to make them rich.Origen informs us that the city churches sent their missionaries to thevillages. The seed grew up while men slept, and brought forth fruit,first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.Every Christian told his neighbor, the laborer to his fellow-laborer,the slave to his fellow-slave, the servant to his master and mistress,the story of his conversion, as a mariner tells the story of the rescuefrom shipwreck.

The gospel was propagated chiefly by living preaching and by personalintercourse; to a considerable extent also through the sacredScriptures, which were early propagated and translated into varioustongues, the Latin (North African and Italian), the Syriac (theCuretonian and the Peshito), and the Egyptian (in three dialects, theMemphitic, the Thebaic, and the Bashmuric). Communication among thedifferent parts of the Roman empire from Damascus to Britain wascomparatively easy and safe. The highways built for commerce and for theRoman legions, served also the messengers of peace and the silentconquests of the cross. Commerce itself at that time, as well as now,was a powerful agency in carrying the gospel and the seeds of Christiancivilization to the remotest parts of the Roman empire.

The particular mode, as well as the precise time, of the introductionof Christianity into the several countries during this period is for themost part uncertain, and we know not much more than the fact itself. Nodoubt much more was done by the apostles and their immediate disciples,than the New Testament informs us of. But on the other hand themediaeval tradition assigns an apostolic origin to many national andlocal churches which cannot have arisen before the second or thirdcentury. Even Joseph of Arimathaea, Nicodemus, Dionysius the Areopagite,Lazarus, Martha and Mary were turned by the legend into missionaries toforeign lands.

§ 7. Extent ofChristianity in the Roman Empire.

Justin Martyr says, about the middle of the second century: "There isno people, Greek or barbarian, or of any other race, by whatsoeverappellation or manners they may be distinguished, however ignorant ofarts or agriculture, whether they dwell in tents or wander about incovered wagons—among whom prayers and thanksgivings are not offered inthe name of the crucified Jesus to the Father and Creator of allthings." Half a century later, Tertullian addresses the heathendefiantly: "We are but of yesterday, and yet we already fill yourcities, islands, camps, your palace, senate and forum; we have left toyou only your temples."(2) These, and similar passages of Irenaeus andArnobius, are evidently rhetorical exaggerations. Origen is morecautious and moderate in his statements. But it may be fairly asserted,that about the end of the third century the name of Christ was known,revered, and persecuted in every province and every city of the empire.Maximian, in one of his edicts, says that "almost all" had abandoned theworship of their ancestors for the new sect.

In the absence of statistics, the number of the Christians must bepurely a matter of conjecture. In all probability it amounted at theclose of the third and the beginning of the fourth century to nearlyone-tenth or one-twelfth of the subjects of Rome, that is to about tenmillions of souls.

But the fact, that the Christians were a closely united body, fresh,vigorous, hopeful, and daily increasing, while the heathen were for themost part a loose aggregation, daily diminishing, made the trueprospective strength of the church much greater.

The propagation of Christianity among the barbarians in the provincesof Asia and the north-west of Europe beyond the Roman empire, was atfirst, of course, too remote from the current of history to be of anygreat immediate importance. But it prepared the way for the civilizationof those regions, and their subsequent position in the world.

Notes.

Gibbon and Friedländer (III. 531) estimate the number of Christiansat the accession of Constantine (306) probably too low at one-twentieth;Matter and Robertson too high at one-fifth of his subjects. Some olderwriters, misled by the hyperbolical statements of the early Apologists,even represent the Christians as having at least equalled if notexceeded the number of the heathen worshippers in the empire. In thiscase common prudence would have dictated a policy of toleration longbefore Constantine. Mosheim, in his Hist. Commentaries, etc.(Murdock’s translation I. p. 274 sqq.) discusses at length the number ofChristians in the second century without arriving at definiteconclusions. Chastel estimates the number at the time of Constantine at1/15 in the West, 1/10 in the East, 1/12 on an average (Hist. de ladestruct. du paganisme, p. 36). According to Chrysostom, theChristian population of Antioch in his day (380) was about 100,000, orone-half of the whole.

§ 8. Christianity in Asia.

Asia was the cradle of Christianity, as it was of humanity andcivilization. The apostles themselves had spread the new religion overPalestine, Syria, and Asia Minor. According to the younger Pliny, underTrajan, the temples of the gods in Asia Minor were almost forsaken, andanimals of sacrifice found hardly any purchasers. In the second centuryChristianity penetrated to Edessa in Mesopotamia, and some distance intoPersia, Media, Bactria, and Parthia; and in the third, into Armenia andArabia. Paul himself had, indeed, spent three years in Arabia, butprobably in contemplative retirement preparing for his apostolicministry. There is a legend, that the apostles Thomas and Bartholomewcarried the gospel to India. But a more credible statement is, that theChristian teacher Pantaeus of Alexandria journeyed to that country about190, and that in the fourth century churches were found there.

The transfer of the seat of power from Rome to Constantinople, andthe founding of the East Roman empire under Constantine I. gave to AsiaMinor, and especially to Constantinople, a commanding importance in thehistory of the Church for several centuries. The seven oecumenicalCouncils from 325 to 787 were all held in that city or its neighborhood,and the doctrinal controversies on the Trinity and the person of Christwere carried on chiefly in Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt.

In the mysterious providence of God those lands of the Bible and theearly church have been conquered by the prophet of Mecca, the Biblereplaced by the Koran, and the Greek church reduced to a condition ofbondage and stagnation; but the time is not far distant when the Eastwill be regenerated by the undying spirit of Christianity. A peacefulcrusade of devoted missionaries preaching the pure gospel and leadingholy lives will reconquer the holy land and settle the Easternquestion.

§ 9. Christianity in Egypt.

In Africa Christianity gained firm foothold first in Egypt, and thereprobably as early as the apostolic age. The land of the Pharaohs, of thepyramids and sphinxes, of temples and tombs, of hieroglyphics andmummies, of sacred bulls and crocodiles, of despotism and slavery, isclosely interwoven with sacred history from the patriarchal times, andeven imbedded in the Decalogue as "the house of bondage." It was thehome of Joseph and his brethren, and the cradle of Israel. In Egypt theJewish Scriptures were translated more than two hundred years before ourera, and this Greek version used even by Christ and the apostles, spreadHebrew ideas throughout the Roman world, and is the mother of thepeculiar idiom of the New Testament. Alexandria was full of Jews, theliterary as well as commercial centre of the East, and the connectinglink between the East and the West. There the largest libraries werecollected; there the Jewish mind came into close contact with the Greek,and the religion of Moses with the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle.There Philo wrote, while Christ taught in Jerusalem and Galilee, and hisworks were destined to exert a great influence on Christian exegesisthrough the Alexandrian fathers.

Mark, the evangelist, according to ancient tradition, laid thefoundation of the church of Alexandria. The Copts in old Cairo, theBabylon of Egypt, claim this to be the place from which Peter wrote hisfirst epistle (1 Pet. 5:13); but he must mean either the Babylon on theEuphrates, or the mystic Babylon of Rome. Eusebius names, as the firstbishops of Alexandria, Annianos (a.d. 62–85), Abilios (to 98), andKerdon (to 110). This see naturally grew up to metropolitan andpatriarchal importance and dignity. As early as the second century atheological school flourished in Alexandria, in which Clement and Origentaught as pioneers in biblical learning and Christian philosophy. FromLower Egypt the gospel spread to Middle and Upper Egypt and the adjacentprovinces, perhaps (in the fourth century) as far as Nubia, Ethiopia,and Abyssinia. At a council of Alexandria in the year 235, twentybishops were present from the different parts of the land of theNile.

During the fourth century Egypt gave to the church the Arian heresy,the Athanasian orthodoxy, and the monastic piety of St. Antony and St.Pachomius, which spread with irresistible force over Christendom.

The theological literature of Egypt was chiefly Greek. Most of theearly manuscripts of the Greek Scriptures—including probably theinvaluable Sinaitic and Vatican MSS.—were written in Alexandria. Butalready in the second century the Scriptures were translated into thevernacular language, in three different dialects. What remains of theseversions is of considerable weight in ascertaining the earliest text ofthe Greek Testament.

The Christian Egyptians are the descendants of the PharaonicEgyptians, but largely mixed with negro and Arab blood. Christianitynever fully penetrated the nation, and was almost swept away by theMohammedan conquest under the Caliph Omar (640), who burned themagnificent libraries of Alexandria under the plea that if the booksagreed with the Koran, they were useless, if not, they were perniciousand fit for destruction. Since that time Egypt almost disappears fromchurch history, and is still groaning, a house of bondage under newmasters. The great mass of the people are Moslems, but the Copts—abouthalf a million of five and a half millions—perpetuate the nominalChristianity of their ancestors, and form a mission field for the moreactive churches of the West.

§ 10. Christianity in NorthAfrica.

Böttiger: Geschichte der Carthager. Berlin, 1827.

Movers: Die Phönizier. 1840–56, 4 vols. (A standardwork.)

Th. Mommsen: Röm. Geschichte, I. 489 sqq. (Book III. chs.1–7, 5th ed.)

N. Davis: Carthage and her Remains. London & N. York,1861.

R. Bosworth Smith: Carthage and the Carthaginians. Lond. 2nded. 1879. By the same: Rome and Carthage. N. York, 1880.

Otto Meltzer: Geschichte der Karthager. Berlin, vol. I.1879.

These books treat of the secular history of the ancientCarthaginians, but help to understand the situation and antecedents.

Julius Lloyd; The North African Church. London, 1880. Comesdown to the Moslem Conquest.

The inhabitants of the provinces of Northern Africa were of Semiticorigin, with a language similar to the Hebrew, but became Latinized incustoms, laws, and language under the Roman rule. The church in thatregion therefore belongs to Latin Christianity, and plays a leading partin its early history.

The Phoenicians, a remnant of the Canaanites, were the English ofancient history. They carried on the commerce of the world; while theIsraelites prepared the religion, and the Greeks the civilization of theworld. Three small nations, in small countries, accomplished a moreimportant work than the colossal empires of Assyria, Babylon, andPersia, or even Rome. Occupying a narrow strip of territory on theSyrian coast, between Mount Lebanon and the sea, the Phoenicians senttheir merchant vessels from Tyre and Sidon to all parts of the old worldfrom India to the Baltic, rounded the Cape of Good Hope two thousandyears before Vasco de Gama, and brought back sandal wood from Malabar,spices from Arabia, ostrich plumes from Nubia, silver from Spain, goldfrom the Niger, iron from Elba, tin from England, and amber from theBaltic. They furnished Solomon with cedars from Lebanon, and helped himto build his palace and the temple. They founded on the northernmostcoast of Africa, more than eight hundred years before Christ, the colonyof Carthage.(3) From that favorable position they acquired the controlover the northern coast of Africa from the pillars of Hercules to theGreat Syrtes, over Southern Spain, the islands of Sardinia and Sicily,and the whole Mediterranean sea. Hence the inevitable rivalry betweenRome and Carthage, divided only by three days’ sail; hence the threePunic wars which, in spite of the brilliant military genius of Hannibal,ended in the utter destruction of the capital of North Africa (b.c.146).(4) "Delenda est Carthago," was the narrow and cruelpolicy of the elder Cato. But under Augustus, who carried out the wiserplan of Julius Caesar, there arose a new Carthage on the ruins of theold, and became a rich and prosperous city, first heathen, thenChristian, until it was captured by the barbarous Vandals (a.d. 439),and finally destroyed by a race cognate to its original founders, theMohammedan Arabs (647). Since that time "a mournful and solitarysilence" once more brooded over its ruins.(5)

Christianity reached proconsular Africa in the second, perhapsalready at the close of the first century, we do not know when and how.There was constant intercourse with Italy. It spread very rapidly overthe fertile fields and burning sands of Mauritania and Numidia. Cypriancould assemble in 258 a synod of eighty-seven bishops, and in 308 theschismatical Donatists held a council of two hundred and seventy bishopsat Carthage. The dioceses, of course, were small in those days.

The oldest Latin translation of the Bible, miscalled "Itala" (thebasis of Jerome’s "Vulgata"), was made probably in Africa and forAfrica, not in Rome and for Rome, where at that time the Greek languageprevailed among Christians. Latin theology, too, was not born in Rome,but in Carthage. Tertullian is its father. Minutius Felix, Arnobius, andCyprian bear witness to the activity and prosperity of AfricanChristianity and theology in the third century. It reached its highestperfection during the first quarter of the fifth century in the sublimeintellect and burning heart of St. Augustin, the greatest among thefathers, but soon after his death (430) it was buried first beneath theVandal barbarism, and in the seventh century by the Mohammedan conquest.Yet his writings led Christian thought in the Latin church throughoutthe dark ages, stimulated the Reformers, and are a vital force to thisday.

§ 11. Christianity in Europe.

"Westward the course of Empire takes its way."

This law of history is also the law of Christianity. From Jerusalemto Rome was the march of the apostolic church. Further and further Westhas been the progress of missions ever since.

The church of Rome was by far the most important one for all theWest. According to Eusebius, it had in the middle of the third centuryone bishop, forty-six presbyters, seven deacons with as manysub-deacons, forty-two acolyths, fifty readers, exorcists, anddoor-keepers, and fifteen hundred widows and poor persons under itscare. From this we might estimate the number of members at some fifty orsixty thousand, i.e. about one-twentieth of the population ofthe city, which cannot be accurately determined indeed, but must haveexceeded one million during the reign of the Antonines.(6) The strengthof Christianity in Rome is also confirmed by the enormous extent of thecatacombs where the Christians were buried.

From Rome the church spread to all the cities of Italy. The firstRoman provincial synod, of which we have information, numbered twelvebishops under the presidency of Telesphorus (142–154). In the middle ofthe third century (255) Cornelius of Rome held a council of sixtybishops.

The persecution of the year 177 shows the church already planted inthe south of Gaul in the second century. Christianity came hitherprobably from the East; for the churches of Lyons and Vienne wereintimately connected with those of Asia Minor, to which they sent areport of the persecution, and Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, was a discipleof Polycarp of Smyrna. Gregory of Tours states, that in the middle ofthe third century seven missionaries were sent from Rome to Gaul. One ofthese, Dionysius, founded the first church of Paris, died a martyr atMontmartre, and became the patron saint of France. Popular superstitionafterwards confounded him with Dionysius the Areopagite, who wasconverted by Paul at Athens.

Spain probably became acquainted with Christianity likewise in thesecond century, though no clear traces of churches and bishops theremeet us till the middle of the third. The council of Elvira in 306numbered nineteen bishops. The apostle Paul once formed the plan of amissionary journey to Spain, and according to Clement of Rome hepreached there, if we understand that country to be meant by "the limitof the West," to which he says that Paul carried the gospel.(7) Butthere is no trace of his labors in Spain on record. The legend, indefiance of all chronology, derives Christianity in that country fromJames the Elder, who was executed in Jerusalem in 44, and is said to beburied at Campostella, the famous place of pilgrimage, where his boneswere first discovered under Alphonse II, towards the close of the eighthcentury.1(8)

When Irenaeus speaks of the preaching of the gospel among the Germansand other barbarians, who, "without paper and ink, have salvationwritten in their hearts by the Holy Spirit," he can refer only to theparts of Germany belonging to the Roman empire (Germaniacisrhenana).

According to Tertullian Britain also was brought under the power ofthe cross towards the end of the second century. The Celtic churchexisted in England, Ireland, and Scotland, independently of Rome, longbefore the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons by the Roman mission ofAugustine; it continued for some time after that event and sentoffshoots to Germany, France, and the Low Countries, but was ultimatelyat different dates incorporated with the Roman church. It took itsorigin probably from Gaul, and afterwards from Italy also. The legendtraces it to St. Paul and other apostolic founders. The venerable Bede(†735) says, that the British king Lucius (about 167) applied to theRoman bishop Eleutherus for missionaries. At the council of Arles, inGaul (Arelate), in 314, three British bishops, of Eboracum (York),Londinum (London), and Colonia Londinensium (i.e. eitherLincoln or more probably Colchester), were present.

The conversion of the barbarians of Northern and Western Europe didnot begin in earnest before the fifth and sixth centuries, and willclaim our attention in the history of the Middle Ages.

Original Footnotes

(1; original 4): Acts 8:4; 11:19.

(2; original 5): "Sola vobis relinqitimustempla."Apol.c. 37. Long before Tertullian the heathenPliny, in his famous letter to Trajan (Epp. x. 97) had spokenof "desolata templa" and "sacra solemnia diuintermissa, " in consequence of the spread of the Christiansuperstition throughout the cities and villages of Asia Minor.

(3; original 6): The Phoenician or Punic name is Karthada,the Greek Karchedon (Karchdwvn), the LatinCarthago. It means New City (Neapolis). The wordKereth or Carth enters also into the names of othercities of Phoenician origin, as Cirta in Numidia.

(4; original 7): See the masterly comparison of Rome and Carthage byMommsen, Book III.ch. 1. (vol. I. 506), of the destruction of Carthagein Book IV. ch. 1. (vol. II. 22 sqq.)

(5; original 8): On the ruins of Carthage see the descriptions of N.Davis and B. Smith (Rome and Carthage, ch. xx. 263-291). Therecent conquest of Tunis by France (1881) gives new interest to the pastof that country, and opens a new chapter for its future. Smith describesTunis as the most Oriental of Oriental towns, with a gorgeous mixture ofraces—Arabs, Turks, Moors, and Negroes—held together by the religion ofIslam.

(6; original 9): Gibbon, in his; thirty-first chapter, and Milmanestimate the population of Rome at 1,200,000; Hoeck (on the basis of theMonumentum Ancyranum), Zumpt and Howson at two millions; Bunsen somewhatlower; while Dureau de la Malle tries to reduce it to half a million, onthe ground that the walls of Servius Tullius occupied an area onlyone-fifth of that of Paris. But these walls no longer marked the limitsof the city since its reconstruction after the conflagration under Nero,and the suburbs stretched to an unlimited extent into the country. Comp.vol. I. p. 359

(7; original 10): Rom. 15:24; Clem. R. Ad Cor. c. 5 (to;tevrma th'" duvsew")

(8; original 11): See J. B. Gams (R.C.): Die Kirchengeschichtevon Spanien, Regensburg, 1862-1879, 5 vols. The first vol. (422pages) is taken up with the legendary history of the first threecenturies. 75 pages are given to the discussion of Paul’s journey toSpain. Gams traces Christianity in that country to Paul and to sevendisciples of the Apostles sent to Rome, namely, Torquatus, Ctesiphon,Secundus, Indaletius, Caecilius, Hesychius, and Euphrasius (according tothe Roman Martyrologium, edited by Baronius, 1586).

脚注

Best guess 对照表

正文及中文脚注中带上标 * 的外文为 bestguess，尚未逐项核实；原始字串保留如下。

原字串Best guess语言出现位置说明
KarchdwvnΚαρχηδώνGreek脚注 3按旧字体编码还原，h 对应 η，wv 对应 ώ；与迦太基的希腊名称相符。
to; tevrma th'" duvsew"τὸ τέρμα τῆς δύσεωςGreek脚注 7按旧字体字母及重音编码还原，与革利免所述“西方的极处”相符。

  1. 《使徒行传》8:4；11:19。↩︎

  2. “Sola vobis relinqitimustempla”（我们只给你们留下了庙宇）。《护教篇》(Apol.)，第37章。早在德尔图良之前，异教徒普林尼(Pliny) 在他致图拉真 (Trajan) 的著名书信（Epp. x.97）中，就曾说到，由于基督教这一迷信传遍小亚细亚的城乡，以致“desolatatempla”（庙宇荒凉），以及“sacra solemnia diuintermissa”（例行祭礼久已中断）。↩︎

  3. 其腓尼基语或布匿语名称为 Karthada，希腊语为Karchedon（Καρχηδών*），拉丁语为Carthago，意为新城 (Neapolis)。Kereth 或Carth 一词也见于其他源自腓尼基的城市名称，例如努米底亚(Numidia) 的 Cirta。↩︎

  4. 参见蒙森 (Mommsen)对罗马与迦太基的精辟比较，第III编第1章（第I卷，第506页）；关于迦太基的毁灭，见第IV编第1章（第II卷，第22页及后）。↩︎

  5. 关于迦太基 (Carthage) 的遗址，参见 N. 戴维斯 (N. Davis)和 B. 史密斯 (B. Smith) 的描述（《罗马与迦太基》〔Rome andCarthage〕，第xx章，第263–291页）。法国最近对突尼斯 (Tunis)的征服（1881年），使该国的往昔重新引起人们的兴趣，也为其未来开启了新的篇章。史密斯将突尼斯描述为东方城镇中最具东方色彩的一座，阿拉伯人、土耳其人、摩尔人和黑人汇聚于此，绚丽多彩，由伊斯兰教联结在一起。↩︎

  6. 吉本 (Gibbon) 在其第三十一章中，以及米尔曼(Milman)，都估计罗马人口为1,200,000；赫克(Hoeck，依据《安居拉铭文》〔Monumentum Ancyranum〕)、楚姆普特 (Zumpt)和豪森 (Howson) 估计为二百万；本生 (Bunsen) 的估计略低；而迪罗·德·拉马勒(Dureau de la Malle) 则试图将其减至五十万，理由是塞尔维乌斯·图利乌斯(Servius Tullius)城墙所圈定的面积只有巴黎的五分之一。然而，自尼禄时期大火之后重建以来，这些城墙就已不再标示城市的边界，郊区更是无限地伸展到乡间。比较第I卷，第359页。↩︎

  7. 《罗马书》15:24；罗马的革利免 (Clem.R.)：《致哥林多人书》(Ad Cor.)，第5章（τὸτέρμα τῆς δύσεως*，西方的极处）。↩︎

  8. 参见 J. B. 加姆斯 (J. B.Gams，罗马天主教徒)：《西班牙教会史》(Die Kirchengeschichte vonSpanien)，雷根斯堡(Regensburg)，1862–1879年，5卷。第一卷（422页）全用于叙述最初三个世纪的传说史，其中75页用于讨论保罗的西班牙之行。加姆斯将该国基督教的起源追溯至保罗，以及七位被差往罗马的使徒门徒，即托尔夸图斯(Torquatus)、克特西丰 (Ctesiphon)、塞孔杜斯 (Secundus)、因达勒提乌斯(Indaletius)、凯基利乌斯 (Caecilius)、赫叙基乌斯 (Hesychius)和欧弗拉修斯(Euphrasius)（依据巴罗尼乌斯〔Baronius〕于1586年编辑的《罗马殉道者名录》〔RomanMartyrologium〕）。↩︎

§ 74. 文献

参看§ 14关于基督生平的文献，以及§ 20关于使徒时期的文献。

I. 《希腊文新约》(Greek Testament)的校勘版本：拉赫曼(Lachmann)，1842–50年，2卷；蒂申多夫 (Tischendorf)，第八版大型校勘本(ed. octava critics major)，1869–72年，2卷，附C. R. 格雷戈里 (C. R.Gregory) 所撰《绪论》(Prolegomena)，第一部分，莱比锡(Leipz.)，1884年；特雷格尔斯 (Tregelles)，1857–79年；韦斯科特与霍特(Westcott andHort)，1881年，另附《导论与附录》一卷，剑桥与纽约，修订版，1888年。

拉赫曼奠定了基础；蒂申多夫和特雷格尔斯大大扩充了校勘资料，并加以细致甄别；韦斯科特和霍特根据所能获得的最古老资料，恢复了最纯净的文本；他们在原则和结果上都基本一致，给我们提供的是古代大写字体抄本的文本，而非中世纪草写体抄本的文本。

与近来路德译本和钦定本的修订有关，还有两种双语版本值得特别提及。奥斯卡·冯·格布哈特(Oskar von Gebhardt)：《希腊文与德文新约》(Novum Testamentum Graeceet Germanice)，莱比锡(Lips.)，1881年，采用蒂申多夫最后定本的文本（下附特雷格尔斯及韦斯科特与霍特的异读），以及路德译本的修订译文。他的希腊文文本也单独出版，附有双语版所未收录的“校勘注释”("Adnotatiocritica")。《希英对照新约：韦斯科特与霍特希腊文文本及英语修订本分列对页，附沙弗导言》(TheGreek-English New Testament, containing Westcott and Hort’s Greek Textand the Revised English Version on opposite pages, with introduction bySchaff.)，纽约，哈珀兄弟出版社 (Harper &Brothers)，1882年；修订版，1888年。

  1. 以下各家所著的历史批判性《新约导论》，或《新约文学史》：胡格(Hug)、德·韦特 (De Wette)、克雷德纳 (Credner)、盖里克 (Guericke)、霍恩(Horne)、戴维森 (Davidson)、特雷格尔斯 (Tregelles)、格劳(Grau)、希尔根费尔德 (Hilgenfeld)、阿伯勒 (Aberle，罗马天主教)、布利克(Bleek，曼戈尔德〔Mangold〕编第四版，1886年)、罗伊斯(Reuss，第六版，1887年)、霍尔茨曼 (Holtzmann，第二版，1886年)、魏斯(Weiss，1886年)、萨蒙 (Salmon，第三版，1888年)。

  2. 蒂尔施(Thiersch)：《重建新约诸书批判研究的历史立场》(Herstellung deshistorischen Standpunktes für die Kritik der neutestamentl.Schriften)。埃尔朗根(Erlangen)，1845年。（反对鲍尔〔Baur〕及图宾根学派〔TübingenSchool〕。）——爱德华·C. 米切尔 (Edward C.Mitchell)：《新约批判研究手册》(Critical Handbook to the NewTest.，论真确性、正典等)。伦敦 (Lond.) 与安多弗(Andover)，1880年；法译本，巴黎，1882年。——J. P. 兰格 (J. P.Lange)：《圣经知识纲要》(Grundriss der Bibelkunde)。海德堡(Heidelberg)，1881年。——菲利普·沙弗 (PhilipSchaff)：《希腊文新约与英语译本指南》(Companion to the GreekTestament and the English Version.)。纽约 (N. Y.) 与伦敦(Lond.)，1883年；第三版，修订本，1888年。——G. D. 拉德 (G. D.Ladd)：《圣经教义》(The Doctrine of Sacred Scripture,)，纽约(N. York)，1883年，2卷。同书节本，1888年。

  3. 下文所引关于福音书和使徒书信的著作。

V. 关于新约正典，有以下各家的著作：基尔希霍费尔(Kirchhofer)（《史料汇编》等，Quellensammlung，苏黎世〔Zürich〕，1844年；查特里斯〔Charteris〕增订英译本：《正典性》等，Canonicity，爱丁堡〔Edinb.〕，1881年）；克雷德纳(Credner)（《正典史论》，Zur Gesch. desKanon.，哈雷〔Halle〕，1847年；《新约正典史》，福尔克马尔〔Volkmar〕编，Geschichtedes Neutest. § 75. 使徒文献的兴起

基督是人人都当诵读的生命之书。他的宗教不是像摩西律法那样外在的诫命字句，而是自由、使人得生命的灵；不是文学的产物，而是道德的创造；不是为学者设立的一套新神学或哲学体系，而是将神的生命传给人，以救赎整个世界。基督是有位格的上帝之道，是永恒的逻各斯(Logos)，成为肉身，作为真正的舍金纳 (Shekinah)住在地上，在遮蔽之中显出父独生子的荣光，充充满满地有恩典有真理。他开口说话；他口中所出的一切话，从前是、如今仍是灵，是生命。人心所渴求的，不是一位博学、写信、著书的基督，而是一位行神迹、背十架、成就赎罪的救赎主，已经复活，在天上登基，统治世界；同时也为人和天使提供一个永无穷尽的默想、讲论和赞美的主题。

同样，主所拣选的使徒，除保罗一人以外，没有一个出自学者的行列；他没有训练他们从事著述，在他整个地上生活中，也未曾明白吩咐过他们一句，要他们以这种方式劳作。这些加利利的朴实渔夫，不通晓世上的智慧，却充满真理的圣灵和来世的能力；他们奉差遣，靠着已经得荣耀之主的能力，奉他的名，将救恩的佳音传给万民。这位主坐在全能父上帝的右边，并且应许与他们同在，直到世界的末了。

因此，福音最初的传播、教会最初的建立，是凭着使徒及其门徒亲身的口头教导和劝勉，即他们的“宣讲”“见证”“话语”“传承”；事实上，直到今日，活的言语仍是推广基督教不可缺少的手段，至少也是主要手段。《新约》几乎所有的书卷都写于公元50至70年间，距基督复活和教会建立至少已有二十年；约翰的福音书和书信则写得更晚。

随着使徒工作范围的扩展，领域变得过于广大，非他们亲身所能照料，因而需要书信往来。基督教的根本利益和后世的需要，要求有完全可靠的见证人，忠实记录基督的生平和教训。因为在会犯错误的人中间，口头传承容易发生种种偶然的变动，离源头越远，其确定性和可信性便越低，直到最后，再也无法将它与其上积累的增添和讹误清楚地区别开来。此外，那些在使徒在世时就已抬头的犹太化和异教化的谬误传播者，也极有可能蓄意歪曲基督教的历史和教义。因此，对耶稣及其门徒的言行作出真确的文字记录，实在绝不可少；这固然不是为了创立教会，而是为了保守教会不受败坏，并为她提供纯正的信仰与纪律准则。

于是便有了使徒和使徒同人的二十七卷著作，都是在圣灵特殊的感动与引导下写成的。这些著作为我们真实地描绘了原始基督教的历史、信仰和实践，“于教训、督责、使人归正、教导人学义都是有益的。”1

将这些著作汇集成正典，使之既有别于伪经或伪托使徒的作品，又有别于虽属正统却仅出于人的作品，乃是早期教会的工作；教会进行这项工作时，同样受到上帝之灵和健全的真理意识的引导。直到第四世纪末，这项工作才告完成，得到所有人的认可；在此之前，有七卷新约书（优西比乌〔Eusebius〕所谓的“有争议之书”〔Antilegomena〕），即《彼得后书》《约翰二书》《约翰三书》、未署名的《希伯来书》、《雅各书》《犹大书》，以及在某种意义上也包括《约翰启示录》，其作者身份或价值仍受到一些人的怀疑。不过，汇集工作无疑在第一世纪就已仿照旧约正典的模式开始了；2而其中主要的书卷，即诸福音书、《使徒行传》、保罗的十三封书信、《彼得前书》和《约翰一书》，在第二世纪中叶以后便已作为一个整体普遍使用，并仿照犹太会堂的方式，在公共敬拜中整卷或分段诵读，以造就会众。

对于新教基督徒而言，单凭传统的外在见证，并不能判定一卷书是否源于使徒、是否具有正典性质；这必须得到该书本身内在见证的证实。然而，这种见证并不缺少；这十八个世纪以来，基督教世界一致承认，我们称为《新约》的这一小卷书，在属灵能力及对人心智与心灵的影响上，是一本绝无仅有的书，其意趣和价值胜过古今一切经典的总和。上帝若曾向人说话，并且如今仍向人说话，那就是在这本书中。

§ 76. 新约的特质

在这些受默示的著作中，我们所拥有的，虽不等同于基督及其使徒亲身同在、口授教训，却是可靠的替代。写下的话语与口述的话语，仅在形式上有所不同；其实质相同，因此对我们而言，也具有与最初听见这些话的人所经历的同样的权威和使人得生命的能力。这些书卷表面上虽然是由特殊而偶然的契机促成，起初也是写给特定读者群，并适应特殊处境的，然而，它们既以活泼的形式呈现永恒不变的真理，就适用于一切境遇和状况。它们是为当时而写的篇章，也是为万世而写的篇章；它们本为第一世纪的犹太人和希腊人而写，却同样引起第十九世纪英国人和美国人的关切。直到今日，它们不仅是原始基督教唯一可靠而纯净的源泉，也是基督徒信仰与实践无误的准则。教会从这源泉中饮取生命之水，已有五十多代，并且还要继续饮用，直到世界的末了。在这准则中，教会拥有纠正她一切过失的永久依据，以及抵御一切谬误的保障。神学体系兴起又消逝，从这宝库中或多或少地汲取材料，增进我们对真理的认识；然而，它们永不能与那永远长存、无误的上帝之道相提并论。

“我们渺小的体系各有其时，

盛行一时，便归消逝；

它们不过是你破碎的光芒，

上帝啊，你却远超其上。”

《新约》在其文体本身就显出它普及万民的旨趣；仅此一点，便足以使它有别于前后各时代的一切文学作品。它有希腊的躯体、希伯来的灵魂，以及统御两者的基督教精神。它所用的是希腊化语体(Hellenisticidiom)，即基督时代散居各地的犹太人所说的马其顿希腊语；它以一种经过更新的基督教形式，将古代世界两大彼此对立的民族和宗教结合起来。异教世界最优美的语言与希伯来人庄严古老的语言，在这里融为一体，受了基督教精神的洗礼，成为银网子，衬托福音永恒真理的金苹果。圣经的文体，总的说来，格外适合各阶层和各种文化程度的人；它既为儿童的宗教需要提供简单的滋养，也为最深邃的思想家提供取之不尽的研究材料。圣经不只是一本通俗读物，更是一本属于万国、适用于人类一切社会、阶层和境遇的书。它不只是一本书，更是一种统御基督教世界的制度。

《新约》以其特有的方式，呈现出与基督位格相同的神人联合。在这个意义上，也可以说“道成了肉身，住在我们中间”。基督在身体、魂与灵各方面都与我们相同，只是没有罪；同样，那“为他作见证”的圣经，在内容与形式上，在其产生、编集、保存和流传的方式上，也全然具有人性（却没有教义和伦理上的错误）；然而，同时它在思想与言语、起源、生命力、能力和功效上，又全然具有神性。在文字这属人的奴仆形象之下，信心的眼睛辨认出“父独生子的荣光，充充满满地有恩典有真理”。

使徒著作分为三类：历史性的、教导性的和预言性的。福音书与《使徒行传》属于第一类；书信属于第二类；《启示录》属于第三类。它们彼此的关系，犹如重生、成圣与得荣耀，又如根基、房屋与穹顶。耶稣基督是一切的开端、中心和终结。在福音书中，他以人的形象行走于地上，成就救赎的工作。在《使徒行传》和书信中，他建立教会，并借着他的灵充满、引导教会。最后，在《启示录》的异象中，他在荣耀里再来，与他的新妇——众圣徒的教会——在新地的上帝之城中永远作王。

这一顺序与基督教启示的自然进程相合，也为教会普遍采用，惟书信的编排略有差异。《新约》并非以一部编定成书的形式赐下；各卷书乃是在被认可和使用的过程中，依照内在契合的规律，逐渐汇集而成。大多数古代抄本、译本和书目，都依照以下次序排列各卷：福音书、《使徒行传》、大公书信、保罗书信、《启示录》。3 有些则将保罗书信放在大公书信之前。4我们的英文圣经沿用拉丁文《武加大译本》(Vulgate) 的次序。5

II. 批判性讨论

纳撒尼尔·拉德纳 (NathanielLardner，1684–1768年，学识渊博的不从国教派牧师)：《福音历史的可信性》(TheCredibility of the GospelHistory)。初版为八开本17卷，伦敦，1727–1757年；又收入A. 基皮斯 (A.Kippis)所编的《全集》(Works)，伦敦，1788年（共11卷），第I–V卷。论学问之诚实与坚实，无出其右，至今仍有价值。

D. 米夏埃利斯 (J. D.Michaelis) 的《新约导论，附前三部福音书的起源与构成论》(Introductionto the New Test., with a Dissertation on the Origin and Composition ofthe Three FirstGospels)。伦敦，1802年。这是对艾希霍恩假说的修正。
