It isin the fullest sense free, comprehensive, universal. It displays thischaracter, not only in the acceptance of all comers who seek admission,irrespective of race or caste or sex, but also in the instruction andtreatment of those who are already its members. It has no sacred days orseasons, no special sanctuaries, because every time and every placealike are holy. Above all it has no sacerdotal system. It interposes nosacrificial tribe or class between God and man, by whose interventionalone God is reconciled and man forgiven. Each individual member holdspersonal communion with the Divine Head. To Him immediately he isresponsible, and from Him directly he obtains pardon and drawsstrength."

But he immediately proceeds to qualify this statement, and says thatthis is simply the ideal view—"a holy season extending the whole yearround, a temple confined only by the limits of the habitable world, apriesthood co-extensive with the race"—and that the Church of Christ canno more hold together without officers, rules, and institutions than anyother society of men. "As appointed days and set places areindispensable to her efficiency, so also the Church could not fulfil thepurposes for which she exists without rulers and teachers, without aministry of reconciliation, in short, without an order of men who may insome sense be designated a priesthood. In this respect the ethics ofChristianity present an analogy to the politics. Here also the idealconception and the actual realization are incommensurate and in a mannercontradictory."

  1. Nearly all denominations appeal for their church polity to the NewTestament, with about equal right and equal wrong: the Romanists to theprimacy of Peter; the Irvingites to the apostles and prophets andevangelists, and the miraculous gifts; the Episcopalians to the bishops,the angels, and James of Jerusalem; the Presbyterians to the presbytersand their identity with the bishops; the Congregationalists to theindependence of the local congregations and the absence ofcentralization. The most that can be said is, that the apostolic agecontains fruitful germs for various ecclesiastical organizationssubsequently developed, but none of them can claim divine authorityexcept for the gospel ministry, which is common to all. Dean Stanleyasserts that no existing church can find any pattern or platform of itsgovernment in the first century, and thus strongly contrasts theapostolic and post-apostolic organizations (l.c.): "It iscertain that the officers of the apostolical or of any subsequentchurch, were not part of the original institution of the Founder of ourreligion; that of Bishop, Presbyter, and Deacon; of Metropolitan,Patriarch, and Pope, there is not the shadow of a trace in the fourGospels. It is certain that they arose gradually out of the preexistinginstitutions either of the Jewish synagogue, or of the Roman empire, orof the Greek municipalities, or under the pressure of local emergencies.It is certain that throughout the first century, and for the first yearsof the second, that is, through the later chapters of the Acts, theApostolical Epistles, and the writings of Clement and Hermas. Bishop andPresbyter were convertible terms, and that the body of men so-calledwere the rulers—so far as any permanent rulers existed—of the earlychurch. It is certain that, as the necessities of the time demanded,first at Jerusalem, then in Asia Minor, the elevation of one Presbyterabove the rest by the almost universal law, which even in republicsengenders a monarchial element, the word ’Bishop’ gradually changed itsmeaning, and by the middle of the second century became restricted tothe chief Presbyter of the locality. It is certain that in no instancewere the apostles called ’Bishops’ in any other sense than they wereequally called ’Presbyters’ and ’Deacons.’ It is certain that in noinstance before the beginning of the third century the title or functionof the Pagan or Jewish priesthood is applied to the Christian pastors.... It is as sure that nothing like modern Episcopacy existed beforethe close of the first century as it is that nothing like modernPresbyterianism existed after the beginning of the second. That whichwas once the Gordian knot of theologians has at least in this instancebeen untied, not by the sword of persecution, but by the patientunravelment of scholarships."

§ 60. Apostles, Prophets,Evangelists.

The ministry originally coincided with the apostolate; as the churchwas at first identical with the congregation of Jerusalem. No otherofficers are mentioned in the Gospels and the first five chapters of theActs. But when the believers began to number thousands, the apostlescould not possibly perform all the functions of teaching, conductingworship, and administering discipline; they were obliged to create newoffices for the ordinary wants of the congregations, while they devotedthemselves to the general supervision and the further extension of thegospel. Thus arose gradually, out of the needs of the Christian church,though partly at the suggestion of the existing organization of theJewish synagogue, the various general and congregational offices in thechurch. As these all have their common root in the apostolate, so theypartake also, in different degrees, of its divine origin, authority,privileges, and responsibilities.

We notice first, those offices which were not limited to any onecongregation, but extended over the whole church, or at least over agreat part of it. These are apostles, prophets, and evangelists. Paulmentions them together in this order.(6) But the prophecy was a gift andfunction rather than an office, and the evangelists were temporaryofficers charged with a particular mission under the direction of theapostles. All three are usually regarded as extraordinary officers andconfined to the apostolic age; but from time to time God raisesextraordinary missionaries (as Patrick, Columba, Boniface, Ansgar),divines (as Augustin, Anselm, Thomas Aquinas, Luther, Melancthon,Calvin), and revival preachers (as Bernard, Knox, Baxter, Wesley,Whitefield), who may well be called apostles, prophets, and evangelistsof their age and nation.(7)

  1. Apostles. These were originally twelve in number, answering tothe twelve tribes of Israel. In place of the traitor, Judas, Matthiaswas chosen by lot, between the ascension and Pentecost.(8) After theoutpouring of the Holy Spirit, Paul was added as the thirteenth by thedirect call of the exalted Saviour. He was the independent apostle ofthe Gentiles, and afterward gathered several subordinate helpers aroundhim. Besides these there were apostolic men, like Barnabas, and Jamesthe brother of the Lord, whose standing and influence were almost equalto that of the proper apostles. The Twelve (excepting Matthias, who,however, was an eye-witness of the resurrection) and Paul were calleddirectly by Christ, without human intervention, to be hisrepresentatives on earth, the inspired organs of the Holy Spirit, thefounders and pillars of the whole church. Their office was universal,and their writings are to this day the unerring rule of faith andpractice for all Christendom. But they never exercised their divineauthority in arbitrary and despotic style. They always paid tenderregard to the rights, freedom, and dignity of the immortal souls undertheir care. In every believer, even in a poor slave like Onesimus, theyrecognized a member of the same body with themselves, a partaker oftheir redemption, a beloved brother in Christ. Their government of thechurch was a labor of meekness and love, of self-denial and unreserveddevotion to the eternal welfare of the people. Peter, the prince of theapostles, humbly calls himself a "fellow-presbyter," and raises hisprophetic warning against the hierarchical spirit which so easily takeshold of church dignitaries and alienates them from the people.

  2. Prophets. These were inspired and inspiring teachers andpreachers of the mysteries of God. They appear to have had specialinfluence on the choice of officers, designating the persons who werepointed out to them by the Spirit of God in their prayer and fasting, aspeculiarly fitted for missionary labor or any other service in thechurch. Of the prophets the book of Acts names Agabus, Barnabas, Symeon,Lucius, Manaen, and Saul of Tarsus, Judas and Silas.(9) The gift ofprophecy in the wider sense dwelt in all the apostles, pre-eminently inJohn, the seer of the new covenant and author of the Revelation. It wasa function rather than an office.

  3. Evangelists, itinerant preachers, delegates, and fellow-laborersof the apostles—such men as Mark, Luke, Timothy, Titus, Silas, Epaphras,Trophimus, and Apollos.(10) They may be compared to modern missionaries.They were apostolic commissioners for a special work. "It is theconception of a later age which represents Timothy as bishop of Ephesus,and Titus as bishop of Crete. St. Paul’s own language implies that theposition which they held was temporary. In both cases their term ofoffice is drawing to a close when the apostle writes."(11)

§61. Presbyters or Bishops. The Angels of the Seven Churches. James ofJerusalem.

We proceed to the officers of local congregations who were chargedwith carrying forward in particular places the work begun by theapostles and their delegates. These were of two kinds, Presbyters orBishops, and Deacons or Helpers. They multiplied in proportion asChristianity extended, while the number of the apostles diminished bydeath, and could, in the nature of the case, not be filled up bywitnesses of the life and resurrection of Christ. The extraordinaryofficers were necessary for the founding and being of the church, theordinary officers for its preservation and well-being.

The terms Presbyter (or Elder)(12) and Bishop (or Overseer,Superintendent)(13) denote in the New Testament one and the same office,with this difference only, that the first is borrowed from theSynagogue, the second from the Greek communities; and that the onesignifies the dignity, the other the duty.(14)

  1. The identity of these officers is very evident from thefollowing facts:

a. They appear always as a plurality or as a college in oneand the same congregation, even in smaller cities) as Philippi.(15)

b. The same officers of the church of Ephesus arealternately called presbyters(16) and bishops.

c. Paul sends greetings to the "bishops" and "deacons" ofPhilippi, but omits the presbyters because they were included in thefirst term; as also the plural indicates.(17)

d. In the Pastoral Epistles, where Paul intends to give thequalifications for all church officers, he again mentions only two,bishops and deacons, but uses the term presbyter afterwards forbishop.(18)

Peter urges the "presbyters" to "tend the flock of God," and to"fulfil the office of bishops" with disinterested devotion and without"lording it over the charge allotted to them."(19)

e. The interchange of terms continued in use to the close ofthe first century, as is evident from the Epistle of Clement of Rome(about 95), and the Didache, and still lingered towards theclose of the second.(20)

With the beginning of the second century, from Ignatius onward, thetwo terms are distinguished and designate two offices; the bishop beingregarded first as the head of a congregation surrounded by a council ofpresbyters, and afterwards as the head of a diocese and successor of theapostles. The episcopate grew out of the presidency of the presbytery,or, as Bishop Lightfoot well expresses it: "The episcopate was formed,not out of the apostolic order by localization, but out of thepresbyteral by elevation; and the title, which originally was common toall, came at length to be appropriated to the chief among them."(21)Nevertheless, a recollection of the original identity was preserved bythe best biblical scholars among the fathers, such as Jerome (who taughtthat the episcopate rose from the presbyterate as a safeguard againstschism), Chrysostom, and Theodoret.(22)

The reason why the title bishop (and not presbyter) was givenafterwards to the superior officer, may be explained from the fact thatit signified, according to monumental inscriptions recently discovered,financial officers of the temples, and that the bishops had the chargeof all the funds of the churches, which were largely charitableinstitutions for the support of widows and orphans, strangers andtravellers, aged and infirm people in an age of extreme riches andextreme poverty.(23)

  1. The origin of the presbytero-episcopal office is notrecorded in the New Testament, but when it is first mentioned in thecongregation at Jerusalem, a.d. 44, it appears already as a settledinstitution.(24) As every Jewish synagogue was ruled by elders, it wasvery natural that every Jewish Christian congregation should at onceadopt this form of government; this may be the reason why the writer ofthe Acts finds it unnecessary to give an account of the origin; while hereports the origin of the deaconate which arose from a special emergencyand had no precise analogy in the organization of the synagogue. TheGentile churches followed the example, choosing the already familiarterm bishop. The first thing which Paul and Barnabas did after preachingthe gospel in Asia Minor was to organize churches by the appointment ofelders.(25)

  2. The office of the presbyter-bishops was to teach and to rule theparticular congregation committed to their charge. They were the regular"pastors and teachers."(26) To them belonged the direction of publicworship, the administration of discipline, the care of souls, and themanagement of church property. They were usually chosen from the firstconverts, and appointed by the apostles or their delegates, with theapproval of the congregation, or by the congregation itself, whichsupported them by voluntary contributions. They were solemnly introducedinto their office by the apostles or by their fellow presbyters throughprayers and the laying on of hands.(27)

The presbyters always formed a college or corporation, a presbytery;as at Jerusalem, at Ephesus, at Philippi, and at the ordination ofTimothy.(28) They no doubt maintained a relation of fraternal equality.The New Testament gives us no information about the division of laboramong them, or the nature and term of a presidency. It is quite probablethat the members of the presbyteral college distributed the variousduties of their office among themselves according to their respectivetalents, tastes, experience, and convenience. Possibly, too, thepresident, whether temporary or permanent, was styled distinctively thebishop; and from this the subsequent separation of the episcopate fromthe presbyterate may easily have arisen. But so long as the generalgovernment of the church was in the hands of the apostles and theirdelegates, the bishops were limited in their jurisdiction either to onecongregation or to a small circle of congregations.

The distinction of "teaching presbyters" or ministers proper, and"ruling presbyters" or lay-elders, is a convenient arrangement ofReformed churches, but can hardly claim apostolic sanction, since theone passage on which it rests only speaks of two functions in the sameoffice.(29) Whatever may have been the distribution and rotation ofduties, Paul expressly mentions ability to teach among the regularrequisites for the episcopal or presbyteral office.(30)

  1. The Angels of the Seven Churches in Asia Minor must be regardedas identical with the presbyter-bishops or local pastors. They representthe presiding presbyters, or the corps of regular officers, as theresponsible messengers of God to the congregation.(31) At the death ofPaul and Peter, under Nero, the congregations were ruled by a college ofelders, and if the Apocalypse, as the majority of critical commentatorsnow hold, was written before the year 70, there was too little time fora radical change of the organization from a republican to a monarchicalform. Even if we regard the "angels" as single persons, they wereevidently confined to a single church, and subject to St. John; hence,not successors of the apostles, as the latter diocesan bishops claim tobe. The most that can be said is that the angels were congregational, asdistinct from diocesan bishops, and mark one step from the primitivepresbyters to the Ignatian bishops, who were likewise congregationalofficers, but in a monarchical sense as the heads of the presbytery,bearing a patriarchal relation to the congregation and being eminentlyresponsible for its spiritual condition.(32)

  2. The nearest approach to the idea of the ancient catholicepiscopate may be found in the unique position of James, the Brother ofthe Lord. Unlike the apostles, he confined his labors to the motherchurch of Jerusalem. In the Jewish Christian traditions of the secondcentury he appears both as bishop and pope of the church universal.(33)But in fact he was only primus inter pares. In his last visitto Jerusalem, Paul was received by the body of the presbyters, and tothem he gave an account of his missionary labors.(34) Moreover, thisauthority of James, who was not an apostle, was exceptional and duechiefly to his close relationship with the Lord, and his personalsanctity, which won the respect even of the unconverted Jews.

The institution of episcopacy proper cannot be traced to theapostolic age, so far as documentary evidence goes, but is very apparentand well-nigh universal about the middle of the second century. Itsorigin and growth will claim our attention in the next period.

§ 62. Deacons and Deaconesses.

Deacons,(35) or helpers, appear first in the church of Jerusalem,seven in number. The author of the Acts 6 gives us an account of theorigin of this office, which is mentioned before that of the presbyters.It had a precedent in the officers of the synagogue who had charge ofthe collection and distribution of alms.(36) It was the first relief ofthe heavy burden that rested on the shoulders of the apostles, whowished to devote themselves exclusively to prayer and the ministry ofthe word. It was occasioned by a complaint of the Hellenistic Christiansagainst the Hebrew or Palestinian brethren, that their widows wereneglected in the daily distribution of food (and perhaps money). In theexercise of a truly fraternal spirit the congregation elected sevenHellenists instead of Hebrews, if we are to judge from their Greeknames, although they were not uncommon among the Jews in that age. Afterthe popular election they were ordained by the apostles.

The example of the mother church was followed in all othercongregations, though without particular regard to the number. Thechurch of Rome, however, perpetuated even the number seven for severalgenerations.(37) In Philippi the deacons took their rank after thepresbyters, and are addressed with them in Paul’s Epistle.

The office of there deacons, according to the narrative in Acts, wasto minister at the table in the daily love-feasts, and to attend to thewants of the poor and the sick. The primitive churches were charitablesocieties, taking care of the widows and orphans, dispensing hospitalityto strangers, and relieving the needs of the poor. The presbyters werethe custodians, the deacons the collectors and distributors, of thecharitable funds. To this work a kind of pastoral care of souls verynaturally attached itself, since poverty and sickness afford the bestoccasions and the most urgent demand for edifying instruction andconsolation. Hence, living faith and exemplary conduct were necessaryqualifications for the office of deacon.(38)

Two of the Jerusalem deacons, Stephen and Philip, labored also aspreachers and evangelists, but in the exercise of a personal gift ratherthan of official duty.

In post-apostolic times, when the bishop was raised above thepresbyter and the presbyter became priest, the deacon was regarded asLevite, and his primary function of care of the poor was lost in thefunction of assisting the priest in the subordinate parts of publicworship and the administration of the sacraments. The diaconate becamethe first of the three orders of the ministry and a stepping-stone tothe priesthood. At the same time the deacon, by his intimacy with thebishop as his agent and messenger, acquired an advantage over thepriest.

Deaconesses,(39) or female helpers, had a similar charge of the poorand sick in the female portion of the church. This office was the moreneedful on account of the rigid separation of the sexes at that day,especially among the Greeks and Orientals. It opened to pious women andvirgins, and chiefly to widows, a most suitable field for the regularofficial exercise of their peculiar gifts of self-denying charity anddevotion to the welfare of the church. Through it they could carry thelight and comfort of the gospel into the most private and delicaterelations of domestic life, without at all overstepping their naturalsphere. Paul mentions Phoebe as a deaconess of the church of Cenchreae,the port of Corinth, and it is more than probable that Prisca(Priscilla), Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, and Persis, whom he commends fortheir labor in the Lord, served in the same capacity at Rome.(40)

The deaconesses were usually chosen from elderly widows. In theEastern churches the office continued to the end of the twelfthcentury.(41)

§ 63. Church Discipline.

Holiness, like unity and catholicity or universality, is an essentialmark of the Church of Christ, who is himself the one, holy Saviour ofall men; but it has never yet been perfectly actualized in hermembership on earth, and is subject to gradual growth with manyobstructions and lapses. The church militant, as a body, like everyindividual Christian, has to pass through a long process ofsanctification, which cannot be complete till the second coining of theLord.

Even the apostles, far as they tower above ordinary Christians, andinfallible as they are in giving all the instruction necessary tosalvation, never during their earthly life claimed sinless perfection ofcharacter, but felt themselves oppressed with manifold infirmities, andin constant need of forgiveness and purification.

Still less can we expect perfect moral purity in their churches. Infact, all the Epistles of the New Testament contain exhortations toprogress in virtue and piety, warnings against unfaithfulness andapostasy, and reproofs respecting corrupt practices among the believers.The old leaven of Judaism and heathenism could not be purged away atonce, and to many of the blackest sins the converts were for the firsttime fully exposed after their regeneration by water and the Spirit. Inthe churches of Galatia many fell back from grace and from the freedomof the gospel to the legal bondage of Judaism and the "rudiments of theworld." In the church of Corinth, Paul had to rebuke the carnal spiritof sect, the morbid desire for wisdom, participation in the idolatrousfeasts of the heathen, the tendency to uncleanness, and a scandalousprofanation of the holy Supper or the love-feasts connected with it.Most of the churches of Asia Minor, according to the Epistles of Pauland the Apocalypse, were so infected with theoretical errors orpractical abuses, as to call for the earnest warnings and reproofs ofthe Holy Spirit through the apostles.(42)

These facts show how needful discipline is, both for the churchherself and for the offenders. For the church it is a process ofself-purification, and the assertion of the holiness and moral dignitywhich essentially belong to her. To the offender it is at once a meritedpunishment and a means of repentance and reform. For the ultimate end ofthe agency of Christ and his church is the salvation of souls; and Paulstyles the severest form of church discipline the delivering of thebackslider "to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spiritmay be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus."(43)

The means of discipline are of various degrees of severity; first,private admonition, then public correction, and, finally, when theseprove fruitless, excommunication, or temporary exclusion from all themeans of grace and from Christian intercourse.(44) Upon sincererepentance, the fallen one is restored to the communion of the church.The act of discipline is that of the whole congregation in the name ofChrist; and Paul himself, though personally absent, excommunicated thefornicator at Corinth with the concurrence of the congregation, and asbeing, in spirit united with it. In one of the only two passages whereour Lord uses the term ecclesia, he speaks of it as a courtwhich, like the Jewish synagogue, has authority to decide disputes andto exercise discipline.(45) In the synagogue, the college of presbytersformed the local court for judicial as well as administrative purposes,but acted in the name of the whole congregation.

The two severest cases of discipline in the apostolic church were thefearful punishment of Ananias and Sapphira by Peter for falsehood andhypocrisy in the church of Jerusalem in the days of her first love,(46)and the excommunication of a member of the Corinthian congregation byPaul for adultery and incest.(47) The latter case affords also aninstance of restoration.(48)

§ 64. The Council at Jerusalem.

(Comp. § 34, pp. 835 sqq. and 346 sq.)

The most complete outward representation of the apostolic church as ateaching and legislative body was the council convened at Jerusalem inthe year 50, to decide as to the authority of the law of Moses, andadjust the difference between Jewish and Gentile Christianity.(49)

We notice it here simply in its connection with the organization ofthe church.

It consisted not of the apostles alone, but of apostles, elders, andbrethren. We know that Peter, Paul, John, Barnabas, and Titus werepresent, perhaps all the other apostles. James—not one of theTwelve—presided as the local bishop, and proposed the compromise whichwas adopted. The transactions were public, before the congregation; thebrethren took part in the deliberations; there was a sharp discussion,but the spirit of love prevailed over the pride of opinion; the apostlespassed and framed the decree not without, but with the elders and withthe whole church and sent the circular letter not in their own nameonly, but also in the name of "the brother elders" or "elder brethren"to "the brethren" of the congregations disturbed by the question ofcircumcision.(50)

All of which plainly proves the right of Christian people to takepart in some way in the government of the church, as they do in the actsof worship. The spirit and practice of the apostles favored a certainkind of popular self-government, and the harmonious, fraternalco-operation of the different elements of the church. It countenanced noabstract distinction of clergy and laity. All believers are called tothe prophetic, priestly, and kingly offices in Christ. The bearers ofauthority and discipline should therefore never forget that their greatwork is to train the governed to freedom and independence, and by thevarious spiritual offices to build them up unto the unity of faith andknowledge, and to the perfect manhood of Christ.

The Greek and Roman churches gradually departed from the apostolicpolity and excluded not only the laity, but also the lower clergy fromall participation in the legislative councils.

The conference of Jerusalem, though not a binding precedent, is asignificant example, giving the apostolic sanction to the synodical formof government, in which all classes of the Christian community arerepresented in the management of public affairs and in settlingcontroversies respecting faith and discipline. The decree which itpassed and the pastoral letter which it sent, are the first in the longline of decrees and canons and encyclicals which issued fromecclesiastical authorities. But it is significant that this firstdecree, though adopted undoubtedly under the guidance of the HolySpirit, and wisely adapted to the times and circumstances of the mixedchurches of Jewish and Gentile converts, was after all merely "atemporary expedient for a temporary emergency," and cannot be quoted asa precedent for infallible decrees of permanent force. The spirit offraternal concession and harmony which dictated the Jerusalemcompromise, is more important than the letter of the decree itself. Thekingdom of Christ is not a dispensation of law, but of spirit and oflife.

Notes.

I. There is an interesting difference of reading in Acts15:23 (see the critical editions), but it does not affect thecomposition of the conference, at least as far as the elders areconcerned. The textus receptus reads: oiJ ajpovstoloi, kai; oiJpresbuvteroi, kai; oiJ ajdelfoiv (a’, H, L, P, Syr., etc.), "Theapostles, and the elders, and the brethren send greeting untothe brethren," etc. So the E. V., except that it omits the articletwice. The Revised V., following the better attested reading: oiJajpovstoloi, kai; oiv presbuvteroi ajdelfoiv, renders in the text: "Theapostles, and the elders, brethren," and in the margin: "The apostlesand the elder brethren" (omitting the comma). But it may also betranslated: "The apostles, and brother-elders," considering that Peteraddresses the elders as sumpresbuvtero", or "fellow-elder" (1 Pet. 5:1).The textus rec. agrees better with Acts 15:22, and the omission of kai;oiJ may possibly have arisen from a desire to conform the text to thelater practice which excluded the laity from synods, but it is stronglysupported by aBellarmin and other Roman Catholic and certain Episcopaldivines get over the fact of the participation of the elders andbrethren in a legislative council by allowing the elders and brethrensimply a silent consent. So Becker (as quoted by Bishop Jacobson, inSpeaker’s Commentary on Acts 15:22):, "The apostles join the elders andbrethren with themselves ... not to allow them equal authority, butmerely to express their concurrence." Very different is the view of Dr.Plumptre on Acts 15:22: "The latter words [’with the whole church’] areimportant as showing the position occupied by the laity. If theyconcurred in the latter, it must have been submitted to their approval,and the right to approve involves the power to reject and probably tomodify." Bishop Cotterill (Genesis of the Church, p. 379)expresses the same view. "It was manifestly," he says, "a free council,and not a mere private meeting of some office-bearers. It was in factmuch what the Agora was in archaic times, as described inHomer: in which the council of the nobles governed the decisions, butthe people were present and freely expressed their opinion. And it mustbe remembered that the power of free speech in the councils of thechurch is the true test of the character of these assemblies. Freediscussion, and arbitrary government, either by one person or by aprivileged class, have been found, in all ages and under all polities,to be incompatible with each other. Again, not only were the multitudepresent, but we are expressly told that the whole church concurred inthe decision and in the action taken upon it."

  1. The authority of the Jerusalem conference as a precedentfor regular legislative councils and synods has been often overrated. Onthe other hand, Canon Farrar (Life and Work of St. Paul, I.431) greatly underrates it when he says: "It is only by an unwarrantableextension of terms that the meeting of the church of Jerusalem can becalled a ’council,’ and the word connotes a totally different order ofconceptions to those that were prevalent at that early time. Theso-called Council of Jerusalem in no way resembled the General Councilsof the Church, either in its history, its constitution, or its object.It was not a convention of ordained delegates, but a meeting of theentire church of Jerusalem to receive a deputation from the church ofAntioch. Even Paul and Barnabas seem to have had no vote in thedecision, though the votes of a promiscuous body could certainly not bemore enlightened than theirs, nor was their allegiance due in any way toJames. The church of Jerusalem might out of respect be consulted, but ithad no claim to superiority, no abstract prerogative to bind itsdecisions on the free church of God. The ’decree’ of the ’council’ waslittle more than the wise recommendation of a single synod, addressed toa particular district, and possessing only a temporary validity. It was,in fact, a local concordat. Little or no attention has beenpaid by the universal church to two of its restrictions; a third, notmany years after, was twice discussed and settled by Paul, on the samegeneral principles, but with a by no means identical conclusion. Theconcession which it made to the Gentiles, in not insisting on thenecessity of circumcision, was equally treated as a dead letter by theJudaizing party, and cost Paul the severest battle of his lifetime tomaintain. If this circular letter is to be regarded as a binding andfinal decree, and if the meeting of a single church, not by delegates,but in the person of all its members, is to be regarded as a council,never was the decision of a council less appealed to, and never was adecree regarded as so entire inoperative alike by those who repudiatedthe validity of its concessions, and by those who discussed, as thoughthey were still an open question, no less than three of its fourrestrictions."

§ 65. The Church and theKingdom of Christ.

Thus the apostolic church appears as a free, independent, andcomplete organism, a system of supernatural, divine life in a humanbody. It contains in itself all the offices and energies required forits purposes. It produces the supply of its outward wants from its ownfree spirit. It is a self-supporting and self-governing institution,within the state, but not of the state. Of a union with the state,either in the way of hierarchical supremacy or of Erastiansubordination, the first three centuries afford no trace. The apostleshonor the civil authority as a divine institution for the protection oflife and property, for the reward of the good and the punishment of theevil-doer; and they enjoin, even under the reign of a Claudius and aNero, strict obedience to it in all civil concerns; as, indeed, theirheavenly Master himself submitted in temporal matters to Herod and toPilate, and rendered unto Caesar the things that were Caesar’s. But intheir spiritual calling they allowed nothing to be prescribed orforbidden to them by the authorities of the state. Their principle was,to "obey God rather than men." For this principle, for their allegianceto the King of kings, they were always ready to suffer imprisonment,insult, persecution, and death, but never to resort to carnal weapons,or stir up rebellion and revolution. "The weapons of our warfare," saysPaul, "are not carnal, but mighty through God." Martyrdom is a farnobler heroism than resistance with fire and sword, and leads withgreater certainty at last to a thorough and permanent victory.

The apostolic church, as to its membership, was not free fromimpurities, the after-workings of Judaism and heathenism and the naturalman. But in virtue of an inherent authority it exercised rigiddiscipline, and thus steadily asserted its dignity and holiness. It wasnot perfect; but it earnestly strove after the perfection of manhood inChrist, and longed and hoped for the reappearance of the Lord in glory,to the exaltation of his people. It was as yet not actually universal,but a little flock compared with the hostile hosts of the heathen andJewish world; yet it carried in itself the principle of truecatholicity, the power and pledge of its victory over all otherreligions, and its final prevalence among all nations of the earth andin all classes of society.

Paul defines the church as the body of Jesus Christ.(51) He thusrepresents it as an organic living system of various members, powers,and functions, and at the same time as the abode of Christ and the organof his redeeming and sanctifying influence upon the world. Christ is, inone view, the ruling head, in another the all-pervading soul, of thisbody. Christ without the church were a head without a body, a fountainwithout a stream, a king without subjects, a captain without soldiers, abridegroom without a bride. The church without Christ were a bodywithout soul or spirit—a lifeless corpse. The church lives only asChrist lives and moves and works in her. At every moment of herexistence she is dependent on him, as the body on the soul, or thebranches on the vine. But on his part he perpetually bestows upon herhis heavenly gifts and supernatural powers, continually reveals himselfin her, and uses her as his organ for the spread of his kingdom and thechristianizing of the world, till all principalities and powers shallyield free obedience to him, and adore him as the eternal Prophet,Priest, and King of the regenerate race. This work must be a gradualprocess of history. The idea of a body, and of all organic life,includes that of development, of expansion and consolidation. And hencethe same Paul speaks also of the growth and edification of the body ofChrist, "till we all attain unto the unity of the faith, and of theknowledge of the Son of God, unto a full-grown man, unto the measure ofthe stature of the fulness of Christ."(52)

This sublime idea of the church, as developed in the First Epistle tothe Corinthians, and especially in the Epistle to the Ephesians, whenPaul was a prisoner chained to a heathen soldier, soars high above theactual condition of the little flocks of peasants, freedmen, slaves, andlowly, uncultured people that composed the apostolic congregations. Ithas no parallel in the social ideals of ancient philosophers andstatesmen. It can only be traced to divine inspiration.

We must not confound this lofty conception of the church as the bodyof Christ with any particular ecclesiastical organization, which at bestis only a part of the whole, and an imperfect approach to the ideal. Normust we identify it with the still higher idea of the kingdom of God orthe kingdom of heaven. A vast amount of presumption, bigotry, andintolerance has grown out of such confusion. It is remarkable thatChrist speaks only once of the church in the organic or universalsense.(53) But be very often speaks of the kingdom, and nearly all hisparables illustrate this grand idea. The two conceptions are closelyrelated, yet distinct. In many passages we could not possibly substitutethe one for the other without manifest impropriety.(54) The church isexternal, visible, manifold, temporal; the kingdom of heaven isinternal, spiritual, one, and everlasting. The kingdom is older and morecomprehensive; it embraces all the true children of God on earth and inheaven, before Christ and after Christ, inside and outside of thechurches and sects. The historical church with its various ramificationsis a paedagogic institution or training-school for the kingdom ofheaven, and will pass away as to its outward form when its mission isfulfilled. The kingdom has come in Christ, is continually coming, andwill finally come in its full grown strength and beauty when the Kingwill visibly appear in his glory.

The coming of this kingdom in and through the visible churches, withvarying conflicts and victories, is the proper object of church history.It is a slow, but sure and steady progress, with many obstructions,delays, circuitous turns and windings, but constant manifestations ofthe presence of him who sits at the helm of the ship and directs itthrough rain, storm, and sunshine to the harbor of the other and betterworld.

Interpr.，该词条，另参ἐπισκοπή* 和ἐπισκοπέω*两词条）。在埃及，它用来称呼庙宇的官员；在希腊，则泛指监督者或监护人，或指市政官员及财政官员。在雅典，派往殖民地和属邦进行管理的专员称为ἐπίσκοποι*。斯巴达人派出的ἐπιμεληταί*也担任同样的职务。这一用语不仅用于常任官员，也用于治理机构本身，或该机构下设的委员会。阴性词ἐπισκοπή*并非古典用语，而是从《七十士译本》进入希腊文新约（《使徒行传》1:20；《提摩太前书》3:1）及教父用语中，意为主教的工作或职分（inspectio,visitatio，监察、巡视）。见莱特福特(Lightfoot)，《腓立比书》(Philippians)，第93页及后；格布哈特与哈纳克(Gebhardt and Harnack)，Patr. I. 42

    , 47). Noch im zweitenJahrh. findet man die Bischöfe auch Gr. presbuteroi genannt,nicht aber umgekeht. Sofort fixirt sich dann der Sprachgebrauch: der B.ist der Vorsteher derπαροικία*,διοίκησις*, alsNachfolger der Apostel; ihm unterstehen Volk und Geistlichkeit; ihmwohnt die Fülle der priesterlichen Gewaltinne.”（“最初，这两个术语往往以相同的意义使用〔《使徒行传》20:17、28；《提多书》1:5；革利免，《致哥林多人书》I.42、44、47〕。即使到了第二世纪，仍可见主教也被称作希腊文的presbuteroi，但反过来却不然。随后用语便固定下来：主教作为使徒的继承人，是教区的领袖；信众和教牧都隶属于他；他具有完备的祭司权柄。”）然而，祭司观念并非与主教职的升高同时出现，而是在稍后才进入教会。↩︎

L’absorption del’Eglise par les ’presbyteri’est un fait accompliavant la fin du premier. Dans l’èpître de Clément Romain, etc.,ce n’est pas encore l’épiscopat, c’est le presbytérat qui est en cause.On n’y trouve pas trace d’un ’presbyteros’’supérieur aux autres etdevant détrôner les autres. Mais l’auteur proclame hautement que lepresbytérat, to clergé, est antérieur aupeuple.”（“主教制的创立是第二世纪的工作。教会被‘长老们’吸纳，在第一世纪结束以前已成事实。在罗马的革利免书信等文献中，所涉及的还不是主教职，而是长老职。其中找不到任何迹象，表明有一个‘长老’高于其他人，并将取代其他人的地位。但作者大声宣告，长老职，也就是教牧阶层，先于信众而存在。”）另比较勒南的《圣保罗》(SaintPaul)，第238页及下页，以及《基督教会》(L’EgliseChrétienne)，第VI章，第85页及后。因此，这一问题可以视为在学者中已有定论。同时，持平而论，也应承认：长老权力向主教集中的趋势，可以追溯到使徒时期的末叶。↩︎

  27. 《使徒行传》14:23；《提多书》1:5；《提摩太前书》5:22；4:14；《提摩太后书》1:6。关于教牧的选举、按立和供养，见我的《使徒教会史》(Hist.Ap. Ch.)，第500–506页。↩︎

  28. 《使徒行传》11:30；14:23；15:2、4、6、23；16:4；20:17、28；21:18；《腓立比书》1:1；《提摩太前书》4:14；《雅各书》5:14；《彼得前书》5:1。↩︎

  29. 《提摩太前书》5:17：“那善于管理教会的长老（οἱκαλῶς προεστῶτες*πρεσβύτεροι*），当以为配受加倍的敬奉（διπλῆςτιμῆς*）；那劳苦传道教导人的（ἐνλόγῳ καὶ*διδασκαλίᾳ*/），更当如此。”有些释经家强调καλῶς*；有些把“加倍的敬奉”理解为更高的等级与地位，另一些理解为更优厚的报酬，还有一些认为两者兼而有之。↩︎

  30. 《提摩太前书》3:2：“作监督的，必须……善于教导（διδακτικόν*）。”《提多书》1:9、《使徒行传》20:28和《希伯来书》13:17也含有同样的意思。莱特福特的看法是正确的（第192页）：“虽然治理可能是对这一职分最初的理解，但教导的工作必定从一开始就落在长老身上，并且随着时间推移而愈加突出。”关于教导长老和治理长老的问题，除其他论著外，可比较彼得·科林·坎贝尔(Peter Colin Campbell) 的《治理长老职理论》(The Theory of RulingEldership)（爱丁堡与伦敦，1866年），以及 R. D. 希区柯克博士 (R. D.Hitchcock) 和 E. F. 哈特菲尔德博士 (E. F.Hatfield)（两人均属长老会）发表于1868年4月和10月《美国长老会评论》(AmericanPresbyterian Review)的两篇精辟文章。这些作者都不赞同加尔文对《提摩太前书》5:17的解释，即该节教导有两类长老：（1）兼任教导和治理的；（2）只任治理的。不过，坎贝尔根据《哥林多前书》12:28、《罗马书》12:8和《使徒行传》15:22、25，为他所谓的“平信徒陪议员”(LayAssessors)辩护。希区柯克博士认为，原始教会的长老既获授权，也被期望兼任教导和治理。哈特菲尔德博士则力图证明，基督教会的长老与犹太人的长老一样，只应负责治理；教导的职分已交托给使徒、传福音者和其他宣教士。最后这种看法也是南卡罗来纳的桑韦尔博士(Thornwell) 在论《治理长老》(Ruling Elders)时所持的看法；才华卓越的牛津学者、副院长哈奇也以修正的形式提倡此说（前引书〔l.c.〕，第III讲，第35页及后，以及史密斯与奇瑟姆所编著作中的“祭司”一文，II，第1700页）。他认为，基督教会的长老与犹太人的长老一样，最初主要是负责纪律而非崇拜的职员；至于教导的才干和信仰的纯正，则完全从属于治理者所必需的道德品质。他还指出（第1707页），革利免和伊格那丢(Ignatius)都没有在谈到教导时提及长老，而教导乃是一项委派给较有智慧的长老的职能。↩︎

  31. 关于《启示录》中使者的其他解释：1.天上的使者，各教会的守护天使。奥利金 (Origen)、哲罗姆 (Jerome)、德韦特(De Wette)、阿尔福德 (Alford)、莱特福特主教 (Bishop Lightfoot)。2.教会的代表或书记，相当于会堂的 shelichai。维特林加(Vitringa)、约翰·莱特福特 (John Lightfoot)、本格尔 (Bengel)、维纳(Winer)。3. 教会的象征性人格化。阿瑞塔斯 (Arethas)、萨尔马修斯(Salmasius)。4. 严格意义上的主教。见我的《使徒教会史》(Hist. of theAp Ch.)，第537页及后。↩︎

  32. 罗特 (Rothe)、本生 (Bunsen)、蒂尔施 (Thiersch)和莱特福特主教把主教制的设立追溯到小亚细亚的外邦人教会，并主张在公元70至100年这段神秘的时期内，尚存于世的使徒约翰曾给予这一制度某种认可。尼安德(Neander)、鲍尔 (Baur) 和里奇尔 (Ritschl)反对罗特的理论（该理论当时曾在学术界引起相当大的轰动）。罗特并非主教制的信奉者，却认为主教制在古代教会中是一种暂时的历史必然。↩︎

  33. 见 § 27，第264页及后。↩︎

  34. 《使徒行传》21:18；比较11:30；12:17；以及《使徒行传》第15章。↩︎

  35. διάκονος*、diaconus（执事），后来的用法也有διάκων*、diacones（见居普良的著作和教会会议的决议）。↩︎

  36. 莱特福特 (Lightfoot)（Hor.Hebr.，释《使徒行传》6:3）说：“Tralatum erat officiumDiaconatus ... in Ecclesiam Evangelicam ex Judaica. Erant enimin unaquaque Synagoga ג׳פרנסין*, tres Diaconi quibus incubuitista cura(pauperum).”（“执事职分……是从犹太教会传入福音教会的。因为每一座会堂都有三名执事，负责这项照顾穷人的事务。”）↩︎

  37. 据哥尼流 (Cornelius)的一封信，251年罗马教会有四十六名长老，却只有七名执事，见优西比乌(Eusebius)，《教会史》(H. E.)，VI.43。其余职缺由副执事充任。在君士坦丁堡 (Constantinople)，查士丁尼(Justinian) 批准任命一百名执事。↩︎

  38. 《使徒行传》6:3；《提摩太前书》8:8及下。↩︎

  39. ἡδιάκονος*，后来也称διακόνισσα*、diaconissa,diacona（女执事）。↩︎

  40. 《罗马书》16:1，其中称非比为 (ἡ)διάκονος τῆς ἐνΚεγχρεαῖς*。比较16:3、6、12。关于《提摩太前书》3:11；5:9–15所提到的寡妇是否为女执事的问题，见我的《使徒教会史》(Hist.of the Ap. Ch.)，第536页。↩︎

  41. 在罗马教会中，从事慈善工作的修女会已取代了各堂会的女执事；摩拉维亚弟兄会(Moravians)、路德宗、圣公会及其他教会中，也设立了类似的机构（但不立独身誓愿）。罗马天主教的仁爱修女会(Sisters of Charity)，以及凯泽斯韦特 (Kaiserswerth)的福音派女执事会，尤其值得尊崇。见沙弗 (Schaff)《宗教百科全书》(Rel.Cyclop.)，第I卷（1882年），第613页及后，Deacon,Deaconess（执事、女执事）及Deaconesses（女执事团体）条。↩︎

  42. 比较 § 50，第450页。↩︎

  43. 《哥林多前书》5:5。↩︎

  44. 比较《马太福音》18:15–18；《提多书》3:10；《哥林多前书》5:5。↩︎

  45. 《马太福音》18:17。“告诉教会”这句话，不能像《马太福音》16:18中的ἐκκλησία*那样，指普世教会。↩︎

  46. 《使徒行传》5:1–10。↩︎

  47. 《哥林多前书》5:1及下。↩︎

  48. 《哥林多后书》2:5–10。↩︎

  49. 《使徒行传》第15章，以及《加拉太书》第2章。↩︎

  50. 《使徒行传》15:6、12、22、23。见附注。↩︎

  51. 《罗马书》12:5；《哥林多前书》6:15；10:17；12:27；《以弗所书》1:23；4:12；5:23、30；《歌罗西书》1:18、24；2:17。↩︎

  52. 《以弗所书》4:13。↩︎

  53. 《马太福音》16:18。在他谈到ἐκκλησία*的另一处经文，即《马太福音》18:17中，这个词指一个地方会众（一座会堂），正如《使徒行传》和各书信中许多经文的用法一样。我们使用“教会”一词时，另有两种含义，在新约中从未出现，因为当时尚无这些事物，即指教会建筑和宗派（如罗马教会、英国圣公会、路德宗教会）。↩︎

  54. 我们不能说：“愿你的教会降临”（《马太福音》6:9）；“教会正是属于这样的人（小孩子）”（《马可福音》10:14）；“教会来到不是眼所能见的”（《路加福音》17:21）；“淫乱的等等……都不能承受教会”（《哥林多前书》6:10）；“教会不在乎吃喝，只在乎公义、和平并圣灵中的喜乐”（《罗马书》15:17）。另一方面，把上帝的国称为“基督的身体”或“羔羊的新妇”，也不恰当。↩︎

entry.title: 《基督教会史》·第一卷·第九章 使徒时期的敬拜
entry.content:
Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The ChristianChurch

第九章　使徒时期的敬拜

目录

§ 51. 会堂

§ 52. 基督徒的敬拜

§ 53. 敬拜的各个部分

§ 54. 洗礼

§ 55. 圣餐

§ 56. 神圣的场所

§ 57. 神圣的时日——主日

参考文献

Th. 哈纳克 (ThHarnack)：《使徒时期及古代大公教会时期的基督徒会众敬拜》(Derchristliche Gemeindegottesdienst im Apost. und altkathol.Zeitalter)。埃尔朗根(Erlangen)，1854年。同作者：《实践神学》(Prakt.Theol.)，第I卷，1877年。

P. 普罗布斯特 (P.Probst，罗马天主教徒)：《最初三个世纪的礼仪》(Liturgie der dreiersten Jahrhunderte)。图宾根 (Tüb.)，1870年。

W. L. 福尔茨 (W. L. Volz)：《基督教敬拜的起源》(Anfänge deschristl. Gottesdienstes)，载《研究与评论》(Stud. undKrit.)，1872年。

H. 雅各比 (H. Jacoby)：《使徒时期敬拜的构成要素》(Dieconstitutiven Factoren des Apost.Gottesdienstes)，载《德国神学年鉴》(Jahrb. für deutscheTheol.)，1873年。

C. 魏茨泽克 (C. Weizsäcker)：《最早基督徒会众的聚会》(DieVersammlungen der ältestenChristengemeinden)，1876年；及《使徒时期》(Das Apost.Zeitalter)，1886年，第566页及后。

Th. 察恩 (Th Zahn)：《古代教会的主日史》(Gesch. des Sonntags inder alten Kirche)。汉诺威 (Hann.)，1878年。

沙弗 (Schaff)：《使徒教会史》(Hist. of the Apost.Ch.)，第545–586页。

参看第十章的参考文献，以及第II卷第184页关于《十二使徒遗训》(Didache)的参考文献。

§ 51. 会堂

坎佩格·维特林加 (Campeg.Vitringa，1722年卒于弗拉讷克)：《古代会堂三卷》(De Synagoga Veterelibri tres.)。弗拉讷克(Franeker)，1696年，2卷（另有魏森费尔斯版，1726年）。这是一部权威著作，充满圣经及拉比学问。J.L. 伯纳德 (J. L. Bernard) 的节译本题为《会堂与教会》(The Synagogueand the Church)。伦敦，1842年。

C. 博尔尼提乌斯 (C. Bornitius)：《古代希伯来人的会堂》(DeSynagogis veterum Hebraeorum)。维滕贝格(Vitemb.)，1650年。亦收入乌戈利努斯(Ugolinus)：《神圣古物宝库》(Thesaurus Antiquitatumsacrarum)（威尼斯〔Venet.〕，1744–69年），第XXI卷，第495–539页。

Ant. Th. 哈特曼 (Ant. Th. Hartmann)：《旧约与新约的紧密联系》(Dieenge Verbindung des A. Testamenes mit demNeuen)。汉堡，1831年（第225–376页）。

宗茨 (Zunz，犹太拉比)：《犹太人的敬拜讲论》(Diegottesdienstlichen Vorträge der Juden)。柏林，1832年。

约斯特 (Jost)、赫茨费尔德 (Herzfeld) 和米尔曼 (Milman)各自所著的《犹太人史》(Histories of the Jews)。

豪斯拉特 (Hausrath) 所著《新约时代史》(Histories of N. T.Times)（第2版，第I卷，第73页及后），以及许勒尔 (Schürer)的同类著作（第463–475页，及该处所列文献）。

“会堂”条（“Synag.”）：金斯伯格 (Ginsburg)撰，载“基托”(Kitto)；普伦普特里 (Plumptre)撰，载“史密斯”(Smith)（附哈克特〔Hackett〕增补，美版第IV卷，第3133页）；莱勒尔(Leyrer)撰，载“赫尔佐格”(Herzog)（初版，第XV卷，第299页）；克诺伊克尔(Kneuker) 撰，载“申克尔”(Schenkel)（第V卷，第443页）。

正如基督教会在历史上以犹太教会为基础，基督徒的敬拜和会众组织也以会堂的敬拜和组织为基础；不了解会堂，就无法充分理解这些。

会堂过去是、如今仍是一个具有巨大保守力量的制度。正如耶路撒冷的圣殿是犹太人民族生活的中心，会堂则是他们地方宗教生活和社会生活的中心。它既是学校，也是教会，是这个独特民族一切独有事物的培育所和守护者。它大概起源于被掳及以斯拉的时代。1到了基督和使徒的时代，它的组织已十分完备，并为他们所用，成为公开施教的基地。2圣殿被毁后，它仍存留下来，延续至今，其基本特征未变，仍是犹太民族性与宗教的主要培育所和保障。3

“会堂”一词（如同我们所用的“教会”一词），首先指会众，继而也指会众聚集进行公共敬拜的建筑。4每一个城镇，无论多么微小，都有一所会堂，或至少有一处祷告的地方，设在私人住宅中或露天之处（通常靠近河边或海滨，为的是便于行洁净的礼）。十个男子就足以组成一个宗教聚会。“因为从古以来，摩西的书在各城有人传讲，每逢安息日，在会堂里诵读。”5建造会堂被视为一项虔诚而有益于公众的善工。6在亚历山大 (Alexandria)和罗马这样的大城市，会堂为数众多；耶路撒冷约有四百所，供各宗派及来自不同国家、讲希腊语的犹太人使用。7

  1. 建筑是一座朴素的长方形大厅，没有特殊的建筑风格，内部布置与会幕和圣殿略为相似。里面设有长凳，较高的座位（“首位”）留给长老和较富裕的成员；8另有读经台或讲台，以及存放圣卷的木柜或壁橱（称为“Copheret”，即施恩座，又称“Aaron”）。最后这一项相当于会幕和圣殿中的至圣所。堂内仿照圣殿的灯光，点着一盏长明的圣灯，象征神的律法；不过，《塔木德》(Talmud)并未提及此事。其他灯盏则由虔诚的敬拜者在安息日开始时（星期五晚上）带来。会堂门旁如同圣殿一样，设有奉献箱，一个为耶路撒冷的穷人募款，另一个供本地慈善之用。保罗仿效这一榜样，为耶路撒冷贫穷的基督徒募集捐款。

会堂没有艺术装饰（植物图案除外）；因为第二条诫命严格禁止一切神的形像，视之为偶像崇拜。在这一点上，如同在其他许多方面一样，伊斯兰教清真寺以其严拒偶像的朴素风格，成为会堂的翻版。会堂建在邻近地区最高的地方，任何房屋都不许高过它。若没有居高临下的地势，就从屋顶竖起一根高杆，使它显而易见。9

  1. 组织——每所会堂有一位主管，10若干地位平等的长老 (Zekenim)，11一位诵读员和一位传译员，12一位或数位称为“使者”(Sheliach) 的代表或书记，13以及一位负责较卑微杂务的堂役 (Chazzan)。14另有执事 (Gabaezedaka)，负责募集金钱和农产品形式的赈济品。十位或更多有闲暇的富人，称为Batlanim，在每次礼拜中代表会众。每所会堂构成一个独立的共和体，但与其他会堂保持经常的通信联系。它也是民事和宗教法庭，有权将犯过者逐出会堂并施以鞭打。15

  2. 敬拜——形式简单，但时间颇长，包含敬虔、教导和礼仪三种要素。内容包括祷告、歌唱、诵读和讲解圣经，以及割礼和洁净礼。流血的献祭仅限于圣殿，并随着圣殿的毁灭而终止；它们在十字架上那永远的献祭中得了成全。祷文和诗歌主要取自《诗篇》；《诗篇》可称为第一部礼仪书和赞美诗集。

开始的祷告称为 Shema 或 KeriathShema，包括两段开头的祝颂，诵读十诫（后来取消），以及《摩西五经》中的若干段落，即《申命记》6:4–9；11:13–21；《民数记》15:37–41。接着是十八段祷告和祝颂(Berachoth)。其中一段如下：“求你将平安、幸福、福分、恩典、怜悯和慈悲赐给我们，也赐给你的百姓以色列全家。我们的父啊，求你以你脸上的光一同赐福我们众人，因为，主我们的神啊，你曾在你脸上的光中，赐给我们生命的律法、慈爱、公义、福分、怜悯、生命与平安。愿你乐意时时刻刻赐平安给你的百姓以色列。主啊，你是应当称颂的，你以平安赐福给你的百姓以色列。”《米示拿》(Mishna)将这些祝颂追溯到大公会 (Great Synagogue)的一百二十位长老。它们无疑是逐渐形成的，有些源自马加比 (Maccabean)抗争时期，有些源自罗马掌权时期。祷告由诵读员献上，会众回应“阿们”。这一习俗传入了基督教会。16

敬拜中教导和讲道的部分以希伯来圣经为基础。先用原文诵读一段律法（称为parasha）17和一段先知书（haphthara），18然后用通行的亚兰语或希腊语加以意译，或作注解和讲论（midrash）。最后以祝福和会众的“阿们”结束礼拜。

由于在耶路撒冷以外并无正式的祭司职分，任何成年的犹太人都可以起来诵读经课、献上祷告，并向会众讲话。耶稣和使徒利用这一民主的权利传讲福音，宣告福音是律法和先知的应验。19这种礼拜具有浓厚的教导成分，与异教一切敬拜形式迥然不同，其结果是使各阶层的犹太人，甚至婢女，都熟悉自己的宗教，并使他们远高于异教徒。同时，它也吸引了渴望更纯洁、更属灵敬拜的归信者。

举行公共礼拜的日子是安息日、星期一和星期四；祷告的时辰是第三时（上午9时）、第六时（正午）和第九时（下午3时）。20

男女之间以矮墙或屏障隔开，男子在一边，女子在另一边，正如今日东方（以及欧洲某些地区）仍然实行的那样。祷告时，众人站立，面向耶路撒冷。

§ 52. 基督徒的敬拜

基督徒的敬拜，或称cultus，是奉基督的名向上帝献上的公共崇拜；是信徒作为会众，与他们天上的元首相交的庆典，为要荣耀主，并促进和享受属灵的生命。它首先旨在激发教会自身的虔敬并造就教会，同时也带有宣教的性质，吸引外面的世界。五旬节那天，基督徒的敬拜首次以其独特的面貌出现，情形正是如此。

正如我们的主在少年及成年时亲自在会堂和圣殿中敬拜，他早期的门徒只要还被容纳，也同样如此。就连保罗也曾在大马士革(Damascus)、塞浦路斯 (Cyprus)、彼西底的安提阿 (Antioch inPisidia)、暗妃坡里 (Amphipolis)、庇哩亚 (Beraeea)、雅典 (Athens)、哥林多(Corinth)、以弗所 (Ephesus)的会堂里传讲基督。他“每逢安息日，在会堂里与犹太人辩论”，会堂为他提供了讲台和听众。

犹太基督徒，至少在巴勒斯坦(Palestine)，尽可能严守祖先那些古老而可敬的敬拜形式；这些形式确实是神所设立的，也是基督徒敬拜的生动预表。据我们所知，他们谨慎遵守安息日、犹太人每年的节期、每日祷告的时辰，以及整套摩西礼仪；此外，他们还庆祝基督徒的主日、主的死与复活，并举行圣餐。但这种联合因犹太人的顽固反对而逐渐削弱，最终随着圣殿的毁灭而完全破裂，只有伊便尼派(Ebionites) 和拿撒勒派 (Nazarenes) 仍予保留。

在保罗所建立的外邦基督徒会众中，敬拜从起初就采取了较为独立的形式。旧约礼拜的基本要素固然被移植过来，却脱去了民族和律法的性质，并由福音的精神加以转化。于是，犹太人的安息日转为基督徒的主日；具有预表意义的逾越节和五旬节，成为纪念基督受死与复活，以及圣灵浇灌的节期；流血的献祭，让位于对基督在十字架上那一次、全然充足而永远的献祭的感恩纪念和领受，也让位于个人献上的祷告、代求，以及全然献身于救赎主的事奉；在那非人手所造的圣殿的废墟上，兴起了以心灵和诚实向无所不在的上帝献上的永不止息的敬拜。21早在使徒时期结束时，这种更自由、更属灵的基督教敬拜，无疑已几乎普遍通行；然而，许多犹太教的成分，尤其在东方教会中，仍存留至今。

§ 53. 敬拜的各个部分

使徒时期公共敬拜的各个部分如下：

  1. 福音的宣讲。在最初时期，这大多采取向尚未归信者传道的形式；也就是简明而生动地陈述耶稣生平的主要事实，并切实劝勉人悔改归信。被钉十字架并已复活的基督是光辉的中心，从那里发出使人成圣的光，照耀人生的一切关系。这种宣讲从充盈的心中涌流出来，直达人心；它发自内在的生命，也在乐于领受的听众里面点燃生命——一种新的、属神的生命。这是最纯正意义上的奋兴布道。《使徒行传》保存了彼得和保罗所作的几篇见证，作为这种原始基督教见证的实例。

从广义上说，使徒书信也可以视为讲道，不过它们是写给信徒的，旨在滋养已经栽植的基督徒生命。

  1. 诵读旧约经文，22并作切合实际的讲解和应用；这是从犹太会堂移入基督教会的。23后来又适时加入了新约选读经文，也就是正典福音书和使徒书信的经文；这些书信大多是写给整个会众的，原本就打算供公开使用。24使徒去世以后，他们的著作代替了他们口头的教导和劝勉，对教会的重要性倍增，在敬拜中的使用也远比旧约频繁。

  2. 祷告，包括祈求、代求和感恩等各种形式。这同样承袭自犹太教，事实上，甚至一切异教也都以祷告为基本要素；但如今，人开始奉耶稣的名，以儿女般的信赖，向已经与人和好的父祈祷，为各阶层、各处境的人，甚至为仇敌和逼迫者祷告。最初的基督徒在公共和私人生活中，每逢重要行动，都伴以这一神圣礼仪；保罗也劝勉读者要“不住地祷告”。在庄严的场合，他们禁食祷告，以帮助自己专心敬虔，虽然新约没有任何地方直接吩咐人禁食。25他们照着圣灵的感动，按具体的需要和处境，自由地从心里祷告。《使徒行传》第四章就有一个实例。没有任何迹象表明当时存在一种统一而排他的礼拜仪式；这样的仪式与使徒教会的活力和自由是不相容的。同时，根据犹太人的惯例、主对他所赐祷告范本的指示、26最初基督徒之间强烈的团契意识，以及古代教会的礼仪精神，我们可以确实推知，他们经常使用诗篇和简短的祷文，如主祷文；因为若无使徒时期及使徒后时期的某些先例，这种礼仪精神就不可能在东西方如此普遍地盛行。最古老的形式，是《十二使徒遗训》(Didache)中的圣餐祷文，以及《革利免一书》中为执政者所作的祈求；后者与尼禄和图密善残酷的敌意，构成了极其美好的对照。27

  3. 歌唱，这是祷告的一种形式，披着诗歌的节庆盛装，运用受默感而发的崇高语言，使会众的虔敬达到最高境界，并使他们得以参与众圣徒在天上的和声。这种形式随着旧约诗篇——那些取之不尽的属灵经历、造就和安慰的宝库——直接从圣殿和会堂进入基督教会。主自己在设立圣餐时，率先将唱诗引入新约，28保罗也明确吩咐信徒唱“诗章、颂词、灵歌”，作为彼此造就的途径。29然而，对于这份承自往昔的宝贵遗产，直到如今，人们才在新约启示的光照下首次充分认识其价值；教会又以起初爱心的热忱，加上原创而具有鲜明基督教特色的诗章、颂歌、颂荣和祝福，为随后各世纪的圣诗和圣乐提供了极其丰富的素材。例如，救主降生时天军的歌唱；30 西面的“Nuncdimittis”（《西面颂》）；31童贞女马利亚的“Magnificat”（《尊主颂》）；32撒迦利亚的“Benedictus”（《撒迦利亚颂》）；33彼得蒙神迹拯救后的感恩；34使徒教会中的说方言，无论是歌唱还是祷告，总是使用热忱洋溢的崇高语言；散见于各书信的颂歌片段；35以及《启示录》中抒情和礼仪性的段落、颂荣与应答歌。36

  4. 信仰告白。上述一切敬拜行为，也都是信心的行为。第一个明确的信仰告白，是彼得见证耶稣是基督，是永生神的儿子。其次是三一的洗礼公式。由此逐渐产生了所谓的《使徒信经》(Apostles’Creed)，其结构同样以三一为纲，却将关于基督的告白置于中心，并给予最大的篇幅。它现今的形式虽不能追溯至第四世纪以前，在第二、第三世纪也见于长短不一的各种形式，但其实质完全源于使徒，并且无与伦比地概括了三一上帝的启示中，从创造世界到身体复活的主要事实；其表达又人人可以理解，极其适合公共敬拜和教理问答之用。我们将在第二时期更详尽地论及它。

  5. 最后是圣礼的施行，也就是基督所设立的神圣礼仪；藉着适当的象征和可见的记号，属灵的恩赐与不可见的恩典得以表明、印证，并施予那些配领受的人。

洗礼和圣餐这两项圣礼，是旧约割礼和逾越节所预表的实体，由基督设立，作为新约恩典的有效记号、凭据和施恩途径。两者之间的关系，犹如重生与成圣，或基督徒生命的开始与成长。新约提及的其他宗教礼仪，如坚振礼和按立礼，在尊荣上不能与圣礼并列，因为它们并非基督所命定的。

  1. 洗礼的观念。洗礼由基督在升天前不久庄严设立，吩咐人奉父、子、圣灵的名施行。它取代了割礼，作为教会成员身份的记号和印证。它是作基督门徒的外在标志，也是进入恩典之约的入门礼。它是悔改（归信）、罪得赦免，以及靠圣灵大能重生的圣礼。37按其本质，洗礼只应领受一次。它使悔改的罪人加入有形教会，使他有权享有这一团契的一切特权，也使他有义务履行其中的一切责任。若缺少悔改与信心的条件，祝福就会变为咒诅（如同圣餐和圣道的宣讲一样）；上帝原定作为叫人活的香气，便因人的不忠而成为叫人死的死气。

有人根据《约翰福音》3:5和《马可福音》16:16，推论洗礼是得救所必需的；然而，我们固然受上帝所定规例的约束，上帝自己却是自由的，可以随己意拯救任何人，也可以使用任何途径施行拯救。教会始终坚持这一原则：单单缺少圣礼并不使人被定罪，惟有藐视圣礼才使人被定罪。否则，一切未受洗便夭折的婴孩都将灭亡。圣奥古斯丁和罗马教会，的确曾从洗礼被认为是绝对必需这一前提，推导出这种可怕的教义；但这与福音的精神，以及基督对待孩童的态度直接冲突，因为天国正是属于这样的人。

这一圣礼首次按其完整的基督教意义施行，是在教会诞生之日，使徒首次独立宣讲之后。约翰的洗礼更多具有消极的性质，只是为圣灵的洗礼作预备。按理论而言，基督教洗礼之前是归信，即人以悔改和信心离罪归向上帝的行动；之后是重生，即上帝赦免罪，并施行内在洁净与更新的行动。然而在实际中，外在的记号与内在的状态及果效并不总是一致；行邪术的西门(Simon Magus) 是受了水洗却未受圣灵之洗的例子，哥尼流 (Cornelius)则是在施用水礼以前便已领受圣灵的例子。就婴孩而言，归信作为意志的自觉行动，既不可能，也无必要。就成人而言，在这一庄严礼仪之前，先有福音的宣讲，或对福音主要事实的简要教导，之后再更加深入地灌输使徒的教义。后来，接纳归信者必须十分谨慎，教理教导与考验的时期便大为延长。

  1. 洗礼通常采用的形式是浸水。这可从希腊文 βαπτίζειν 和 βαπτισμός的原义推知；38也可从约翰在约旦河施洗的类比推知；还可从使徒将这神圣礼仪比作神迹般地经过红海、方舟脱离洪水、洁净而使人舒畅的沐浴，以及埋葬与复活推知；最后，也可从古代教会的一般惯例推知，这惯例在东方一直延续至今。39不过，在很早的时候，对患病和垂死的人，以及一切无法全身或部分浸水的情形，也施行洒水礼，或者更确切地说，施行大量浇水的洗礼。有些作者认为，五旬节那三千人首次受洗时，情形便是如此；因为耶路撒冷的供水和私人浴池都很不足，汲沦溪(Kedron)只是一条小溪，夏季又会干涸；不过，城中也有若干水池和蓄水池。在希腊化时代的用法中，有关词语有时也可具有洗涤、沐浴、洒水和礼仪性洁净等较广的含义。40毫无疑问，浸水比浇水或洒水更能完整地表达洗礼作为全人洁净与更新的观念；但以水的数量或性质，或用水的方式，来限制圣灵的运行，并不符合福音的精神。水是圣灵洁净与重生能力的恰当象征，因此是洗礼绝对必需的；但水多水少、冷暖、淡咸，取自河流、蓄水池还是泉源，相对而言都无关紧要，不能影响这一礼仪的有效性。

  2. 关于洗礼的对象：不但浸信会(Baptists)，就连许多赞成婴孩洗礼的神学家，也否认婴孩洗礼源于使徒。浸信会断言，婴孩洗礼违背这圣礼本身的观念，因而是一种不合圣经的败坏。他们说，洗礼必然以教会宣讲福音，以及领受礼仪的人悔改并相信为先决条件；婴孩既不能明白所传的道，也不能悔改相信，就不是洗礼的适当对象，因为洗礼只为成年的归信者而设。诚然，使徒教会是一个宣教的教会，必须先建立一个母体群体，惟有在其中，洗礼的恩典才能借着基督教教育得到培育。因此，即使在旧约之下，割礼也是先施于成年的亚伯拉罕；同样，如今所有在异教地区工作的基督教宣教士，也都从传道和为成人施洗开始。诚然，新约没有为婴孩施洗的明确命令；这样的命令也不符合福音自由的精神。在政教联合以前，也没有强制或普遍施行的婴孩洗礼；第一位基督徒皇帝君士坦丁(Constantine)将洗礼推迟到临终才领受（正如今日许多人推迟悔改一样）；即使在君士坦丁以后，也有一些杰出教师，如拿先斯的贵格利(Gregory Nazianzen)、奥古斯丁 (Augustin)、金口约翰(Chrysostom)，虽有基督徒母亲，却直到成年初期归信时才受洗。

然而，新约更没有禁止婴孩洗礼；若婴孩洗礼不当，鉴于犹太人普遍在婴孩出生后第八日以割礼使其加入旧约团契的习俗，我们本可期待新约加以禁止。

相反，我们有推定性的和确实的论据，支持婴孩洗礼的使徒起源与性质。首先，割礼确实预表了洗礼，正如逾越节预表圣餐一样；其次，基督徒父母与儿女之间有着有机的关系；新约的性质比旧约更为广泛包容；基督作为一切性别、阶层和年龄之人的救赎主，其功效普及所有人，尤其是他自己的婴孩时期具有重要意义，救赎并圣化了婴孩的年龄；他明确邀请孩童到他那里，保证他们有分于天国，因此，他必不会使他们缺少这种成员身份的记号与印证；他设立洗礼的话，显然着眼于使整国整族，而不仅是个别人归于基督，其中自然包括孩童；彼得在首次施行洗礼时，明确宣告这赦罪和赐下圣灵的应许是给犹太人“和他们的儿女”的；新约记载了五次全家受洗，其中大多数家庭有孩童的可能性，远比所有家庭都没有孩童的可能性大；最后，早期教会普遍施行婴孩洗礼，德尔图良(Tertullian) 孤立的抗议，并不比他其他古怪见解和孟他努派 (Montanistic)的特异主张更有证明力；相反，他的激烈抗议恰恰表明婴孩洗礼已普遍施行。他主张出于审慎而推迟洗礼，免得受洗者再度犯罪，便永远丧失这礼仪所赐的益处；但他从未否认早期受洗的使徒起源或正当性。

不过，我们必须补充说，除非有基督徒父母或监护人的照管，并有基督教教育的保证，否则婴孩洗礼便毫无意义，施行它也是一种亵渎。它还需要由个人献身的行动加以完成：孩童在福音上受到适当教导以后，明白而自由地承认基督，献身服事他，随后庄严地被接纳，完全参与教会的团契，并领受圣餐。有人认为，坚信礼(confirmation)最早的痕迹，可以在使徒于洗礼后按手、即象征性地授予圣灵的惯例中找到。41

§ 55. 圣餐

圣餐这一圣礼，是基督在最庄严的情境下设立的；那时，他即将献上自己为祭，以拯救世人。它是一个筵席，使人满怀感恩地记念并领受他赎罪之死的益处，使信徒与他有生命的联合，也彼此相交。正如逾越节使人鲜明地记得那神迹般地脱离为奴之地的拯救，同时又指向将要来到的上帝的羔羊；圣餐也照样将如今已经成就的、脱离罪与死的救赎表明、印证并施予人，直到世界的末了。在这里，基督教最深的奥秘不断重新得到体现，十字架的事迹重现在我们面前。在这里，喂饱五千人的神迹在属灵意义上延续下去。在这里，那坐在上帝右边、却又真实临在于他教会中直到世界末了的基督，将他为我们献上的身体和宝血，也就是他自己、他的生命，以及他赎罪之死的功效，作为属灵的食物，作为从天上来的真粮，赐给一切经过适当自省、饥渴赴这天上筵席的人。因此，圣餐始终被视为基督教崇拜最内在的圣所。

在使徒时期，圣餐每天举行，并与一种出于弟兄之爱的简单聚餐，即爱筵((agape))相连；基督徒在其中与他们共同的救赎主相交，忘却地位、财富和教养的一切差别，感到自己同属上帝的一个家庭。然而，随着教会人数增加，这种孩童般纯真的弟兄合一表现变得越来越困难，并导致种种弊端，正如我们所见保罗在哥林多人中责备的那些事。因此，爱筵逐渐与圣餐分离，并在第二、第三世纪期间渐渐消失；其实，爱筵和耶路撒冷的财物公用一样，都不是律法所强令的。

使徒要求基督徒42以自省来预备领受圣餐，也就是认真省察自己是否有悔改与信心；没有这些，他们不但不能从圣礼领受祝福，反而招致上帝的审判。这一警戒产生了一个合宜的习俗，即在圣餐之前举行特别的预备聚会。

随着时间的推移，这神圣的爱之筵席，竟像洗礼这圣礼，甚至像基督自身的位格一样，成了激烈争论的对象。对于设立圣餐的简单话语（“这是我的身体”等），有三种不同的解释，由此推导出三种彼此冲突的理论——化质说(transubstantiation)、同质说 (consubstantiation) 和基督属灵临在说(spiritualpresence)。然而，使徒当时亲自在主面前，又记得他曾警告他们，不可按属肉体的意思误解他关于吃他肉的讲论，实在不大可能误解这些话。43中世纪及十六世纪的圣餐争论，是基督教历史上最无益于造就、最少结果的争论之一。然而，这些争论也不可能全然徒劳。各种理论各自代表着某些真理的成分；这些成分虽被经院哲学的繁琐辨析所遮蔽或歪曲，却仍可以得到净化，并彼此结合。圣餐是：（1）一种纪念性的礼仪，记念基督在十字架上所献的赎罪之祭；（2）信徒与救主有生命联合的筵席，借此他们真实地，也就是在属灵上、凭着信心，领受基督和他一切的恩惠，并以他的生命为滋养，直到永生；（3）信徒作为基督同一奥秘身体的肢体，彼此相交；（4）向基督献上我们自身和服事的感恩祭或感谢祭，因为他为我们死，为要使我们为他而活。

幸而，圣餐的福分并不取决于对设立圣餐之话语的经院式解释和理解，而在于主的应许，以及对他如孩童般的信心。因此，即使在今日，分属不同宗派、持有不同意见的基督徒，仍能一同围聚在他们共同的主和救主的桌前，感到自己与他合一，并在他里面彼此合一。

§ 56. 神圣的场所

上帝是无所不在的灵，宇宙就是他的殿，因此，人虽可在宇宙各处敬拜他，44但我们有限而依赖感官的本性，以及共同敬拜的需要，仍要求有专门奉献给他、供敬拜之用的场所或圣所。最初的基督徒效法主的榜样，只要他们与摩西制度的关系仍容许，就经常前往耶路撒冷的圣殿和各会堂。不过，除此以外，他们从一开始也在私人住宅中聚会，尤其为举行圣餐和爱筵。教会本身就是在五旬节那日，在一所简陋住宅的楼房上建立的。

教会中显要的成员和最初的归信者，如耶路撒冷约翰·马可的母亲马利亚、凯撒利亚(Caesarea) 的哥尼流、腓立比 (Philippi) 的吕底亚、帖撒罗尼迦(Thessalonica) 的耶孙、哥林多 (Corinth) 的犹士都、以弗所 (Ephesus)的百基拉、歌罗西 (Colosse)的腓利门，都乐意开放自己的住宅，供众人共同敬拜。在罗马这样的大城市，基督徒群体分为若干个这样的家庭聚会，45然而，书信总是把他们作为一个整体来称呼。

使徒时期的基督徒不可能建造专门的礼拜堂；即使不说他们普遍贫穷，单是他们遭受犹太人和外邦人的逼迫，就足以排除这种可能；而整座会堂归信新信仰的情形，无疑也极为罕见。正如世界的救主生于马厩，又从山上升天，他的使徒以及直到第三世纪的继承者，也是在街道、市场、山上、船中、坟墓、洞穴、旷野，以及归信者的家中传道。然而，此后世界各地，为尊荣那位被钉十字架的救赎主，已经建造、并且仍在不断建造多少成千上万座华贵的教堂和礼拜堂！他在降卑的日子里，却连自己的枕头之地也没有！46

英语中有极其丰富的安息日文献，多具通俗和实用性质。关于英美对基督教安息日的理论及其历史，可参阅作者的论文《英美的安息日》(TheAnglo-AmericanSabbath)，纽约，1863年（有英文和德文版）；纽约安息日委员会 (NewYork Sabbath Committee) 在1857–1886年间的出版物；威尔·C. 伍德(Will. C. Wood) 编《安息日论文集》(SabbathEssays)，波士顿（公理会出版协会，Congreg. Publ.Soc.），1879年；以及 A. E. 沃弗尔 (A. E. Waffle)：《主日》(TheLord’s Day)，费城 (Philad.)，1886年。

正如每一个地方一样，每一天、每一个时辰对上帝也同样是神圣的；他充满一切空间和时间，人可以随时随地敬拜他。然而，我们地上生活所必有的限制，以及群体和公共敬拜的性质，使专设神圣时日的做法应运而生。使徒教会大体沿袭犹太人的惯例，却除去了其中的迷信，并赋予它信心与自由的精神。

  1. 因此，除了不受时间约束的纯属个人的灵修之外，信徒也习惯遵守犹太人每日祷告的时辰，尤其是早晨和晚上。

  2. 主日取代了犹太人的安息日，成为每周公共敬拜的日子。实质保留了，形式却改变了。每周定期设立一日，使身体和灵魂得享安息，这一制度植根于我们的身体和道德本性，与人类同样古老，正如婚姻一样，可以追溯到乐园之中。47我们的主那句深刻的话，已包含这一层意思：“安息日是为人设立的。”

这一制度被纳入十诫，也就是道德律法之中；基督来不是要废掉这律法，乃是要成全。若从中删去一条诫命，就必损害其余一切诫命。

与此同时，犹太人的安息日又被许多民族性和礼仪性的限制所围绕；这些限制原非为永久存留而设，却逐渐被抬高到如此显要的地位，以致遮蔽了安息日重大的道德目的，使人成为安息日的奴仆，而不是使安息日为人服务。被掳以后，在法利赛人手中，它与其说是一项特权和福分，不如说成了律法的束缚。基督作为安息日的主，反对这种机械的礼仪主义，恢复了这一制度的真实精神和仁慈目的。48当法利赛人那种奴役人、迷信而又自以为义的严守安息日主义，悄悄进入加拉太众教会，并被当作称义的条件时，保罗便斥责这是重新陷入犹太教。49

这日子由一周的第七日移到第一日，并非根据某项特定的命令，而是出于福音自由的精神，以及构成基督教会根基的若干重大事实的力量。正是在这一天，基督从死里复活；向马利亚、往以马忤斯的门徒，以及聚集的众使徒显现；浇灌他的圣灵，建立教会；50又向他所爱的门徒启示未来的奥秘。因此，早在使徒时期，一周的第一日就已被尊称为“主日”。在这一天，保罗与特罗亚(Troas)的门徒聚集，讲道直到半夜。他吩咐加拉太和哥林多的基督徒，在这一天按各人的力量，为慈善目的献上每周的捐项；这无疑是与敬拜聚会相连的。因此，从新约本身就可看出，星期日被守为敬拜的日子，特别记念基督的复活，救赎之工借此得以完成。51

第二世纪普遍而无异议地遵守主日，只有一个事实能够解释，就是这种做法植根于使徒的实践。这样的遵守更值得珍视，因为在君士坦丁(Constantine)时代以前，民事立法并不予以支持；而且，考虑到大多数基督徒社会地位卑微，又依赖异教的主人和雇主，遵守主日必定带来许多不便。于是，经过一种平易而自然的转变，星期日成为基督教的安息日，或每周休息的日子；它既应验了犹太人安息日的预表意义，本身又成为上帝子民在天上迦南永享安息的预表。52在福音的安排中，安息日并不是贬低一周其余的日子，而是把这些日子提升到更高的层次，以使一切时间和一切工作都分别为圣。它不是律法礼仪的束缚，而是宝贵的恩典之赐，是一项特权，是在世界的纷扰中安息于上帝里面，是在与上帝相交、与众圣徒团契中使心灵重新得力的日子，是对天上永无止境之安息日的预尝和凭据。

在恰当地遵守主日这一点上，英格兰、苏格兰和美国的众教会胜过欧洲大陆的众教会，并由此获得不可估量的益处。这样的遵守是一所施行有益管教的学校，是使民众蒙恩的途径，是公共道德和宗教的保障，是抵御不信的堡垒，也是教会、国家和家庭无量福分的源泉。仅次于教会和圣经，主日是基督教社会的主要支柱。

犹太基督徒除了遵守基督教的主日，也遵守他们古老的安息日，直到耶路撒冷被毁。此后，这一犹太习惯只在伊便尼派(Ebionites) 和拿撒勒派 (Nazarenes) 中继续存留。

正如主日专为记念救主的复活，被守为感恩和喜乐的日子，星期五也至迟在第二世纪——即使不是更早——开始被守为悔改的日子，人们以祷告和禁食，记念基督的受苦和受死。

  1. 每年的节期。使徒著作对于遵守这些节期，并无直接或间接的命令，正如十诫也没有为它们提供根据一样。但基督曾遵守这些节期，而其中的逾越节和五旬节，很容易经历一种转变，类似于犹太安息日转变为基督教的安息日。将书信中的一些暗示53，与第二世纪教会普遍而无异议的惯例相互参照，就可以推断，每年记念基督受死、复活及圣灵浇灌的庆典，起源于使徒时期。事实上，那被钉十字架、已经复活并活在教会中的基督，是早期基督徒全心专注的唯一思想；这一思想既表现为每周遵守主日，也就很自然地会把旧约中两个具有预表意义的大节期，转变为基督教的复活节和圣灵降临节。第二世纪的逾越节争论，所涉及的不是要不要守复活节，而是在什么时候守；士每拿的坡旅甲(Polycarp of Smyrna) 和罗马的阿尼塞图 (Anicet ofRome)，都把各自的习俗追溯到使徒本身在实践上一个无关紧要的差异。

至于其他每年的节期，新约中连最微小的痕迹也没有。圣诞节于第四世纪出现，是教会年这一观念自然发展的结果，成为一种按年代次序排列的民众信经。随着尼西亚(Nicene)及后尼西亚时期圣徒崇拜的传播，记念马利亚、使徒、圣徒和殉道者的节期逐渐接踵而来，直到几乎每一天都先成为圣日，继而成为假日。正如圣徒遮蔽了主，圣徒的节日也遮蔽了主日。

§ 51. The Synagogue.

Campeg. Vitringa (d. at Franeker, 1722): De Synagoga Vetere libritres. Franeker, 1696. 2 vols. (also Weissenfels, 1726). A standardwork, full of biblical and rabbinical learning. A condensed translationby J. L. Bernard: The Synagogue and the Church. London,1842.

Art. "Synag.," by Ginsburg in "Kitto"; Plumptre: in "Smith" (withadditions by Hackett, IV. 3133, Am. ed.); Leyrer in "Herzog" (XV. 299,first ed.); Kneuker in "Schenkel" (V. 443).

As the Christian Church rests historically on the Jewish Church, soChristian worship and the congregational organization rest on that ofthe synagogue, and cannot be well understood without it.

The synagogue was and is still an institution of immense conservativepower. It was the local centre of the religious and social life of theJews, as the temple of Jerusalem was the centre of their national life.It was a school as well as a church, and the nursery and guardian of allthat is peculiar in this peculiar people. It dates probably from the ageof the captivity and of Ezra.(1) It was fully organized at the time ofChrist and the apostles, and used by them as a basis of their publicinstruction.(2) It survived the temple, and continues to this dayunaltered in its essential features, the chief nursery and protection ofthe Jewish nationality and religion.(3)

The term "synagogue" (like our word church) signifies first thecongregation, then also the building where the congregation meet forpublic worship.(4) Every town, however small, had a synagogue, or atleast a place of prayer in a private house or in the open air (usuallynear a river or the sea-shore, on account of the ceremonial washings).Ten men were sufficient to constitute a religious assembly. "Moses fromgenerations of old hath in every city them that preach him, being readin the synagogues every Sabbath."(5) To erect a synagogue was considereda work of piety and public usefulness.(6) In large cities, as Alexandriaand Rome, there were many; in Jerusalem, about four hundred for thevarious sects and the Hellenists from different countries.(7)

  1. The building was a plain, rectangular ball of no peculiarstyle of architecture, and in its inner arrangement somewhat resemblingthe Tabernacle and the Temple. It had benches, the higher ones ("theuppermost seats") for the elders and richer members,(8) a reading-deskor pulpit, and a wooden ark or closet for the sacred rolls (called"Copheret" or Mercy Seat, also "Aaron"). The last corresponded to theHoly of Holies in the Tabernacle and the Temple. A sacred light was keptburning as a symbol of the divine law, in imitation of the light in theTemple, but there is no mention made of it in the Talmud. Other lampswere brought in by devout worshippers at the beginning of the Sabbath(Friday evening). Alms-boxes were provided near the door, as in theTemple, one for the poor in Jerusalem, another for local charities. Paulimitated the example by collecting alms for the poor Christians inJerusalem.

There was no artistic (except vegetable) ornamentation; for thesecond commandment strictly forbids all images of the Deity asidolatrous. In this, as in many other respects, the Mohammedan mosque,with its severe iconoclastic simplicity, is a second edition of thesynagogue. The building was erected on the most elevated spot of theneighborhood, and no house was allowed to overtop it. In the absence ofa commanding site, a tall pole from the roof rendered itconspicuous.(9)

  1. Organization.—Every synagogue had a president,(10) anumber of elders (Zekenim) equal in rank,(11) a reader andinterpreter,(12) one or more envoys or clerks, called "messengers"(Sheliach),(13) and a sexton or beadle (Chazzan) forthe humbler mechanical services.(14) There were also deacons (Gabaezedaka) for the collection of alms in money and produce. Ten ormore wealthy men at leisure, called Batlanim, represented thecongregation at every service. Each synagogue formed an independentrepublic, but kept up a regular correspondence with other synagogues. Itwas also a civil and religious court, and had power to excommunicate andto scourge offenders.(15)

  2. Worship.—It was simple, but rather long, and embracedthree elements, devotional, didactic, and ritualistic. It includedprayer, song, reading, and exposition of the Scripture, the rite ofcircumcision, and ceremonial washings. The bloody sacrifices wereconfined to the temple and ceased with its destruction; they werefulfilled in the eternal sacrifice on the cross. The prayers and songswere chiefly taken from the Psalter, which may be called the firstliturgy and hymn book.

The opening prayer was called the Shema or KeriathShema, and consisted of two introductory benedictions, the readingof the Ten Commandments (afterward abandoned) and several sections ofthe Pentateuch, namely, Deut. 6:4–9; 11:13–21; Num. 15:37–41. Thenfollowed the eighteen prayers and benedictions (Berachoth).This is one of them: "Bestow peace, happiness, blessing, grace, mercy,and compassion upon us and upon the whole of Israel, thy people. OurFather, bless us all unitedly with the light of thy countenance, for inthe light of thy countenance didst thou give to us, O Lord our God, thelaw of life, lovingkindness, justice, blessing, compassion, life, andpeace. May it please thee to bless thy people lsrael at all times, andin every moment, with peace. Blessed art thou, O Lord, who blessest thypeople Israel with peace." These benedictions are traced in the Mishnato the one hundred and twenty elders of the Great Synagogue. They wereno doubt of gradual growth, some dating from the Maccabean struggles,some from the Roman ascendancy. The prayers were offered by a reader,and the congregation responded "Amen." This custom passed into theChristian church.(16)

The didactic and homiletical part of worship was based on the HebrewScriptures. A lesson from the Law (called parasha),(17) and onefrom the Prophets (haphthara) were read in the original,(18)and followed by a paraphrase or commentary and homily (midrash)in the vernacular Aramaic or Greek. A benediction and the "Amen" of thepeople closed the service.

As there was no proper priesthood outside of Jerusalem, any Jew ofage might get up to read the lessons, offer prayer, and address thecongregation. Jesus and the apostles availed themselves of thisdemocratic privilege to preach the gospel, as the fulfilment of the lawand the prophets.(19) The strong didactic element which distinguishedthis service from all heathen forms of worship, had the effect offamiliarizing the Jews of all grades, even down to the servant-girls,with their religion, and raising them far above the heathen. At the sametime it attracted proselytes who longed for a purer and more spiritualworship.

The days of public service were the Sabbath, Monday, and Thursday;the hours of prayer the third (9 a.m.), the sixth (noon), and the ninth(3 p.m.).(20)

The sexes were divided by a low wall or screen, the men on the oneside, the women on the other, as they are still in the East (and in someparts of Europe). The people stood during prayer with their faces turnedto Jerusalem.

§ 52. Christian Worship.

Christian worship, or cultus, is the public adoration of God in thename of Christ; the celebration of the communion of believers as acongregation with their heavenly Head, for the glory of the Lord, andfor the promotion and enjoyment of spiritual life. While it aimsprimarily at the devotion and edification of the church itself, it hasat the same time a missionary character, and attracts the outside world.This was the case on the Day of Pentecost when Christian worship in itsdistinctive character first appeared.

As our Lord himself in his youth and manhood worshipped in thesynagogue and the temple, so did his early disciples as long as theywere tolerated. Even Paul preached Christ in the synagogues of Damascus,Cyprus, Antioch in Pisidia, Amphipolis, Beraeea, Athens, Corinth,Ephesus. He "reasoned with the Jews every sabbath in the synagogues"which furnished him a pulpit and an audience.

The Jewish Christians, at least in Palestine, conformed as closely aspossible to the venerable forms of the cultus of their fathers, which intruth were divinely ordained, and were an expressive type of theChristian worship. So far as we know, they scrupulously observed theSabbath, the annual Jewish feasts, the hours of daily prayer, and thewhole Mosaic ritual, and celebrated, in addition to these, the ChristianSunday, the death and the resurrection of the Lord, and the holy Supper.But this union was gradually weakened by the stubborn opposition of theJews, and was at last entirely broken by the destruction of the temple,except among the Ebionites and Nazarenes.

In the Gentile-Christian congregations founded by Paul, the worshiptook from the beginning a more independent form. The essential elementsof the Old Testament service were transferred, indeed, but divested oftheir national legal character, and transformed by the spirit of thegospel. Thus the Jewish Sabbath passed into the Christian Sunday; thetypical Passover and Pentecost became feasts of the death andresurrection of Christ, and of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; thebloody sacrifices gave place to the thankful remembrance andappropriation of the one, all-sufficient, and eternal sacrifice ofChrist on the cross, and to the personal offering of prayer,intercession, and entire self-consecration to the service of theRedeemer; on the ruins of the temple made without hands arose the neverceasing worship of the omnipresent God in spirit and in truth.(21) Soearly as the close of the apostolic period this more free and spiritualcultus of Christianity had no doubt become well nigh universal; yet manyJewish elements, especially in the Eastern church, remain to thisday.

§ 53. The Several Parts ofWorship.

The several parts of public worship in the time of the apostles wereas follows:

  1. The Preaching of the gospel. This appears in the first period mostlyin the form of a missionary address to the unconverted; that is, asimple, living presentation of the main facts of the life of Jesus, withpractical exhortation to repentance and conversion. Christ crucified andrisen was the luminous centre, whence a sanctifying light was shed onall the relations of life. Gushing forth from a full heart, thispreaching went to the heart; and springing from an inward life, itkindled life—a new, divine life—in the susceptible hearers. It wasrevival preaching in the purest sense. Of this primitive Christiantestimony several examples from Peter and Paul are preserved in the Actsof the Apostles.

The Epistles also may be regarded in the wider sense as sermons,addressed, however, to believers, and designed to nourish the Christianlife already planted.

  1. The Reading of portions of the Old Testament,(22) with practicalexposition and application; transferred from the Jewish synagogue intothe Christian church.(23) To these were added in due time lessons fromthe New Testament; that is, from the canonical Gospels and the apostolicEpistles, most of which were addressed to whole congregations andoriginally intended for public use.(24) After the death of the apostlestheir writings became doubly important to the church, as a substitutefor their oral instruction and exhortation, and were much more used inworship than the Old Testament.

  2. Prayer, in its various forms of petition, intercession, andthanksgiving. This descended likewise from Judaism, and in fact belongsessentially even to all heathen religions; but now it began to beoffered in childlike confidence to a reconciled Father in the name ofJesus, and for all classes and conditions, even for enemies andpersecutors. The first Christians accompanied every important act oftheir public and private life with this holy rite, and Paul exhorts hisreaders to "pray without ceasing." On solemn occasions they joinedfasting with prayer, as a help to devotion, though it is nowheredirectly enjoined in the New Testament.(25) They prayed freely from theheart, as they were moved by the Spirit, according to special needs andcircumstances. We have an example in the fourth chapter of Acts. Thereis no trace of a uniform and exclusive liturgy; it would be inconsistentwith the vitality and liberty of the apostolic churches. At the sametime the frequent use of psalms and short forms of devotion, as theLord’s Prayer, may be inferred with certainty from the Jewish custom,from the Lord’s direction respecting his model prayer,(26) from thestrong sense of fellowship among the first Christians, and finally fromthe liturgical spirit of the ancient church, which could not have sogenerally prevailed both in the East and the West without some apostolicand post-apostolic precedent. The oldest forms are the eucharisticprayers of the Didache, and the petition for rulers in thefirst Epistle of Clement, which contrasts most beautifully with thecruel hostility of Nero and Domitian.(27)

  3. The Song, a form of prayer, in the festive dress of poetry andthe elevated language of inspiration, raising the congregation to thehighest pitch of devotion, and giving it a part in the heavenlyharmonies of the saints. This passed immediately, with the psalms of theOld Testament, those inexhaustible treasures of spiritual experience,edification, and comfort, from the temple and the synagogue into theChristian church. The Lord himself inaugurated psalmody into the newcovenant at the institution of the holy Supper,(28) and Paul expresslyenjoined the singing of "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs," as ameans of social edification.(29) But to this precious inheritance fromthe past, whose full value was now for the first time understood in thelight of the New Testament revelation, the church, in the enthusiasm ofher first love, added original, specifically Christian psalms, hymns,doxologies, and benedictions, which afforded the richest material forSacred poetry and music in succeeding centuries; the song of theheavenly hosts, for example, at the birth of the Saviour;(30) the "Nuncdimittis" of Simeon;(31) the "Magnificat" of the Virgin Mary;(32) the"Benedictus" of Zacharias;(33) the thanksgiving of Peter after hismiraculous deliverance;(34) the speaking with tongues in the apostolicchurches, which, whether song or prayer, was always in the elevatedlanguage of enthusiasm; the fragments of hymns scattered through theEpistles;(35) and the lyrical and liturgical passages, the doxologiesand antiphonies of the Apocalypse.(36)

  4. Confession Of Faith. All the above-mentioned acts of worship arealso acts of faith. The first express confession of faith is thetestimony of Peter, that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of the livingGod. The next is the trinitarian baptismal formula. Out of thisgradually grew the so-called Apostles’ Creed, which is also trinitarianin structure, but gives the confession of Christ the central and largestplace. Though not traceable in its present shape above the fourthcentury, and found in the second and third in different longer orshorter forms, it is in substance altogether apostolic, and exhibits anincomparable summary of the leading facts in the revelation of thetriune God from the creation of the world to the resurrection of thebody; and that in a form intelligible to all, and admirably suited forpublic worship and catechetical use. We shall return to it more fully inthe second period.

  5. Finally, the administration of the Sacraments, or sacred ritesinstituted by Christ, by which, under appropriate symbols and visiblesigns, spiritual gifts and invisible grace are represented, sealed, andapplied to the worthy participators.

The two sacraments of Baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the antitypes ofcircumcision and the passover under the Old Testament, were institutedby Christ as efficacious signs, pledges, and means of the grace of thenew covenant. They are related to each other as regeneration andsanctification, or as the beginning and the growth of the Christianlife. The other religious rites mentioned in the New Testament, asconfirmation and ordination, cannot be ranked in dignity with thesacraments, as they are not commanded by Christ.
