CHAPTERVIII. CHRISTIAN LIFE IN THE APOSTOLIC CHURCH.

Sources.

The teaching and example of Christ as exhibited in the Gospels,and of the apostles in the Acts and Epistles; compared andcontrasted with the rabbinical ethics and the state of Jewish society,and with the Greek systems of philosophy and the moral condition of theRoman empire, as described in the writings of Seneca, Tacitus, the Romansatirists, etc.

Literature.

I. The respective sections in the Histories of the Apost.Church by Neander: I. 229–283 (Germ. ed.); Schaff: §§109–123 (pp. 433–492); Lange: II. 495–534; Weizsäcker: 647–698.

II The works on the Theology of the Apostolic Age, bySchmid, Reuss, Baur, Weiss, etc.

  1. The Systems of Christian Ethics bySchleiermacher, Rothe, Neander, Schmid, Wuttke,Harless, Martensen, Luthardt, and Lecky’s History of EuropeanMorals (1869), vol I. 357 sqq.

  2. A. Thoma (pastor in Mannheim): Geschichte der christlichenSittenlehre in der Zeit des Neuen Testamentes, Haarlem, 1879 (380pp.). A crowned prize-essay of the Teyler Theol. Society. The firstattempt of a separate critical history of N. T. ethics, but written fromthe negative standpoint of the Tübingen school, and hence veryunsatisfactory. It is divided in three parts: I. The Ethics of Jesus;II. The Ethics of Paul; III. The Ethics of the Congregation.

V. Works which treat of Christian life in the post-apostolic age(Cave, Arnold, Schmidt, Chastel, Pressensé, etc.) will be noticed in thesecond period.

§ 44. The Power ofChristianity.

Practical Christianity is the manifestation of a new life; aspiritual (as distinct from intellectual and moral) life; a supernatural(as distinct from natural) life; it is a life of holiness and peace; alife of union and communion with God the Father, the Son, and theSpirit; it is eternal life, beginning with regeneration and culminatingin the resurrection. It lays hold of the inmost centre of man’spersonality, emancipates him from the dominion of sin, and brings himinto vital union with God in Christ; from this centre it acts as apurifying, ennobling, and regulating force upon all the faculties ofman—the emotions, the will, and the intellect—and transforms even thebody into a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Christianity rises far above all other religions in the theory andpractice of virtue and piety. It sets forth the highest standard of loveto God and to man; and this not merely as an abstract doctrine, or anobject of effort and hope, but as a living fact in the person of JesusChrist, whose life and example have more power and influence than allthe maxims and precepts of sages and legislators. Deeds speak louderthan words. Praecepta docent, exempla trahunt. The finestsystems of moral philosophy have not been able to regenerate and conquerthe world. The gospel of Christ has done it and is doing it constantly.The wisest men of Greece and Rome sanctioned slavery, polygamy,concubinage, oppression, revenge, infanticide; or they belied theirpurer maxims by their conduct. The ethical standard of the Jews was muchhigher; yet none of their patriarchs, kings, or prophets claimedperfection, and the Bible honestly reports the infirmities and sins, aswell as the virtues, of Abraham, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon.

But the character of Christ from the manger to the cross is withoutspot or blemish; he is above reproach or suspicion, and acknowledged byfriend and foe to be the purest as well as the wisest being that everappeared on earth. He is the nearest approach which God can make to man,and which man can make to God; he represents the fullest imaginable andattain able harmony of the ideal and real, of the divine and human. TheChristian church may degenerate in the hands of sinful men, but thedoctrine and life of her founder are a never-failing fountain ofpurification.

The perfect life of harmony with God and devotion to the welfare ofthe human race, is to pass from Christ to his followers. Christian lifeis an imitation of the life of Christ. From his word and spirit, livingand ruling in the church, an unbroken stream of redeeming, sanctifying,and glorifying power has been flowing forth upon individuals, families,and nations for these eighteen centuries, and will continue to flow tillthe world is transformed into the kingdom of heaven, and God becomes allin all.

One of the strongest proofs of the supernatural origin ofChristianity, is its elevation above the natural culture and moralstandard of its first professors. The most perfect doctrine and lifedescribed by unschooled fishermen of Galilee, who never before had beenoutside of Palestine, and were scarcely able to read and to write! Andthe profoundest mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, the incarnation,redemption, regeneration, resurrection, taught by the apostles tocongregations of poor and illiterate peasants, slaves and freedmen! For"not many wise after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble" werecalled, "but God chose the foolish things of the world, that he mightput to shame them that are wise; and God chose the weak things of theworld, that he might put to shame the things that are strong; and thebase things of the world, and the things that are despised, did Godchoose, yea, and the things that are not, that he might bring to naughtthe things that are: that no flesh should glory before God. But of himare ye in Christ Jesus, who was made unto us wisdom from God, andrighteousness and sanctification and redemption: that, according as itis written, he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord."(1)

If we compare the moral atmosphere of the apostolic churches with theactual condition of surrounding Judaism and heathenism, the contrast isas startling as that between a green oasis with living fountains andlofty palm trees, and a barren desert of sand and stone. Judaism in itshighest judicatory committed the crime of crimes, the crucifixion of theSaviour of the world, and hastened to its doom. Heathenism was fitlyrepresented by such imperial monsters as Tiberius, Caligula, Nero, andDomitian, and exhibited a picture of hopeless corruption and decay, asdescribed in the darkest colors not only by St. Paul, but by his heathencontemporary, the wisest Stoic moralist, the teacher and victim ofNero.(2)

Notes.

The rationalistic author of Supernatural Religion (vol. II.487) makes the following remarkable concession: "The teaching of Jesuscarried morality to the sublimest point attained, or even attainable, byhumanity. The influence of his spiritual religion has been rendereddoubly great by the unparalleled purity and elevation of his character.Surpassing in his sublime simplicity and earnestness the moral grandeurof Sâkya Muni, and putting to the blush the sometimes sullied, thoughgenerally admirable, teaching of Socrates and Plato, and the whole roundof Greek philosophers, he presented the rare spectacle of a life, so faras we can estimate it, uniformly noble and consistent with his own loftyprinciples, so that the ’imitation of Christ’ has become almost thefinal word in the preaching of his religion, and must continue to be oneof the most powerful elements of its permanence."

Lecky, likewise a rationalistic writer and historian of great abilityand fairness, makes this weighty remark in his History of EuropeanMorals (vol. II. 9):, "It was reserved for Christianity to presentto the world an ideal character, which through all the changes ofeighteen centuries has inspired the hearts of men with an impassionedlove; has shown itself capable of acting on all ages, nations,temperaments, and conditions; has been not only the highest pattern ofvirtue, but the strongest incentive to its practice, and has exercisedso deep an influence that it may be truly said that the simple record ofthree short years of active life has done more to regenerate and tosoften mankind than all the disquisitions of philosophers and all theexhortations of moralists. This has, indeed, been the wellspring ofwhatever is best and purest in Christian life. Amid all the sins andfailings, amid all the priestcraft and persecution and fanaticism thathave defaced the Church, it has preserved, in the character and exampleof its Founder, an enduring principle of regeneration."

To this we may add the testimony of the atheistic philosopher, JohnStuart Mill from his essay on Theism, written shortly beforehis death (1873), and published, 1874, in Three Essays onReligion. (Am. ed., p. 253): "Above all, the most valuable part ofthe effect on the character which Christianity has produced, by holdingup in a divine person a standard of excellence and a model forimitation, is available even to the absolute unbeliever, and can nevermore be lost to humanity. For it is Christ rather than God whomChristianity has held up to believers as the pattern of perfection forhumanity. It is the God incarnate more than the God of the Jews, or ofnature, who, being idealized, has taken so great and salutary a hold onthe modem mind. And whatever else may be taken away from us by rationalcriticism, Christ is still left; a unique figure, not more unlike allhis precursors than all his followers, even those who had the directbenefit of his personal teaching. It is of no use to say that Christ, asexhibited in the Gospels, is not historical, and that we know not howmuch of what is admirable has been super-added by the tradition of hisfollowers. The tradition of followers suffices to insert any number ofmarvels, and may have inserted all the miracles which he is reputed tohave wrought. But who among his disciples, or among their proselytes,was capable of inventing the sayings ascribed to Jesus, or of imaginingthe life and character revealed in the Gospels? Certainly not thefishermen of Galilee; as certainly not St. Paul, whose character andidiosyncrasies were of a totally different sort; still less the earlyChristian writers, in whom nothing is more evident than that the goodwhich was in them was all derived, as they always professed that it wasderived, from the higher source."

§ 45. The Spiritual Gifts.

Comp. the Commentaries on Rom. 12:3–9, and 1 Cor. 12–14.

The apostolic church was endowed from the day of Pentecost with allthe needful spiritual gifts for the moral regeneration of the world.They formed, as it were, her bridal garment and her panoply againstJewish and Gentile opposition. They are called charisms(3) or gifts ofgrace, as distinguished from, though not opposed to, natural endowments.They are certain special energies and manifestations of the Holy Spiritin believers for the common good.(4) They are supernatural, therefore,in their origin; but they correspond to natural virtues, and inoperation they follow all the mental and moral faculties of Dian,raising them to higher activity, and consecrating them to the service ofChrist. They all rest on faith, that "gift of gifts."

The spiritual gifts may be divided into three classes: first,intellectual gifts of knowledge, mainly theoretical in theircharacter, and concerned primarily with doctrine and theology; secondly,emotional gifts of feeling, appearing chiefly in divine worship and forimmediate edification; and thirdly, practical gifts of will,devoted to the organization, government, and discipline of the church.They are not, however, abstractly separate, but work togetherharmoniously for the common purpose of edifying the body of Christ. Inthe New Testament ten charisms are specially mentioned; the first fourhave to do chiefly, though not exclusively, with doctrine, the next twowith worship, and the remaining four with government and practicalaffairs.

  1. The gift of Wisdom and Knowledge,(5) or of deep insight into thenature and system of the divine word and the doctrines of the Christiansalvation.

  2. The gift of Teaching.(6) or of practically applying the gift ofknowledge; the power of clearly expounding the Scriptures for theinstruction and edification of the people.

  3. The gift of Prophecy,(7) akin to the two preceding, but addressedrather to pious feeling than to speculative reflection, and employingcommonly the language of higher inspiration, rather than that of logicalexposition and demonstration. It is by no means confined to theprediction of future events, but consists in disclosing the hiddencounsel of God, the deeper sense of the Scriptures, the secret state ofthe heart, the abyss of sin, and the glory of redeeming grace. Itappears particularly in creative periods, times of mighty revival; whilethe gift of reaching suits better a quiet state of natural growth in thechurch. Both act not only in the sphere of doctrine and theology, butalso in worship, and might in this view be reckoned also among the giftsof feeling.

  4. The gift of Discerning Spirits,(8) serves mainly as a guide tothe third gift, by discriminating between true prophets and false,between divine inspiration and a merely human or satanic enthusiasm. Ina wider sense it is a deep discernment in separating truth and error,and in judging of moral and religious character; a holy criticism stillever necessary to the purity of Christian doctrine and theadministration of the discipline of the church.

  5. The gift of Tongues,(9) or of an utterance proceeding from astate of unconscious ecstasy in the speaker, and unintelligible to thehearer unless interpreted—thus differing from prophecy, which requires aself-conscious though highly elevated state of feeling, serves directlyto profit the congregation, and is therefore preferred by Paul.(10) Thespeaking with tongues is an involuntary psalm-like prayer or song,uttered from a spiritual trance, and in a peculiar language inspired bythe Holy Spirit. The soul is almost entirely passive, an instrument onwhich the Spirit plays his heavenly melodies. This gift has, therefore,properly, nothing to do with the spread of the church among foreignpeoples and in foreign languages, but is purely an act of worship, forthe edification primarily of the speaker himself, and indirectly,through interpretation, for the hearers. It appeared, first, indeed, onthe day of Pentecost, but before Peter’s address to the people,which was the proper mission-sermon; and we meet with it afterwards inthe house of Cornelius and in the Corinthian congregation, as a means ofedification for believers, and not, at least not directly, forunbelieving hearers, although it served to them as a significantsign,(11) arresting their attention to the supernatural power in thechurch.

  6. The gift of Interpretation (12) is the supplement of theglossolalia, and makes that gift profitable to the congregation bytranslating the prayers and songs from the language of the spirit and ofecstasy(13) into that of the understanding and of soberself-consciousness.(14) The preponderance of reflection here puts thisgift as properly in the first class as in the second.

  7. The gift of Ministry and Help,(15) that is, of specialqualification primarily for the office of deacon and deaconess, or forthe regular ecclesiastical care of the poor and the sick, and, in thewide sense, for all labors of Christian charity andphilanthropy.

  8. The gift of church Government and the Care of souls,(16)indispensable to all pastors and rulers of the church, above all to theapostles and apostolic men, in proportion to the extent of theirrespective fields of labor. Peter warns his co-presbyters against thetemptation to hierarchical arrogance and tyranny over conscience, ofwhich so many priests, bishops, patriarchs, and popes have since beenguilty; and points them to the sublime example of the great Shepherd andArchbishop, who, in infinite love, laid down his life for thesheep.(17)

  9. The gift of Miracles(18) is the power possessed by the apostlesand apostolic men, like Stephen, to heal all sorts of physical maladies,to cast out demons, to raise the dead, and perform other similar works,in virtue of an extraordinary energy or faith, by word, prayer, and thelaying on of hands in the name of Jesus, and for his glory. Thesemiracles were outward credentials and seals of the divine mission of theapostles in a time and among a people which required such sensible helpsto faith. But as Christianity became established in the world, it couldpoint to its continued moral effects as the best evidence of its truth,and the necessity for outward physical miracles ceased.

  10. Finally, the gift of Love, the greatest, most precious, mostuseful, most needful, and most enduring of all, described and extolledby St. Paul in the thirteenth chapter of 1 Corinthians with the pen ofan angel in the vision and enjoyment of the God of infinite lovehimself.(19) Love is natural kindness and affection sanctified andraised to the spiritual sphere, or rather a new heavenly affectioncreated in the soul by the experience of the saving love of God inChrist. As faith lies at the bottom of all charisms, so love is notproperly a separate gift, but the soul of all the gifts, guarding themfrom abuse for selfish and ambitious purposes, making them available forthe common good, ruling, uniting, and completing them. It alone givesthem their true value, and without love even the speaking with tonguesof angels, and a faith which removes mountains, are nothing before God.It holds heaven and earth in its embrace. It "believeth all things," andwhen faith fails, it "hopeth all things," and when hope fails, it"endureth all things," but it "never fails." As love is the most needfulof all the gifts on earth, so it will also outlast all the others and bethe ornament and joy of the saints in heaven. For love is the inmostessence, the heart, as it were, of God, the ground of all hisattributes, and the motive of all his works. It is the beginning and theend of creation, redemption, and sanctification—the link which unites uswith the triune God, the cardinal virtue of Christianity, the fulfillingof the law, the bond of perfectness, and the fountain of bliss.

§ 46. Christianity inIndividuals.

The transforming spiritual power of Christianity appears first in thelives of individuals. The apostles and primitive Christians rose to amorality and piety far above that of the heroes of heathen virtue andeven that of the Jewish saints. Their daily walk was a living union withChrist, ever seeking the glory of God and the salvation of men. Many ofthe cardinal virtues, humility, for example, and love for enemies, wereunknown before the Christian day.

Peter, Paul, and John represent the various leading forms or types ofChristian piety, as well as of theology. They were not without defect,indeed they themselves acknowledged only one sinless being, their Lordand Master, and they confessed their own shortcomings;(20) yet they wereas nearly perfect as it is possible to be in a sinful world; and themoral influence of their lives and writings on all generations of thechurch is absolutely immeasurable. Each exhibits the spirit and life ofChrist in a peculiar way. For the gospel does not destroy, but redeemsand sanctifies the natural talents and tempers of men. It consecratesthe fire of a Peter, the energy of a Paul, and the pensiveness of a Johnto the same service of God. It most strikingly displays its new creatingpower in the sudden conversion of the apostle of the Gentiles from amost dangerous foe to a most efficient friend of the church. Upon Paulthe Spirit of God came as an overwhelming storm; upon John, as a gentle,refreshing breeze. But in all dwelt the same new, supernatural, divineprinciple of life. All are living apologies for Christianity, whoseforce no truth-loving heart can resist.

Notice, too, the moral effects of the gospel in the female charactersof the New Testament. Christianity raises woman from the slavishposition which she held both in Judaism and in heathendom, to her truemoral dignity and importance; makes her an heir of the same salvationwith man,(21) and opens to her a field for the noblest and loveliestvirtues, without thrusting her, after the manner of modernpseudo-philanthropic schemes of emancipation, out of her appropriatesphere of private, domestic life, and thus stripping her of her fairestornament and peculiar charm.

The Virgin Mary marks the turning point in the history of the femalesex. As the mother of Christ, the second Adam, she corresponds to Eve,and is, in a spiritual sense, the mother of all living.(22) In her, the"blessed among women," the whole sex wass blessed, and the curse removedwhich had hung over the era of the fall. She was not, indeed, free fromactual and native sin, as is now, taught, without the slightest groundin Scripture, by the Roman church since the 8th of December, 1854. Onthe contrary, as a daughter of Adam, she needed, like all men,redemption and sanctification through Christ, the sole author of sinlessholiness, and she herself expressly calls God her Saviour.(23) But inthe mother and educator of the Saviour of the world we no doubt may andshould revere, though not worship, the model of female Christian virtue,of purity, tenderness, simplicity, humility, perfect obedience to God,and unreserved surrender to Christ. Next to her we have a lovely groupof female disciples and friends around the Lord: Mary, the wife ofClopas; Salome, the mother of James and John; Mary of Bethany, who satat Jesus’ feet; her busy and hospitable sister, Martha; Mary of Magdala,whom the Lord healed of a demoniacal possession; the sinner, who washedhis feet with her tears of penitence and wiped them with her hair; andall the noble women, who ministered to the Son of man in his earthlypoverty with the gifts of their love,(24) lingered last around hiscross,(25) and were the first at his open sepulchre on the, morning ofthe resurrection.(26)

Henceforth we find woman no longer a slave of man and tool of lust,but the pride and joy of her husband, the fond mother training herchildren to virtue and godliness, the ornament and treasure of thefamily, the faithful sister, the zealous servant of the congregation inevery work of Christian charity, the sister of mercy, the martyr withsuperhuman courage, the guardian angel of peace, the example of purity,humility, gentleness, patience, love, and fidelity unto death. Suchwomen were unknown before. The heathen Libanius, the enthusiasticeulogist of old Grecian culture, pronounced an involuntary eulogy onChristianity when he exclaimed, as he looked at the mother ofChrysostom: "What women the Christians have!"

§ 47. Christianity and theFamily.

H. Gregoire: De l’influence du christianisme sur la condition desfemmes. Paris, 1821.

F. Münter: Die Christin im heidnischen Hause vor den ZeitenConstantin’s des Grossen. Kopenhagen, 1828.

Julia Kavanagh: Women of Christianity, Exemplary for Acts ofPiety and Charity. Lond., 1851; N. York, 1866.

Thus raising the female sex to its true freedom and dignity,Christianity transforms and sanctifies the entire family life. Itabolishes polygamy, and makes monogamy the proper form of marriage; itcondemns concubinage with all forms of unchastity and impurity. Itpresents the mutual duties of husband and wife, and of parents andchildren, in their true light, and exhibits marriage as a copy of themystical union of Christ with his bride, the church; thus imparting toit a holy character and a heavenly end.(27)

Henceforth the family, though still rooted, as before, in the soil ofnature, in the mystery of sexual love, is spiritualized and becomes anursery of the purest and noblest virtues, a miniature church, where thefather, as shepherd, daily leads his household into the pastures of thedivine word, and, as priest, offers to the Lord the sacrifice of theircommon petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise.

With the married state, the single also, as an exception to the rule,is consecrated by the gospel to the service of the kingdom of God; as wesee in a Paul, a Barnabas, and a John,(28) and in the history ofmissions and of ascetic piety. The enthusiasm for celibacy, which spreadso soon throughout the ancient church, must be regarded as a one-sided,though natural and, upon the whole, beneficial reaction against therotten condition and misery of family life among the heathen.

§ 48. Christianity and Slavery.

Literature.

H. Wallon (Prof. of Modern History in Paris): Histoire del’esclavage dans l’antiquité, Par. 1879, 3 vols., treats verythoroughly of Slavery in the Orient, among the Greeks and the Romans,with an Introduction on modern negro slavery in the Colonies.

Augustin Cochin (ancien maire et conseiller municipal de la Ville deParis): L’abolition de l’esclavage, Paris, 1862, 2 vols. Thiswork treats not only of the modern abolition of slavery, but includes invol. II., p. 348–470, an able discussion of the relation of Christianityand slavery.

Möhler (R. C., d. 1848): Bruchstücke aus der Geschichte derAufhebung der Sklaverei, 1834. ("Vermischte Schriften," vol. II.,p. 54.)

H. Wiskemann: Die Sklaverei. Leiden, 1866. A crownedprize-essay.

P. Allard: Les esclaves chrétiens depuis les premiers temps del’église jusqu’ à la fin de la domination romaine en OccidentParis, 1876 (480 pp.).

G. V. Lechler: Sklaverei und Christenthum. Leipz.1877–78.

Ph. Schaff: Slavery and the Bible, in his "Christ andChristianity," N. York and London, 1885, pp. 184–212.

Compare the Commentaries on the Epistle of Paul to Philemon,especially Braune, and Lightfoot (in Colossians and Philemon,1875).

The numerous American works on slavery by Channing, Parker, Hodge,Barnes, Wilson, Cheever, Bledsoe, and others, relate to the question ofnegro slavery, now providentially abolished by the civil war of1861–65.

To Christianity we owe the gradual extinction of slavery.

This evil has rested as a curse on all nations, and at the time ofChrist the greater part of the existing race was bound in beastlydegradation—even in civilized Greece and Rome the slaves being morenumerous than the free-born and the freedmen. The greatest philosophersof antiquity vindicated slavery as a natural and necessary institution;and Aristotle declared all barbarians to be slaves by birth, fit fornothing but obedience. According to the Roman law, "slaves had no headin the State, no name, no title, no register;" they had no rights ofmatrimony, and no protection against adultery; they could be bought andsold, or given away, as personal property; they might be tortured forevidence, or even put to death, at the discretion of their master. Inthe language of a distinguished writer on civil law, the slaves in theRoman empire "were in a much worse state than any cattle whatsoever."Cato the elder expelled his old and sick slaves out of house and home.Hadrian, one of the most humane of the emperors, wilfully destroyed theeye of one of his slaves with a pencil. Roman ladies punished theirmaids with sharp iron instruments for the most trifling offences, whileattending half-naked, on their toilet. Such legal degradation and crueltreatment had the worst effect upon the character of the slaves. Theyare described by the ancient writers as mean, cowardly, abject, false,voracious, intemperate, voluptuous, also as hard and cruel when placedover others. A proverb prevailed in the Roman empire: "As many slaves,so many enemies." Hence the constant danger of servile insurrections,which more than once brought the republic to the brink of ruin, andseemed to justify the severest measures in self-defence.

Judaism, indeed, stood on higher ground than this; yet it toleratedslavery, though with wise precautions against maltreatment, and with thesignificant ordinance, that in the year of jubilee, which prefigured therenovation of the theocracy, all Hebrew slaves should go free.(29)

This system of permanent oppression and moral degradation the gospelopposes rather by its whole spirit than by any special law. It nowhererecommends outward violence and revolutionary measures, which in thosetimes would have been worse than useless, but provides an internalradical cure, which first mitigates the evil, takes away its sting, andeffects at last its entire abolition. Christianity aims, first of all,to redeem man, without regard to rank or condition, from that worstbondage, the curse of sin, and to give him true spiritual freedom; itconfirms the original unity of all men in the image of God, and teachesthe common redemption and spiritual equality of all before God inChrist;(30) it insists on love as the highest duty and virtue, whichitself inwardly levels social distinctions; and it addresses the comfortand consolation of the gospel particularly to all the poor, thepersecuted, and the oppressed. Paul sent back to his earthly master thefugitive slave, Onesimus, whom he had converted to Christ and to hisduty, that he might restore his character where he had lost it; but heexpressly charged Philemon to receive and treat the bondman hereafter asa beloved brother in Christ, yea, as the apostle’s own heart. It isimpossible to conceive of a more radical cure of the evil in those timesand within the limits of established laws and customs. And it isimpossible to find in ancient literature a parallel to the littleEpistle to Philemon for gentlemanly courtesy and delicacy, as well asfor tender sympathy with a poor slave.

This Christian spirit of love, humanity, justice, and freedom, as itpervades the whole New Testament, has also, in fact, gradually abolishedthe institution of slavery in almost all civilized nations, and will notrest till all the chains of sin and misery are broken, till the personaland eternal dignity of man redeemed by Christ is universallyacknowledged, and the evangelical freedom and brotherhood of men areperfectly attained.

Noteon the Number and Condition of Slaves in Greece and Rome.

Attica numbered, according to Ctesicles, under the governorship ofDemetrius the Phalerian (309 b.c.), 400,000 slaves, 10,000 foreigners,and only 21,000 free citizens. In Sparta the disproportion was stillgreater.

As to the Roman empire, Gibbon estimates the number of slaves underthe reign of Claudius at no less than one half of the entire population,i.e., about sixty millions (I. 52, ed. Milman, N. Y., 1850).According to Robertson there were twice as many slaves as free citizens,and Blair (in his work on Roman slavery, Edinb. 1833, p. 15) estimatesover three slaves to one freeman between the conquest of Greece (146b.c.) and the reign of Alexander Severna (a.d. 222–235). The proportionwas of course very different in the cities and in the rural districts.The majority of the plebs urbana were poor and unable to keepslaves; and the support of slaves in the city was much more expensivethan in the country. Marquardt assumes the proportion of slaves tofreemen in Rome to have been three to two. Friedländer(Sittengeschichte Roms. l. 55, fourth ed.) thinks it impossibleto make a correct general estimate, as we do not know the number ofwealthy families. But we know that Rome a.d. 24 was thrown intoconsternation by the fear of a slave insurrection (Tacit. Ann.IV. 27). Athenaeus, as quoted by Gibbon (I. 51) boldly asserts that heknew very many (πάμπολλοι) Romans who possessed, not for use, butostentation, ten and even twenty thousand slaves. In a single palace atRome, that of Pedanius Secundus, then prefect of the city, four hundredslaves were maintained, and were all executed for not preventing theirmaster’s murder (Tacit. Ann. XIV. 42, 43).

The legal condition of the slaves is thus described by Taylor onCivil Law, as quoted in Cooper’s Justinian, p. 411:"Slaves were held pro nullis, pro mortuis, pro quadrupedibus;nay, were in a much worse state than any cattle whatsoever. They had nohead in the state, no name, no title, or register; they were not capableof being injured; nor could they take by purchase or descent; they hadno heirs, and therefore could make no will; they were not entitled tothe rights and considerations of matrimony, and therefore had no reliefin case of adultery; nor were they proper objects of cognation oraffinity, but of quasi-cognation only; they could be sold, transferred,or pawned, as goods or personal estate, for goods they were, and as suchthey were esteemed; they might be tortured for evidence, punished at thediscretion of their lord, and even put to death by his authority;together with many other civil incapacities which I have no room toenumerate." Gibbon (I. 48) thinks that "against such internal enemies,whose desperate insurrections had more then once reduced the republic tothe brink of destruction, the most severe regulations and the most crueltreatment seemed almost justifiable by the great law ofself-preservation."

The individual treatment of slaves depended on the character of themaster. As a rule it was harsh and cruel. The bloody spectacles of theamphitheatre stupefied the finer sensibilities even in women. Juvenaldescribes a Roman mistress who ordered her female slaves to beunmercifully lashed in her presence till the whippers were worn out;Ovid warns the ladies not to scratch the face or stick needles into thenaked arms of the servants who adorned them; and before Hadrian amistress could condemn a slave to the death of crucifixion withoutassigning a reason. See the references in Friedländer, I. 466. It is butjust to remark that the philosophers of the first and second century,Seneca, Pliny, and Plutarch, entertained much milder views on thissubject than the older writers, and commend a humane treatment of theslaves; also that the Antonines improved their condition to some extent,and took the oft abused jurisdiction of life and death over the slavesout of private hands and vested it in the magistrates. But at that timeChristian principles and sentiments already freely circulated throughoutthe empire, and exerted a silent influence even over the educatedheathen. This unconscious atmospheric influence, so to speak, iscontinually exerted by Christianity over the surrounding world, whichwithout this would be far worse than it actually is.

§ 49. Christianity and Society.

Christianity enters with its leaven-like virtue the whole civil andsocial life of a people, and leads it on the path of progress in allgenuine civilization. It nowhere prescribes, indeed, a particular formof government, and carefully abstains from all improper interferencewith political and secular affairs. It accommodates itself tomonarchical and republican institutions, and can flourish even underoppression and persecution from the State, as the history of the firstthree centuries sufficiently shows. But it teaches the true nature andaim of all government, and the duties of rulers and subjects; itpromotes the abolition of bad laws and institutions, and theestablishment of good; it is in principle opposed alike to despotism andanarchy; it tends, under every form of government, towards order,propriety, justice, humanity, and peace; it fills the ruler with a senseof responsibility to the supreme king and judge, and the ruled with thespirit of loyalty, virtue, and piety.

Finally, the Gospel reforms the international relations by breakingdown the partition walls of prejudice and hatred among the differentnations and races. It unites in brotherly fellowship and harmony aroundthe same communion table even the Jews and the Gentiles, once sobitterly separate and hostile. The spirit of Christianity, trulycatholic or universal, rises above all national distinctions. Like thecongregation at Jerusalem, the whole apostolic church was of "one heartand of one soul."(31) It had its occasional troubles, indeed, temporarycollisions between a Peter and a Paul, between Jewish and GentileChristians; but instead of wondering at these, we must admire theconstant victory of the spirit of harmony and love over the remainingforces of the old nature and of a former state of things. The poorGentile Christians of Paul’s churches in Greece sent their charities tothe poor Jewish Christians in Palestine, and thus proved their gratitudefor the gospel and its fellowship, which they had received from thatmother church.(32) The Christians all felt themselves to be "brethren,"were constantly impressed with their common origin and their commondestiny, and considered it their sacred duty to "keep the unity of thespirit in the bond of peace."(33) While the Jews, in their spiritualpride and "odium generis humani" abhorred all Gentiles; whilethe Greeks despised all barbarians as only half men; and while theRomans, with all their might and policy, could bring their conquerednations only into a mechanical conglomeration, a giant body without asoul; Christianity, by purely moral means) founded a universal spiritualempire and a communion of saints, which stands unshaken to this day, andwill spread till it embraces all the nations of the earth as its livingmembers, and reconciles all to God.

§50. Spiritual Condition of the Congregations.—The Seven Churches inAsia.

We must not suppose that the high standard of holiness set up indoctrine and example by the evangelists and apostles was fully realizedin their congregations. The dream of the spotless purity and perfectionof the apostolic church finds no support in the apostolic writings,except as an ideal which is constantly held up before our vision tostimulate our energies. If the inspired apostles themselves disclaimedperfection, much less can we expect it from their converts, who had justcome from the errors and corruptions of Jewish and heathen society, andcould not be transformed at once without a miracle in violation of theordinary laws of moral growth.

We find, in fact, that every Epistle meets some particular difficultyand danger. No letter of Paul can be understood without the admission ofthe actual imperfection of his congregations. He found it necessary towarn them even against the vulgar sins of the flesh as well as againstthe refined sins of the spirit. He cheerfully and thankfully commendedtheir virtues, and as frankly and fearlessly condemned their errors andvices.

The same is true of the churches addressed in the Catholic Epistles,and in the Revelation of John.(34)

The seven Epistles in the second and third chapters of the Apocalypsegive us a glimpse of the church in its light and shade in the last stageof the apostolic age—primarily in Asia Minor, but through it also inother lands. These letters are all very much alike in their plan, andpresent a beautiful order, which has been well pointed out by Bengel.They contain (1) a command of Christ to write to the "angel" of thecongregation. (2) A designation of Jesus by some imposing title, whichgenerally refers to his majestic appearance (Rev. 1:13 sqq.), and servesas the basis and warrant of the subsequent promises and threatenings.(3) The address to the angel, or the responsible head of thecongregation, be it a single bishop or the college of pastors andteachers. The angels are, at all events, the representatives of thepeople committed to their charge, and what was said to them applies atthe same time to the churches. This address, or the epistle proper,consists always of (a) a short sketch of the present moralcondition of the congregation—both its virtues and defects—withcommendation or censure as the case may be; (b) an exhortationeither to repentance or to faithfulness and patience, according to theprevailing character of the church addressed; (c) a promise tohim who overcomes, together with the admonition: "He that hath an ear,let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches," or the same inthe reverse order, as in the first three epistles. This latter variationdivides the seven churches into two groups, one comprising the firstthree, the other the remaining four, just as the seven seals, the seventrumpets, and the seven vials are divided. The ever-recurringadmonition: "He that hath an ear," etc., consists of ten words. This isno unmeaning play, but an application of the Old Testament system ofsymbolical numbers, in which three was the symbol of the Godhead; fourof the world or humanity; the indivisible number seven, the sum of threeand four (as also twelve, their product), the symbol of the indissolublecovenant between God and man; and ten (seven and three), the roundnumber, the symbol of fulness and completion.

As to their moral and religious condition, the churches and therepresentatives fall, according to the Epistles, into three classes:

  1. Those which were predominantly good and pure, viz., thoseof Smyrna and Philadelphia. Hence, in the messages to these two churcheswe find no exhortation to repentance in the strict sense of the word,but only an encouragement to be steadfast, patient, and joyful undersuffering.

The church of Smyrna (a very ancient, still flourishing commercialcity in Ionia, beautifully located on the bay of Smyrna) was externallypoor and persecuted, and had still greater tribulation in view, but ischeered with the prospect of the crown of life. It was in the secondcentury ruled by Polycarp, a pupil of John, and a faithful martyr.

Philadelphia (a city built by king Attalus Philadelphus, and namedafter him, now Ala-Schär), in the province of Lydia, a rich wine region,but subject to earthquakes, was the seat of a church likewise poor andsmall outwardly, but very faithful and spiritually flourishing—a churchwhich was to have all the tribulations and hostility it met with onearth abundantly rewarded in heaven.

  1. Churches which were in a predominantly evil and criticalcondition, viz., those of Sardis and Laodicea. Here accordingly wefind severe censure and earnest exhortation to repentance.

The church at Sardis (till the time of Croesus the flourishingcapital of the Lydian empire, but now a miserable hamlet of shepherds)had indeed the name and outward form of Christianity, but not its inwardpower of faith and life. Hence it was on the brink of spiritual death.Yet Rev. 3:4 sq., distinguishes from the corrupt mass a few souls whichhad kept their walk undefiled, without, however, breaking away from thecongregation as separatists, and setting up an opposition sect forthemselves.

The church of Laodicea (a wealthy commercial city of Phrygia, not farfrom Colosse and Hierapolis, where now stands only a desolate village bythe name of Eski-Hissar) proudly fancied itself spiritually rich andfaultless, but was in truth poor and blind and naked, and in that mostdangerous state of indifference and lukewarmness from which it is moredifficult to return to the former decision and ardor, than it was topass at first from the natural coldness to faith. Hence the fearfulthreatening: "I will spew thee out of my mouth." (Lukewarm waterproduces vomiting.) Yet even the Laodiceans are not driven to despair.The Lord, in love, knocks at their door and promises them, on conditionof thorough repentance, a part in the marriage-supper of the lamb(3:20).

  1. Churches of a mixed character, viz., those of Ephesus,Pergamum, and Thyatira. In these cases commendation and censure, promiseand threatening are united.

Ephesus, then the metropolis of the Asian church, had withstood,indeed, the Gnostic errorists predicted by Paul, and faithfullymaintained the purity of the doctrine delivered to it; but it had lostthe ardor of its first love, and it is, therefore, earnestly exhorted torepent. It thus represents to us that state of dead, petrifiedorthodoxy, into which various churches oftentimes fall. Zeal for puredoctrine is, indeed, of the highest importance, but worthless withoutliving piety and active love. The Epistle to the angel of the church ofEphesus is peculiarly applicable to the later Greek church as awhole.

Pergamum in Mysia (the northernmost of these seven cities, formerlythe residence of the kings of Asia of the Attalian dynasty, and renownedfor its large library of 200,000 volumes and the manufacture ofparchment; hence the name charta Pergamena;—now Bergamo, avillage inhabited by Turks, Greeks, and Armenians) was the seat of achurch, which under trying circumstances had shown great fidelity, buttolerated in her bosom those who held dangerous Gnostic errors. For thiswant of rigid discipline she also is called on to repent.

The church of Thyatira (a flourishing manufacturing and commercialcity in Lydia, on the site of which now stands a considerable Turkishtown called Ak-Hissar, or "the White Castle," with nine mosques and oneGreek church) was very favorably distinguished for self-denying, activelove and patience, but was likewise too indulgent towards errors whichcorrupted Christianity with heathen principles and practices.

The last two churches, especially that of Thyatira, form thus theexact counterpart to that of Ephesus, and are the representatives of azealous practical piety in union with theoretical latitudinarianism. Asdoctrine always has more or less influence on practice, this also is adangerous state. That church alone is truly sound and flourishing inwhich purity of doctrine and purity of life, theoretical orthodoxy andpractical piety are harmoniously united and promote one another.

With good reason have theologians in all ages regarded these, sevenchurches of Asia Minor as a miniature of the whole Christian church."There is no condition, good, bad, or mixed, of which these epistles donot present a sample, and for which they do not give suitable andwholesome direction." Here, as everywhere, the word of God and thehistory of the apostolic church evince their applicability to all timesand circumstances, and their inexhaustible fulness of instruction,warning, and encouragement for all states and stages of religiouslife.

  29. 利25:10：“你们要将第五十年分别为圣，在遍地给一切的居民宣告自由。”参赛41:1；路4:19。↩︎

  30. 加8:28；西3:11。↩︎

  31. 徒4:32。↩︎

  32. 加2:10；林后9:12–15；罗15:25–27。↩︎

  33. 加8:28；弗4:3。↩︎

  34. 本段其余部分，有一部分取自我的《使徒教会史》(Hist.of the Apost.Church，§108，第427页及下页)，在那里，这些内容与圣约翰的生平和工作相联系。另参特伦奇(Trench) 和普伦普特里 (Plumptre) 关于七教会的专题著作，以及兰格 (Lange)对《启示录》第2、3章的注释。↩︎

entry.title: 《基督教会史》·第一卷·第七章: 圣约翰与使徒时期的最后阶段: 犹太与外邦基督教的联合巩固
entry.content:
Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The ChristianChurch

第七章圣约翰与使徒时期的最后阶段：犹太与外邦基督教的联合巩固

目录

§ 40. 约翰文献

§ 41. 约翰的生平与品格

§ 42. 约翰的使徒工作

§ 43. 关于约翰的传统1

Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ημῖν, καὶ εθεασάμεθα τὴνδόξαναυτοῦ.——道成了肉身，住在我们中间，我们也见过他的荣光。——《约翰福音》1:14。

§ 40. 约翰文献

I. 史料

  1. 约翰的《福音书、书信与启示录》。对观福音书、《使徒行传》及《加拉太书》2:9中有关约翰的记载。（经文出处见杨氏(Young)《分析经文汇编》〔Analytical Concordance〕。）

  2. 教父传承。爱任纽 (Irenaeus)：《驳异端》 (Adv.Haer.)，II. 22, 5（约翰活到图拉真〔Trajan〕时代）；III. 1,1（约翰在以弗所）；III. 3, 4（约翰与克林妥〔Cerinthus〕）；V. 30,3（约翰与《启示录》）。亚历山大的革利免 (ClemensAlex.)：《哪个财主能得救》 (Quis divessalvus)，第42章（约翰与年轻强盗）。以弗所的波利克拉底(Polycrates)，见优西比乌 (Eusebius)《教会史》 (Hist.Eccl.)，III. 31；V. 24（约翰是 μέγαλαστοιχεῖα〔伟大人物〕之一，又是 ἱερεὺς τὸ πέταλονπεφορηκώς〔佩戴金牌的祭司〕）。德尔图良 (Tertullian)：《论异端的抗辩》(De praescr.haer.)，第36章（关于约翰在罗马被浸入油中受殉道之刑，却蒙神迹保全的传说）。优西比乌：《教会史》(Hist. Eccl.)，III. 第18、23、31章；IV. 14；V.24（逾越节日期之争）。哲罗姆 (Jerome)：《加拉太书注释》 (AdGal.)，6:10（约翰最后的话）；《名人传》 (De vir.ill.)，第9章。奥古斯丁 (Augustin)：《约翰福音讲论》第124篇(Tract. 124 in Evang. Joann.)，载《全集》 (Opera) III.1970，米涅 (Migne) 编。尼基弗鲁斯·卡利斯图斯 (NicephorusCal.)：《教会史》 (Hist. Eccl.)，II. 42。

II. 伪托的传说

《约翰行传》 (Acta Johannis)，康斯特·蒂申多夫 (Const.Tischendorf) 编，载其《使徒伪经行传》 (Acta Apost.Apocr.)，莱比锡 (Lips.)，1851年，第266–276页。参较《序论》(Prolegg.)第LXXIII页及后，其中汇集了教父们关于伪托的《约翰行传》的见证。

《约翰行传：利用C. v. 蒂申多夫遗稿编订》 (Acta Joannis, unterBenutzung von C. v. Tischendorf’s Nachlass bearbeitet)，特奥德·察恩(Theod. Zahn) 编。埃尔朗根(Erlangen)，1880年（正文264页，导论clxxii页）。

这部《行传》包含普罗哥罗 (Prochorus) 所写的 πράξεις τοῦ ... Ἰωάννουτοῦθεολόγου（《神学家……约翰行传》）；他自称是七十门徒之一、耶路撒冷七位执事之一（《使徒行传》6:5），也是圣约翰的门徒；此外还包含约翰的朋友兼门徒琉修斯·卡里努斯(Leucius Charinus) 所写的 περίοδοιἸωάννου（《约翰游历记》）残篇。前者是一部宗教传奇，写于约翰死后约400年；后者据察恩判定，是小亚细亚一位作者在160年以前、很可能在140年以前写成的；它既使用了第四福音书，也使用了对观福音书，就此而言具有某种护教价值。见第cxlviii页。

法国古典语文学家马克斯·博内 (Max Bonnet)允诺出版一部新的《约翰行传》校勘本。见E. 勒鲁 (E. Leroux) 的《评论杂志》(Revue critique)，1880年，第449页。

《约翰启示录》 (Apocalypsis Johannis)，载蒂申多夫(Tischindorf)《摩西、以斯拉、保罗、约翰的伪经启示录，附马利亚安息记》(Apocalypses Apocryphae Mosis, Esdrae, Pauli, Johannis, item MariaeDormitio)。莱比锡 (Lips.)，1866年，第70–94页。

这部伪托约翰的《启示录》自称是圣约翰在基督升天后不久于他泊山 (MountTabor) 写成的。现存抄本可追溯到九世纪，最初由A. 比尔希 (A. Birch)于1804年刊行。

关于圣约翰的传说，参较詹姆森夫人 (Mrs. Jameson)：《神圣与传奇艺术》(Sacred and Legendary Art)，I. 第157–172页，第五版。

III. 传记与批判研究

弗朗西斯·特伦奇 (Francis Trench)：《福音书作者圣约翰的生平与品格》(Life and Character of St. John theEvangelist)。伦敦，1850年。

座堂主任牧师斯坦利 (Dean Stanley，卒于1881年)：《使徒时期讲章与论文》(Sermons and Essays on the ApostolicAge)。牛津与伦敦，1847年；第三版，1874年，第234–281页。

马克斯·克伦克尔 (Max Krenkel)：《使徒约翰》 (Der ApostelJohannes)。莱比锡，1871年。

詹姆斯·M. 麦克唐纳 (James M.Macdonald)：《圣约翰的生平与著作，附座堂主任牧师豪森所撰导论》 (TheLife and Writings of St. John. With Introduction by DeanHowson.)。纽约，1877年（新版，1880年）。

魏茨泽克 (Weizsäcker)：《使徒时期》 (Das Apost.Zeitalter)。1886年，第493–559页。

参较§ 20（第189页）所列有关使徒教会著作中的传记概述；以及吕克(Lücke)、迈耶 (Meyer)、兰格 (Lange)、卢特哈特 (Luthardt)、戈代(Godet)、韦斯科特 (Westcott)、普卢默 (Plummer) 各家注释的导论。

IV. 教义研究

下列学者阐述了约翰式的教义类型：尼安德(Neander)（在其论使徒时期的著作中，第四版，1847年；鲁宾逊〔Robinson〕英译本，纽约〔N.York〕，1865年，第508–531页）；弗罗曼(Frommann)（《约翰的教义观》〔Der JohanneischeLehrbegriff〕，莱比锡〔Leipz.〕，1839年）；C. 莱因哈德·克斯特林 (C.Reinh. Köstlin)（《约翰福音与书信的教义观》〔Der Lehrbegriff des Ev.und der Briefe Johannis〕，柏林，1843年）；罗伊斯(Reuss)（《约翰神学》〔Die Johann.Theologie〕，载斯特拉斯堡《神学研究论集》〔Beiträge zu denTheol. Wissenschaften〕，1847年；《约翰神学》〔La Théologiejohannique〕，巴黎，1879年；以及其《使徒时期神学》〔Theology ofthe Apost. Age〕，第二版，1860年，安妮·哈伍德〔AnnieHarwood〕据法文第三版英译，伦敦〔Lond.〕，1872–74年，2卷）；施密德(Schmid)（在其《新约圣经神学》〔Bibl. Theol. des N.T.〕中，斯图加特〔Stuttg.〕，1853年）；鲍尔(Baur)（在《新约神学讲义》〔Vorlesungen über N. T.Theol.〕中，莱比锡〔Leipz.〕，1864年）；希尔根费尔德(Hilgenfeld)（1849年及1863年）；B. 魏斯 (B.Weiss)（《约翰的教义观》〔Der JohanneischeLehrbegriff〕，柏林，1862年；以及其《新约圣经神学》〔Bibl.Theol. des N.T.〕，第四版，1884年）。此外，魏茨泽克（1862年）、拜施拉格(Beyerschlag)（1866年）等人也有论述约翰的逻各斯教义 (Logos-doctrine)与基督论的专著。

V. 《约翰福音》注释

关于《约翰福音》及其真确性的文献，自1792年至1875年（从埃文森〔Evanson〕到卢特哈特），美国学者卡斯帕·勒内·格雷戈里博士(Dr. Caspar René Gregory) 在他所译的卢特哈特《圣约翰：第四福音书的作者》(St. John, the Author of the Fourth Gospel)附录中，作了格外详尽而准确的列举。爱丁堡(Edinb.)，1875年，第283–360页。又参较以斯拉·阿博特博士 (Dr. Ezra Abbot)在史密斯 (Smith)《圣经辞典》 (Dict. of the Bible)美国版“约翰福音” (John, Gospel of)条目中极为审慎编制的书目（截至1869年），I. 第1437–1439页。

俄利根 (Origen，卒于254年)；金口约翰(Chrysostom，407年)；奥古斯丁（430年）；亚历山大的区利罗 (Cyril ofAlexandria，444年)；加尔文 (Calvin，1564年)；兰佩(Lampe)（1724年，3卷）；本格尔(Bengel)（《释经指要》〔Gnomen〕，1752年）；吕克（1820年，第三版1843年）；奥尔斯豪森(Olshausen)（1832年，埃布拉德〔Ebrard〕编第四版，1861年）；托卢克(Tholuck)（1827年，第七版1857年）；亨斯滕贝格(Hengstesnberg)（1863年；第二版，第I卷，1867年；英译本1865年）；卢特哈特（1852年；第二版完全重写，1875年；格雷戈里英译，2卷，另有一专卷论第四福音书的作者，1875年）；德·韦特—布吕克纳(DeWette-Brückner)（第五版1863年）；迈耶（迈耶本人编的第五版，也是最后一版，1869年；魏斯编第六版，1880年）；埃瓦尔德(Ewald)（1861年）；阿尔福德 (Alford)（第六版1868年）；沃兹沃思(Wordsworth)（第五版1866年）；戈代（1865年，2卷；第二版1877年，英译本3卷；第三版，巴黎，1881年，T.德怀特〔T. Dwight〕译，1886年）；兰格（沙弗译并增订，纽约〔N.Y.〕与爱丁堡，1871年）；沃特金斯(Watkins)（载埃利科特〔Ellicott〕《英语读者新约注释》〔N.T. Com. forEnglishReaders〕，1878年）；韦斯科特（载《议长注释》〔Speaker’sCommentary〕，1879年，亦有单行本）；米利根 (Milligan) 与莫尔顿(Moulton)（载《沙弗通俗注释》〔Schaff’s Popul.Com.〕，1880年）；凯尔 (Keil)（1881年）；普卢默（1881年）；托马(Thoma)（《约翰福音的起源》〔Die Genesis des Joh.Evangeliums〕，1882年）；保罗·尚茨 (PaulSchanz)（图宾根，1885年）。

VI.论第四福音书真确性与可信性的专著

我们没有篇幅列出所有书名，或各注释导论中的相关页码，请读者参阅阿博特与格雷戈里的书目。

  1. 反对其真确性的作者：

E. 埃文森 (E. Evanson)（《四部公认福音书的不协调》〔TheDissonance of the Four generally receivedEvangelists〕，格洛斯特，1792年）。K. G. 布雷特施奈德 (K. G.Bretschneider)（《论使徒约翰福音与书信的性质及起源之可能性》〔Probabiliade Ev. et Ep. Joh. Ap. Indole etOrigine〕，莱比锡〔Leips.〕，1820年；为肖特〔Schott〕、艾希霍恩〔Eichhorn〕、吕克等人所驳斥；作者本人于1828年撤回此说）。D.F. 施特劳斯 (D. F. Strauss)（在其《耶稣传》〔LebenJesu〕中，1835年；1838年第三版撤回，1840年第四版又重新提出，1864年《为德国民众所写的耶稣传》〔LebenJesu für das deutsche Volk〕中亦然）；吕策尔贝格(Lützelberger)（1840年）；布鲁诺·鲍姆 (Bruno Baum)（1840年）。——F. Chr.鲍尔 (F. Chr. Baur)（最初见于图宾根《神学年鉴》〔Theol.Jahrbücher〕1844年所载对这部福音书极为敏锐而精巧的分析，此后又于1847、1848、1853、1855、1859年重申）。他把第四福音书说成文学发展或演化的成熟成果；这一发展依黑格尔(Hegel)的方法，从正题进到反题与合题，亦即从犹太化的彼得派，进到反犹太的保罗派，再进到（伪）约翰式的调和。整个图宾根学派(Tübingen School) 都追随了他：策勒(Zeller)（1845、1847、1853年）；施韦格勒(Schwegler)（1846年）；希尔根费尔德（1849、1854、1855、1875年）；福尔克马尔(Volkmar)（1870、1876年）；申克尔 (Schenkel)（1864及1873年）；霍尔茨曼(Holtzmann)（载申克尔《圣经辞典》〔Bibellexikon〕，1871年，及《导论》〔Einleitung〕，1886年）。凯姆(Keim)（《拿撒勒人耶稣的历史》〔Gesch. Jesu v.Nazara〕，1867年起出版，第I卷，第146页及后、第167页及后；又见其节本第三版，1875年，第40页）；豪斯拉特(Hausrath)（1874年）；曼戈尔德(Mangold)（载布利克〔Bleek〕《导论》〔Introd.〕第四版，1886年）；托马（1882年）。荷兰有斯霍尔滕(Scholten)（莱顿，1865年及1871年）。英国有J. J. 泰勒 (J. J.Tayler)（伦敦，1867年）；塞缪尔·戴维森 (SamuelDavidson)（在其《新约导论》〔Introduction to the N.T.〕新版中，1868年，II. 第323页及后、第357页及后）；《超自然宗教》(Supernatural Religion)的匿名作者（第六版，第II卷，第251页及后，伦敦，1875年）；以及E. A.A.（伦敦的埃德温·A. 阿博特神学博士〔Edwin A. Abbott, D.D.〕，撰《不列颠百科全书》〔Encycl.Brit.〕“福音书”〔Gospels〕条目，第X卷，1879年，第818–843页）。

这些反对者所定的第四福音书成书年代，从110年到170年不等；但他们当中最优秀的学者，已越来越被迫从170年（鲍尔的年代）退到130年（凯姆），甚至退到二世纪之初（110年）。这对他们的理论是致命的；因为在那个时候，约翰许多亲近的朋友和门徒必定仍然在世，足以阻止一部文学虚构之作在教会中被普遍接受为使徒的真作。

罗伊斯（在其《约翰神学》〔Théologiejohannique〕，1879年；其巨著《圣经》〔LaBible〕第六部分；以及《新约圣经著作史》〔Geschichte der heil.Schriften N.T.〕第六版，1887年，第249页及后）对此问题未作定论，尽管倾向于否认约翰为作者。萨巴蒂埃(Sabatier) 先前曾捍卫其真实性（在其《耶稣生平史料论》〔Essai sur lessources de la vie deJésus〕中，1866年），后来追随罗伊斯的脚步，得出否定的结论（见其“约翰”〔Jean〕条目，载利希滕贝格〔Lichtenberger〕《宗教科学百科全书》〔Encycl.des Sciences Relig.〕，第VII卷，巴黎，1880年，第173页及后）。

魏瑟 (Weisse)（1836年）、施韦策(Schweizer)（1841年）、魏茨泽克（1857、1859、1862、1886年）、哈泽(Hase)（在其《耶稣史》〔GeschichteJesu〕中，1875年；他在早期著作中原曾捍卫其真确性），以及勒南(Renan)（1863、1867及1879年），都承认第四福音书中有真实的部分，但对于其范围彼此意见不一。有些人捍卫其中讲论的真确性，却拒绝接受神迹。勒南恰好相反，他在《耶稣传》(Vie de Jésus)第13版第477页及后的一篇专论中，赞同其中历史叙述的部分，却拒绝接受基督的讲论。他在《基督教会》(L’églisechrétienne)，1879年，第47页及后，又改变了看法。他说：“Ce quiparaît le plus probable, c’est qu’un disciple de l’apôtre, dépositairede plusieurs de ses souvenirs, se crut autorisé à parler en son nom et àécrire, vingt-cinq ou trente ans aprés sa mort, ce que l’on regrettaitqu’il n’eût pas lui-même fixé de sonvivant.”（“看来最有可能的是，使徒的一位门徒，保存着他的若干回忆，自认为有权奉他的名说话，并在他死后二十五或三十年，将人们遗憾他生前未曾亲自记录的事写下来。”）他倾向于把这部福音书的编写归给“长老约翰”（此人是否存在，本身就有疑问）和亚里斯提翁(Aristion)，二人都是使徒约翰在以弗所的门徒。他对《约翰福音》中讲论的描述，表明他完全不能领会这部福音书的精神。马修·阿诺德(Matthew Arnold)（《上帝与圣经》〔God and theBible〕，第248页）猜测，以弗所的长老们利用约翰提供的材料编成了这部福音书。

应当指出，鲍尔及其追随者，还有勒南，虽然否认第四福音书的真实性，却极力维护《启示录》出于约翰，把它视为使徒时期确实可靠的文献之一。但凯姆否定约翰曾居留以弗所的整个传承，从而摧毁了鲍尔理论的根基。

b. 以下作者曾捍卫其真确性：

§ 41. 约翰的生平与品格

“Volat avis sine meta,（飞鸟翱翔，无边无际，）

Quo nec votes nec propheta

Evolavit altius:（诗人或先知，未曾飞得比它更高；）

Tam implenda quamimpleta,（无论尚待成就，还是已经成就的事，）

Numquam vidit tot secreta

Purus homopurius.（从无凡人如此纯净地，洞见如此众多的奥秘。）

（圣维克多的亚当〔Adam of St. Victor〕。）

约翰的使命

彼得是代表权柄的犹太人使徒，保罗是代表自由的外邦人使徒；他们在耶路撒冷毁灭以前，已经完成了在世上的工作——既是为他们的时代，也是为将来的一切时代而作的工作；他们已经完成了这工作，并且借着他们著作的影响，至今仍在以永不可取代的方式继续这工作。二人都是建造的能手：一个为基督的教会奠立根基，一个在这根基上建造，而阴间的权柄永不能胜过这教会。

然而，还有一项极其重要的工作尚待完成，就是联合与巩固的工作。这工作是为那位爱的使徒、耶稣的知心朋友所保留的；就人所能反映的神人纯洁与圣洁之理想而言，他已成为耶稣最完美的映照。约翰不像彼得和保罗那样，是宣教士或实干家。据我们所知，他对于基督教向外传播所做的甚少，却为基督教在已经建立之处的内在生命与成长做得更多。对于有形教会的治理、形式和礼仪，他无所论述（甚至“教会”这个名称也未出现在他的福音书和第一封书信中），却更多地论及教会的属灵实质——信徒与基督在生命上的联合，以及信徒彼此间的弟兄相交。他兼为新约的使徒、福音书作者和先见。他活到第一世纪末，为要在使徒时期的根基和上层建筑之上，竖起那宏伟的穹顶，由新天的光辉为之镀金。

他必须在静默的默想中等候，直到教会成熟，足以领受他崇高的教训。我们的主论到约翰时，对彼得所说的那句奥秘的话，就暗示了这一点：“我若要他等到我来的时候，与你何干？”2无疑，主确曾在耶路撒冷所受的可怕审判中临到。约翰本人活过了这场审判，而他的教义与品格类型，也必长存，超越教会历史较早的阶段（彼得和保罗预示并代表了这些阶段），直到主最终降临。在这一较广的意义上，他甚至至今仍在等候；而他的著作，其中尚未探明的深邃与高远，也仍在等待合宜的解释者。最好的总在最后。在以利亚于何烈山(Mount Horeb)所见的异象中，裂山碎石的烈风、地震和火，都在耶和华微小的声音之前。3 智慧女神密涅瓦 (Minerva)的猫头鹰，到黄昏才开始飞翔。战斗的风暴，为和平的筵席预备道路。使徒时期那位伟大的战士，早已奏响了爱的主调，要使基督教世界的两部分和谐一致；而约翰以一切定义中最深刻的定义，揭示至高者内心最深处的本质：“上帝就是爱”，这不过是对保罗的回应。4

福音书中的约翰

约翰是西庇太 (Zebedee) 和撒罗米 (Salome)的儿子（可能是幼子），也是大雅各的兄弟；雅各后来成为使徒中第一位殉道者。5他可能比耶稣年轻十岁左右；古代的见证一致认为，他活到图拉真 (Trajan)在位之时，即98年以后，因此他必定享寿九十余岁。他以捕鱼为业，很可能是加利利的伯赛大(Bethsaida)人（如同彼得、安得烈和腓力）。他的父母家境似乎颇为宽裕。他父亲雇有工人；他母亲属于那群高尚的妇女，她们跟随耶稣，用自己的财物供给他，又买香膏要膏他的身体；她们是最后留在十字架旁、最先来到敞开的坟墓前的人。约翰本人认识大祭司，并在耶路撒冷或加利利拥有一所房屋，将我们主的母亲接到那里奉养。6

按肉身说，他是耶稣的表弟，因为他的母亲是马利亚的姐妹。7这一亲属关系，加上青春的热忱和他天性中炽烈的情感，构成了他与主亲密相交的基础。

他不像保罗那样受过拉比教育；在犹太学者眼中，他和彼得及其他加利利门徒一样，是个“没有学问的小民”。8但他曾在施洗约翰门下受预备性的教导；施洗约翰以耶稣是“上帝的羔羊，除去世人罪孽的”为见证，概括了自己先知的使命，而约翰后来在自己的著作中阐发了这一见证。正是这见证，引领他在约旦河畔来到耶稣面前，经历了那次难忘的会面；半个世纪以后，他甚至还记得当时的时辰。9他不仅是十二使徒之一，更是三位蒙拣选者中的特选者。彼得作为弥赛亚的朋友，在公众面前更为显著；约翰则在亲近的圈子里被人视为耶稣的朋友。10彼得总是注目于基督的职分，询问自己和其他使徒应当做什么；约翰却定睛注视耶稣本身，专心领会夫子所说的话。他们之间的差别，正如忙碌的马大急于服事，而沉思的马利亚以受教为满足。惟有约翰与彼得和他的兄弟雅各一同，目睹了登山变像和客西马尼园的情景——我们主在世生活中最高的荣耀与最深的降卑。在最后的晚餐上，他靠在主的胸膛上，将那些奇妙的临别讲论珍藏在心里，留待日后使用。他跟随主进入该亚法(Caiaphas)的院子。所有门徒中，惟有他在场目睹了钉十字架，并受临终的救主托付，照顾他的母亲。这是一个格外细腻温柔的场景：Materdolorosa（悲痛之母）与蒙爱的门徒仰望十字架，垂死的儿子与主以母子之爱将他们联结起来。这成为那些出于天上的属灵关系的典范，比血缘和利害关系更深、更坚固。约翰既是最后留在十字架旁的人，也是在复活的清晨，继抹大拉的马利亚之后，最先来到敞开的坟墓前向内观看的门徒；他甚至跑在彼得前面。复活的主在加利利湖岸向门徒显现时，也是他首先认出主来。11

他似乎是使徒中最年轻的，因为他比他们所有人都多活了许多年；他无疑是最有天赋、最蒙眷爱的。他具有最高的宗教天才——不是为栽种，而是为浇灌；不是为外在的行动和奋进的工作，而是为内在的默想，洞察基督位格以及在他里面永生的奥秘。品格的纯洁与单纯，情感的深厚与热烈，以及罕见的属灵领悟力与直觉，是他的主要特征；这些特征借着神的恩典，变得高尚，并分别为圣。

关于约翰的生平，没有剧烈转变的记载；他在静默中、不知不觉地成长，进入与主的相交，并愈益效法主的榜样；在这一点上，他与保罗恰成对照。与其他门徒相比，他听得更多，看得更多，说得却更少。他领受了主那些最深刻、却未引起别人注意的话；虽然起初他自己也不明白，却将这些话反复思想，存在心里，直到圣灵使他明白。他与马利亚的亲密关系，也必有助于他从内在了解主的心思和情怀。他始终以蒙爱门徒的形象出现，与主最为亲密，也最能与主心心相印。12

雷子与蒙爱的门徒

符类福音与约翰著作所描绘的约翰，表面上似乎彼此矛盾，正如《启示录》与第四福音之间的差异一样；但仔细考察，就会发现这不过是同一性格的两个方面。福音书中的彼得与他书信中的彼得，也有类似的情形：前者年轻、冲动、急躁、多变，后者则因上帝的恩典而成熟、克制、温厚、纯净。

在《马可福音》中，约翰被称为雷子（Boanerges）。13救主赐给他和他哥哥的这个称号，无疑是一种尊称，预示着他未来的使命，正如赐给西门的彼得之名一样。在希伯来人看来，雷声就是上帝的声音。14它所表达的是热烈的性情、强大的力量和刚烈的性格；至于是善是恶，则取决于动机和目的。同一声雷，既使人惊恐，也借着随之而来的阵雨洁净空气，滋润大地，使之结实。火热的性情若受理性节制，为真理服务，就能成为强大的建设力量；同样的性情若不受约束、误入歧途，则会成为同样强大的破坏力量。约翰燃烧的热忱与献身之心，只需加以管教和明辨，就能成为历代教会的祝福与激励。

西庇太的两个儿子早年并不明白律法与福音的区别；有一个撒马利亚村庄拒绝接待耶稣，他们便大发义怒，想要像古时的以利亚一样，吩咐火从天降，烧灭他们。15但几年之后，约翰前往撒马利亚，坚固新归信的人时，却为他们求下了属神生命与光明的火，就是圣灵的恩赐。16他不容那些在使徒圈子之外奉基督的名行善事的人，其根源也是这种为夫子而发、却误入歧途的热心。17两兄弟渴望在弥赛亚的国里居于最高地位，他们的母亲也有同样的愿望；这同样显明了他们的长处与弱点：他们有一种高贵的志向，愿意亲近基督，即使这意味着亲近烈火与刀剑；然而，这种志向仍未脱尽自私与骄傲，理当受到我们主的责备，而主也将受血洗的前景摆在他们面前。18

这一切与约翰的著作完全一致。在这些著作中，他绝非柔弱多情的人，而是立场鲜明、坚定果决的人。他的性情无疑温柔可爱，但同时也有细腻的感受、炽烈的情怀和坚强的信念。这些特征绝非不能相容。他不知妥协，也不容忠诚有所分割。他里面燃烧着圣洁的火，只是他的激动是在深处，而非浮于表面。在《启示录》中，雷声响亮而有力地震撼着基督及其国度的仇敌；但另一方面，同一卷书里也有安息的片段、平安喜乐的颂歌，以及对天上耶路撒冷的描绘，这一切只能出自那蒙爱的门徒之手。在约翰的福音书和书信中，我们感受到同样的力量，只是受到节制与约束。他既记述救主最严厉的讲论，也记述他最温柔的讲论，视乎主是在向真理的仇敌说话，还是置身门徒之中。没有别的福音书作者，能让我们如此深入地看见基督与犹太教权势集团之间的对立，以及那最终酿成流血毒谋、日益加深的仇恨；也没有一位使徒，比约翰更鲜明地划出光明与黑暗、真理与虚谎、基督与敌基督之间的界线。他的福音书与书信，始终围绕着这些不可调和的对立展开。他不知上帝与巴力之间有何妥协可言。他谈到那卖主的人，以及法利赛人向自己的弥赛亚日益增长的愤怒时，流露出何等圣洁的憎恶！他借主的话，何等严厉地斥责那些心怀杀机、不信的犹太人，称他们为魔鬼的儿女！在书信中，他称凡有辱自己基督徒信仰表白的人为说谎的；凡恨弟兄的为杀人的；凡故意犯罪的为魔鬼的儿女；他又郑重警告人提防那些否认道成肉身奥秘的教师，称他们为敌基督，甚至禁止向他们问安。19他对基督的爱有多深，对敌基督的恨就有多深。因为恨就是反向的爱。爱与恨是同一种激情，只是显露的方向相反。同一个太阳，既给活物光明和温暖，也加速死物的腐朽。

基督教艺术在这一点上充分领会了约翰的双重性格：将他的面容描绘得如女子般纯洁温柔，却并不软弱；又以一只勇猛的鹰作为他的象征，展翅翱翔于云霄之上。20

《启示录》与第四福音

正确理解上述约翰的性格，便消除了将《启示录》与第四福音归于同一作者的主要困难。21两者的性情相同：都是高贵而热烈的天性，能够怀有强烈的爱与恨；所不同的，只是壮年与暮年、战阵的轰鸣与和平的安息之间的差别。两者的神学也是相同的，包括基督论与救恩论最具特色的要点。22没有别的使徒称基督为逻各斯（Logos）。这部福音书就是“属灵化的《启示录》”，或说是理想化的《启示录》。甚至那乍看之下令人惊异的文体差异，经过细察，也就消失了。《启示录》的希腊文是新约各书中最具希伯来色彩的；鉴于它与希伯来预言的密切关系，而古典希腊文又没有相应的表达范式，这是意料之中的。第四福音的希腊文则纯正而无不规则之处；然而，福音书作者约翰毕竟也表现出对希伯来宗教最深的熟悉与洞察，并保存了其中最纯洁、最高贵的成分；他的文体具有旧约全部的赤子般的单纯和格言式的简洁；它不过是由希伯来灵魂赋予生命的希腊躯体。23

要解释《启示录》与约翰其他著作的差异，我们也必须考虑到：直接受默示而写成的先知性作品，与历史性及教导性作品之间必然存在差别；两者写作时间又相隔约二十年。《启示录》写于耶路撒冷被毁之前，第四福音则写于第一世纪末叶，当时他已极其年迈，却如鹰一般返老还童，正如几位最伟大的诗人荷马（Homer）、索福克勒斯（Sophocles）、弥尔顿（Milton）和歌德（Goethe）的情形一样。

附注

I. 雷子与爱的使徒

我从友人戈代博士（Dr.Godet）的著作中，摘引几段论约翰性格的精辟见解（《注释》〔Com.〕I.35，克伦比〔Crombie〕与库辛〔Cusin〕英译）：

“我们该怎样解释这两种表面上如此相反的性格特征呢？有些人性情深沉，善于领受，惯于将所受的感动封存在自己里面；这些感动越是深刻、激荡，他们就越是如此。但一旦这些人失去自制，那些长久压抑的情感便会突然爆发，使周围的人大为惊讶。约翰的性格岂不正属此类吗？耶稣给他和他兄弟起名叫半尼其（Boanerges），就是雷子（《马可福音》3:17），还有比这更贴切的描述吗？我不能认为，耶稣赐下这个称号，是像所有古代作者所相信的那样，为要标明他们出众的口才。我也不能同意，他是要借这称号，让人永远记住他们在上述某一场合中所发的怒气。前面所说的，引导我们作出一种更自然、也更配得上耶稣本人的解释。正如电逐渐积聚在云中，直到忽然化为闪电与霹雳迸发出来；照样，在这两个充满爱与热情的性情之中，种种感动默默积聚，直等到内心满溢，便以出人意料的猛烈之势迸发而出。我们喜欢把圣约翰想象为温柔而非刚强的人，甚至温柔到了软弱的地步。他的著作岂不是首先并且最为强调爱吗？这位老人最后的讲道，岂不就是‘你们要彼此相爱’吗？这固然不错；但我们忘记了他生平最初与最后阶段的另一些不同特征，它们显明他的性情中有某种果决、锐利、绝对，甚至猛烈的成分。如果我们考虑到上述一切事实，就会看出，他属于这样一类敏感而热烈的心灵：他们崇尚理想，一旦遇见在他们看来实现了自己梦想的那一位，便立刻毫无保留地依附于他；而他们的献身之情，也很容易变得排他而不宽容。凡与他们的热情不相契合的事物，都使他们感到排斥。他们不再理解内心何以能有所分割，因为他们自己根本不知如何如此行。以一切报答一切！这就是他们的格言。哪里没有那一切，在他们眼中，哪里就一无所有。这样的情感，总不免掺杂不纯的自我中心。必须有神圣的工作，才能使构成这种情感根基的真正献身之心，最终显出其全部崇高。如果我们没有看错，这就是约翰内心最深处的历程。”参戈代《注释》（Com.）法文第三版，I，第50页。

韦斯科特博士（Dr.Westcott，在其《注释》〔Com.〕第xxxiii页中）说：“约翰知道，与基督同在就是生命，拒绝基督就是死亡；他并不畏缩，乃以旧约时代的精神表达这一思想。随着时日推移，他从主学会了更忠实的忍耐，却没有丢掉那焚烧着他的热烈献身之心。直到最后，那些令人敬畏的警戒之言，犹如宝座周围的雷声，仍显明那隐秘之火的存在。《启示录》的每一页，都激荡着祭坛底下那些灵魂的呼喊：‘要等到几时呢？’（《启示录》6:10）；对于有关基督位格的谬误，也没有别处比他的书信斥责得更严厉（《约翰二书》10节；《约翰一书》4:1及下）。”斯坦利（Stanley）的著作中也有类似的段落。

  1. 约翰的使命

斯坦利座堂主任牧师（DeanStanley，《使徒时期的讲道与论文》〔Sermons and Essays on the Apost.Age,〕，第249页及下页，第3版）说：“约翰所讲的，首要的是灵魂与上帝的联合；但这并非仅凭东方的沉思，或神秘的消融，而是凭着那此时才首次在世界秩序中取得其应有地位的一个字——爱。宣告人心最深处的原则乃是信，这使命留给了圣保罗；宣告上帝本质的属性乃是爱，这使命则留给了圣约翰。旧约已经教导人，‘智慧的开端是敬畏上帝’；新约最后一位使徒还要教导人，‘智慧的终极是爱上帝’。古时，无论犹太人还是异教徒，无论希腊哲学还是东方宗教，都曾教导说，神明喜悦人的献祭、思辨与苦刑；而那项教训——上帝儿女唯一的标记就是‘爱弟兄’——则留给圣约翰来作充分的阐明。正如爱贯穿我们对于他教训的全部理解，爱也贯穿我们对于他品格的全部理解。我们看见他——这想象想必并非毫无根据——随着那个世纪的衰逝而渐渐衰老；他的每一种感官、每一种能力都日益衰弱，惟有那最具神圣性质的能力，燃烧得愈加明亮；我们看见这爱从他每一个眼神、每一个姿态中流露出来，成为他生活行动于其中的氛围里唯一赋予生气的原则；天地、过去、现在与未来，都向他回响着他最后话语中那渐趋低回的曲调：‘我们爱他，因为他先爱我们。’及至他终于在圣经的最后几页中消失于我们的视野，教会传统仍在这结尾处流连不去；在那个感人的故事中——它并不因我们如此熟悉而稍减感人之力——我们看见年迈的使徒由门徒抱着，来到以弗所的聚会中，在那里一遍又一遍地重复同一句话：‘小子们哪，你们要彼此相爱。’后来有人问他，为何只讲这一句而不讲别的，他便用那众所周知、确实配作这位蒙爱门徒临别之言的话回答说：‘因为这是我们主的命令；你们若遵行这一条，就不需要别的了。’”

§ 42. 约翰的使徒工作

《使徒行传》中的约翰

在使徒时期基督教的第一阶段，约翰与彼得及主的兄弟雅各同列为受割礼者教会的三根柱石；保罗与巴拿巴则代表外邦人的教会。24这似乎意味着，他当时尚未充分领会福音的普世性与自由。但在这三人之中，他最为开明，居于雅各、彼得这一方与保罗另一方之间，并已展望犹太基督教与外邦基督教的和解。犹太主义者从未像援引雅各或彼得那样，援引约翰为自己的依据。25我们虽能看到矶法派和雅各派的踪迹，却看不到约翰派的踪迹。他超然于争竞和分裂之上。

在《使徒行传》前几章中，他是这新宗教中仅次于彼得的主要使徒；他与彼得一同医治了圣殿门口的瘸子；与彼得一同被带到公会面前，为基督作见证；又与彼得一同受使徒差遣，从耶路撒冷到撒马利亚，借着将圣灵赐给那些归信基督的人来坚固他们；随后与彼得一同返回耶路撒冷。26但彼得总是先被提名，并且在言语和行动上带头；约翰则以一种神秘的沉默跟随，给人的印象是一股蓄而未发的力量，将在未来某时显露出来。他必定出席了公元50年在耶路撒冷召开的使徒会议，但没有发言，也没有积极参与那场关于割礼及加入教会条件的大辩论。27这一切与福音书赋予他的那种谦逊、沉默却又卓然出众的品格完全一致。

公元50年以后，他似乎离开了耶路撒冷。《使徒行传》不再提到他，也不再提到彼得。保罗第五次、也是最后一次访问圣城时（公元58年），见到了雅各，却没有见到任何一位使徒。28

在以弗所的约翰

约翰后来最重要的工作，保存在他的著作中，我们将在另一章充分考察。这些著作向我们展示了一段几乎全然属于内在与属灵领域的历史，其影响之深远、意义之重大，却不可估量。它们没有提及他的居住与写作的时间和地点。但《启示录》表明，他居于小亚细亚（AsiaMinor）众教会的领袖地位。29古代一致的见证证实了这一点；这见证不容任何合理的怀疑，并指出以弗所（Ephesus）是他晚年的居所。30他在提拉真（Trajan）统治期间，以极高的年寿死于那里；提拉真的统治始于98年。第二世纪时，人们还在那里指认他的坟墓。

我们不知道他何时迁往小亚细亚，但不可能早于63年。因为保罗在对以弗所长老的临别训言中，以及《以弗所书》《歌罗西书》和《提摩太后书》中，都没有提到约翰，并且以小亚细亚众教会监督的权柄发言。很可能是彼得与保罗的殉道，促使约翰接管这些如同失怙、面临严重危险和试炼的教会。31

以弗所是亚细亚行省的首府，是希腊文化、商业和宗教的中心；自古便以荷马（Homer）、阿那克里翁（Anacreon）和弥姆涅尔摩斯（Mimnermus）的诗歌，泰勒斯（Thales）、阿那克西美尼（Anaximenes）和阿那克西曼德（Anaximander）的哲学，以及狄安娜（Diana）的崇拜和宏伟神庙而闻名。保罗曾在那里工作三年（54–57年），建立了一间颇有影响的教会，成为周围异教黑暗中的灯塔。从那里，他最便于与自己在各行省建立的许多教会保持联系。他在那里经历了特殊的喜乐和试炼，也预见到将从内部兴起的异端所带来的巨大危险。32正统基督教与异端基督教的一切势力，都汇集于此。耶路撒冷正走向覆亡；罗马尚未成为第二个耶路撒冷。由于保罗和约翰的工作，以弗所成为第一世纪后半叶及第二世纪大部分时期教会历史的主要舞台。那位元老般的殉道者坡旅甲（Polycarp），以及与诺斯替主义（Gnosticism）争战中的主要神学家爱任纽（Irenaeus），最能代表约翰的精神，并为他的影响作证。惟有约翰能够完成保罗和彼得的工作，赋予教会一种紧密的合一，使她能够抵御外来的逼迫和内部的异端与败坏，保全自己。

若非约翰的著作，第一世纪最后三十年的历史几乎会是一片空白。这些年有如复活与升天之间那神秘的四十天；那时，主仿佛徘徊于天地之间，几乎不触及下面的大地，向门徒显现时，如同来自另一个世界的灵。但第二、第三世纪的神学，显然以约翰的著作为前提，并以他的基督论为出发点，而非保罗的人论与救恩论；后两者几乎被埋没无闻，直到非洲的奥古斯丁（Augustin）才使它们重新发扬起来。

在拔摩的约翰

约翰被放逐到爱琴海（Aegeansea）中、以弗所西南方那座孤寂、多岩而荒瘠的拔摩岛（Patmos，今名Patmo或Palmosa）。这说法依据《启示录》1:9通常所理解的见证：“我约翰，就是你们的弟兄，和你们在耶稣里一同有分于患难、国度、忍耐的，为（由于）上帝的道，并为耶稣的见证，曾在那名叫拔摩的海岛上。”33他在那里“当主日，在灵里”，领受了那些关乎基督教争战与得胜的奇妙启示。

他被放逐到拔摩的事实，得到古代一致见证的证实。34这件事在岛上的传统中长存不灭；除此以外，这座岛并无别的意义。“约翰——这就是拔摩所唤起的思想；这岛属于他，是他的圣所。岛上的石头传讲着他，他活在每个人心中。”35

放逐的时间尚不确定，取决于《启示录》写作年代这一有争议的问题。外部证据指向图密善（Domitian）统治时期，即公元95年；内部证据则指向尼禄统治时期，或他死后不久，即公元68年。

通行的传统——我们可以说，是唯一明确的传统——始于约170年爱任纽这样一位可敬的见证人，将这次放逐定在图密善统治末期；他的统治自81年延续至96年。36他是第二位逼迫基督教的罗马皇帝，而放逐是他惯用的刑罚之一。37这两个事实都支持这一传统。他起初颇有可取之处，后来却变得像尼禄一样残酷嗜血，并且在虚伪和亵渎地自封为神这两方面，更超过尼禄。他在书信开头写道：“我们的主和上帝命令”，并要求臣民如此称呼他。38他下令将自己的金像银像安放在各神庙最神圣的地方。他显得最友善时，正是最危险的时候。无论元老还是执政官，一旦受到他阴暗的猜忌，或妨碍了他的野心，他都不予饶恕。他搜寻大卫的后裔和耶稣的亲属，惧怕他们有所图谋，却发现他们都是贫穷而无辜的人。39许多基督徒在他统治期间因无神论的罪名殉道——其中包括他自己的堂亲、具有执政官身份的弗拉维乌斯·克莱门斯（FlaviusClemens），他被处死；其妻多米提拉（Domitilla）则被放逐到那不勒斯（Naples）附近的潘达特里亚岛（Pandateria）。40支持传统年代的理由，还可以说有一种内在的适切性：这部为正典作结、论述末后之事直至最终成全的书，理应最后写成。

然而，《启示录》本身的内部证据，以及它与第四福音书的比较，都支持一个较早的年代，即耶路撒冷被毁以前、尼禄死后（68年）的帝位空缺时期；那时，兽，也就是罗马帝国，受了伤，却不久就要复原（因韦斯帕芗登基）。早期传统说，有人曾企图在罗马或以弗所以油刑使约翰殉道；倘若这说法有某种根据，自然会指向尼禄的逼迫，那时基督徒被裹上易燃之物，烧作火炬。书中对帝国逼迫的明确暗示，用于尼禄远比用于图密善更为贴切。我们已经提到，《启示录》的希伯来色彩与炽烈气势，和第四福音书纯熟的希腊文与宁静安详之间，存在差异；若前者早写了约二十年，这些差异便更容易解释。这一观点在古代传统中得到一些微弱的支持，41也已为现代大多数批判派历史学家和注释家所采纳。42

因此，我们认为最可能的看法是：约翰在尼禄统治下被放逐到拔摩，在尼禄死后不久，即公元68或69年，写成《启示录》，随后返回以弗所，若干年（也许二十年）后完成福音书和书信，并于公元98年以后、提拉真统治期间安然睡去。

忠实地记述历史中的基督，充分展现他兼具神人二性之位格的丰盛，显明他是所有信徒永生的体现与源泉，再附上一封讲明实际应用的书信——这就是那位蒙爱门徒在第二世纪的门槛上、在使徒时期金色的夕照中所传的最后信息。他对青年时代的回忆，经过长久经验的陶冶，因圣灵而焕然生辉，放射着真理与圣洁的属天光辉，乃是这位最后的使徒留给教会后世万代最宝贵的遗产。

§ 43. 关于约翰的传统43

约翰的形象深深铭刻在教会心中；早期教父保存了不少关于他的轶事，多少显出他的性格，也多少有其可信之处。

第二世纪末，亚历山大的革利免 (Clement of Alexandria)描写约翰是一位忠心而献身的牧者：他年老时，在一次巡访途中，出于爱心去追寻一位自己从前带领归信、后来却沦为强盗的人，使他重归教会。

爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 转述据说出自坡旅甲 (Polycarp)之口的一件事，见证了约翰作为“雷子”的性格：约翰在以弗所的一处公共浴室，遇见否认我们主道成肉身的诺斯替派异端者克林妥(Cerinthus)，44便不肯与他同处一个屋顶之下，恐怕房屋倒塌。这使人想起《路加福音》9:49所记的事，以及使徒在《约翰二书》10、11节所发的严厉警告。这个故事表明，对真理最深切的爱，可以与对谬误和道德邪恶最严厉的斥责并存。45

哲罗姆 (Jerome)将他描绘为爱的门徒：他到了极高龄时，由门徒用臂膀抬到聚会之处，一再重复这句劝勉：“小子们哪，你们要彼此相爱。”又补充说：“这是主的命令；只要实行了这一条，就够了。”在一切关于约翰的传统中，这一则最为可信，也最有益处。

在希腊教会中，约翰有“神学家” (θεολόγος)的称号，因为他最清楚地教导了基督的神性 (τὴν θεότητα τοῦλόγου)。他又因贞洁和被认为终身未婚，而被称为“童贞者” (παρθένος)。46奥古斯丁 (Augustin)说，有人认为，约翰自幼格外贞洁，乃是他与耶稣亲密的缘由。47

第五世纪的修士卡西安 (Cassian)讲述了约翰与猎人的故事：约翰温柔地逗弄着手中的一只鹧鸪，有位猎人见了感到惊讶，他便对猎人说：“不要因我心灵这片刻而轻微的松弛而见怪；若没有这种调剂，精神就会因过度劳累而衰疲，在需要的时候，便不能回应职责的呼召。”赤子般的纯真与活泼，常与真正伟大的心灵相伴。

据优西比乌 (Eusebius) 记载，第二世纪末的以弗所主教波利克拉底(Polycrates)说，约翰在小亚细亚引入了犹太人的习俗，在尼散月十四日守逾越节，不论那天是否为主日。这件事在第二世纪的逾越节争论，以及近代关于《约翰福音》真伪的争论中，都占有重要地位。

这位以弗所的波利克拉底还描写约翰佩戴着犹太大祭司的金牌，或称冠冕（出28:36、37；39:30、31）。这大概是比喻祭司的圣洁；约翰认为一切真信徒都具有这种圣洁（参启2:17），而他身为长老之首，在这方面尤为卓越。48

由于误解了耶稣在《约翰福音》21:22所说的那句隐晦的话，便产生了一种传说：约翰只是在坟墓里睡着，呼吸时坟丘微微起伏，等待着主最后的降临。这传说的另一种说法是，他虽死了，却立刻复活，像以利亚一样被接到天上，将与以利亚一同归来，作基督再临的先驱。49
