§ 41. Life and Character ofJohn

"Volat avis sine meta,

*Quo nec votes nec propheta

Evolavit altius:*

Tam implenda quam impleta,

*Numquam vidit tot secreta

Purus homo purius.*

(Adam of St. Victor.)

The Mission of John.

Peter, the Jewish apostle of authority, and Paul, the Gentile apostleof freedom, had done their work on earth before the destruction ofJerusalem—had done it for their age and for all ages to come; had doneit, and by the influence of their writings are doing it still, in amanner that can never be superseded. Both were master-builders, the onein laying the foundation, the other in rearing the superstructure, ofthe church of Christ, against which the gates of Hades can neverprevail.

But there remained a most important additional work to be done, awork of union and consolidation. This was reserved for the apostle oflove, the bosom-friend of Jesus, who had become his most perfectreflection so far as any human being can reflect the ideal ofdivine-human purity and holiness. John was not a missionary or a man ofaction, like Peter and Paul. He did little, so far as we know, for theoutward spread of Christianity, but all the more for the inner life andgrowth of Christianity where it was already established. He has nothingto say about the government, the forms, and rites of the visible church(even the name does not occur in his Gospel and first Epistle), but allthe more about the spiritual substance of the church—the vital union ofbelievers with Christ and the brotherly communion of believers amongthemselves. He is at once the apostle, the evangelist, and the seer, ofthe new covenant. He lived to the close of the first century, that hemight erect on the foundation and superstructure of the apostolic agethe majestic dome gilded by the light of the new heaven.

He had to wait in silent meditation till the church was ripe for hissublime teaching. This is intimated by the mysterious word of our Lordto Peter with reference to John: "If I will that he tarry till I come,what is that to thee?"(1) No doubt the Lord did come in the terriblejudgment of Jerusalem. John outlived it personally, and his type ofdoctrine and character will outlive the earlier stages of church history(anticipated and typified by Peter and Paul) till the final coming ofthe Lord. In that wider sense he tarries even till now, and hiswritings, with their unexplored depths and heights still wait for theproper interpreter. The best comes last. In the vision of Elijah onMount Horeb, the strong wind that rent the mountains and brake in piecesthe rocks, and the earthquake, and the fire preceded the still smallvoice of Jehovah.(2) The owl of Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, beginsits flight at twilight. The storm of battle prepares the way for thefeast of peace. The great warrior of the apostolic age already soundedthe keynote of love which was to harmonize the two sections ofChristendom; and John only responded to Paul when he revealed the inmostheart of the supreme being by the profoundest of all definitions: "Godis love."(3)

John in the Gospels.

John was a son (probably the younger son) of Zebedee and Salome, anda brother of the elder James, who became the protomartyr of theapostles.(4) He may have been about ten years younger than Jesus, andas, according to the unanimous testimony of antiquity, he lived till thereign of Trajan, i.e., till after 98, he must have attained anage of over ninety years. He was a fisherman by trade, probably ofBethsaida in Galilee (like Peter, Andrew, and Philip). His parents seemto have been in comfortable circumstances. His father kept hiredservants; his mother belonged to the noble band of women who followedJesus and supported him with their means, who purchased spices to embalmhim, who were the last at the cross and the first at the open tomb. Johnhimself was acquainted with the high priest, and owned a house inJerusalem or Galilee, into which he received the mother of ourLord.(5)

He was a cousin of Jesus, according to the flesh, from his mother, asister of Mary.(6) This relationship, together with the enthusiasm ofyouth and the fervor of his emotional nature, formed the basis of hisintimacy with the Lord.

He had no rabbinical training, like Paul, and in the eyes of theJewish scholars he was, like Peter and the other Galilaean disciples, an"unlearned and ignorant man."(7) But he passed through the preparatoryschool of John the Baptist who summed up his prophetic mission in thetestimony to Jesus as the "Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of theworld," a testimony which he afterwards expanded in his own writings. Itwas this testimony which led him to Jesus on the banks of the Jordan inthat memorable interview of which, half a century afterwards, heremembered the very hour.(8) He was not only one of the Twelve, but thechosen of the chosen Three. Peter stood out more prominently before thepublic as the friend of the Messiah; John was known in the privatecircle as the friend of Jesus.(9) Peter always looked at the officialcharacter of Christ, and asked what he and the other apostles should do;John gazed steadily at the person of Jesus, and was intent to learn whatthe Master said. They differed as the busy Martha, anxious to serve, andthe pensive Mary, contented to learn. John alone, with Peter and hisbrother James, witnessed the scene of the transfiguration and ofGethsemane—the highest exaltation and the deepest humiliation in theearthly life of our Lord. He leaned on his breast at the last Supper andtreasured those wonderful farewell discourses in his heart for futureuse. He followed him to the court of Caiaphas. He alone of all thedisciples was present at the crucifixion, and was intrusted by thedeparting Saviour with the care of his mother. This was a scene ofunique delicacy and tenderness: the Mater dolorosa and thebeloved disciple gazing at the cross, the dying Son and Lord unitingthem in maternal and filial love. It furnishes the type of thoseheaven-born spiritual relationships, which are deeper and stronger thanthose of blood and interest. As John was the last at the cross, so hewas also, next to Mary Magdalene, the first of the disciples who,outrunning even Peter, looked into the open tomb on the resurrectionmorning; and he first recognized the risen Lord when he appeared to thedisciples on the shore of the lake of Galilee.(10)

He seems to have been the youngest of the apostles, as he longoutlived them all; he certainly was the most gifted and the mostfavored. He had a religious genius of the highest order—not indeed forplanting, but for watering; not for outward action and aggressive work,but for inward contemplation and insight into the mystery of Christ’sperson and of eternal life in him. Purity and simplicity of character,depth and ardor of affection, and a rare faculty of spiritual perceptionand intuition, were his leading traits, which became ennobled andconsecrated by divine grace.

There are no violent changes reported in John’s history; he grewsilently and imperceptibly into the communion of his Lord and conformityto his example; he was in this respect the antipode of Paul. He heardmore and saw more, but spoke less, than the other disciples. He absorbedhis deepest sayings, which escaped the attention of others; and althoughhe himself did not understand them at first, he pondered them in hisheart till the Holy Spirit illuminated them. His intimacy with Mary mustalso have aided him in gaining an interior view of the mind and heart ofhis Lord. He appears throughout as the beloved disciple, in closestintimacy and in fullest sympathy with the Lord.(11)

The Son of Thunderand the Beloved Disciple.

There is an apparent contradiction between the Synoptic and theJohannean picture of John, as there is between the Apocalypse and thefourth Gospel; but on closer inspection it is only the twofold aspect ofone and the same character. We have a parallel in the Peter of theGospels and the Peter of his Epistles: the first youthful, impulsive,hasty, changeable, the other matured, subdued, mellowed, refined bydivine grace.

In the Gospel of Mark, John appears as a Son of Thunder(Boanerges).(12) This surname, given to him and to his elder brother byour Saviour, was undoubtedly an epithet of honor and foreshadowed hisfuture mission, like the name Peter given to Simon. Thunder to theHebrews was the voice of God.(13) It conveys the idea of ardent temper,great strength and vehemence of character whether for good or for evil,according to the motive and aim. The same thunder which terrifies doesalso purify the air and fructify the earth with its accompanying showersof rain. Fiery temper under the control of reason and in the service oftruth is as great a power of construction as the same temper,uncontrolled and misdirected, is a power of destruction. John’s burningzeal and devotion needed only discipline and discretion to become abenediction and inspiration to the church in all ages.

In their early history the sons of Zebedee misunderstood thedifference between the law and the gospel, when, in an outburst of holyindignation against a Samaritan village which refused to receive Jesus,they were ready, like Elijah of old, to call consuming fire fromheaven.(14) But when, some years afterwards, John went to Samaria toconfirm the new converts, he called down upon them the fire of divinelife and light, the gift of the Holy Spirit.(15) The same mistaken zealfor his Master was at the bottom of his intolerance towards those whoperformed a good work in the name of Christ, but outside of theapostolic circle.(16) The desire of the two brothers, in which theirmother shared, for the highest positions in the Messianic kingdom,likewise reveals both their strength and their weakness, a nobleambition to be near Christ, though it be near the fire and the sword,yet an ambition that was not free from selfishness and pride, whichdeserved the rebuke of our Lord, who held up before them the prospect ofthe baptism of blood.(17)

All this is quite consistent with the writings of John. He appearsthere by no means as a soft and sentimental, but as a positive anddecided character. He had no doubt a sweet and lovely disposition, butat the same time a delicate sensibility, ardent feelings, and strongconvictions. These traits are by no means incompatible. He knew nocompromise, no division of loyalty. A holy fire burned within him,though he was moved in the deep rather than on the surface. In theApocalypse, the thunder rolls loud and mighty against the enemies ofChrist and his kingdom, while on the other hand there are in the samebook episodes of rest and anthems, of peace and joy, and a descriptionof the heavenly Jerusalem, which could have proceeded only from thebeloved disciple. In the Gospel and the Epistles of John, we feel thesame power, only subdued and restrained. He reports the severest as wellas the sweetest discourses of the Saviour, according as he speaks to theenemies of the truth, or in the circle of the disciples. No otherevangelist gives us such a profound inside-view of the antagonismbetween Christ and the Jewish hierarchy, and of the growing intensity ofthat hatred which culminated in the bloody counsel; no apostle draws asharper line of demarcation between light and darkness, truth andfalsehood, Christ and Antichrist, than John. His Gospel and Epistlesmove in these irreconcilable antagonisms. He knows no compromise betweenGod and Baal. With what holy horror does he speak of the traitor, andthe rising rage of the Pharisees against their Messiah! How severelydoes he, in the words of the Lord, attack the unbelieving Jews withtheir murderous designs, as children of the devil! And, in his Epistles,he terms every one who dishonors his Christian profession a liar; everyone who hates his brother a murderer; every one who wilfully sins achild of the devil; and he earnestly warns against teachers who deny themystery of the incarnation, as Antichrists, and he forbids even tosalute them.(18) The measure of his love of Christ was the measure ofhis hatred of antichrist. For hatred is inverted love. Love and hatredare one and the same passion, only revealed in opposite directions. Thesame sun gives light and heat to the living, and hastens the decay ofthe dead.

Christian art has so far well understood the double aspect of John byrepresenting him with a face of womanly purity and tenderness, but notweakness, and giving him for his symbol a bold eagle soaring withoutspread wings above the clouds.(19)

The Apocalypse and theFourth Gospel.

A proper appreciation of John’s character as thus set forth removesthe chief difficulty of ascribing the Apocalypse and the fourth Gospelto one and the same writer.(20) The temper is the same in both: a noble,enthusiastic nature, capable of intense emotions of love and hatred, butwith the difference between vigorous manhood and ripe old age, betweenthe roar of battle and the repose of peace. The theology is the same,including the most characteristic features of Christology andsoteriology.(21) By no other apostle is Christ called the Logos. TheGospel is, "the Apocalypse spiritualized," or idealized. Even thedifference of style, which is startling at first sight, disappears oncloser inspection. The Greek of the Apocalypse is the most Hebraizing ofall the books of the New Testament, as may be expected from its closeaffinity with Hebrew prophecy to which the classical Greek furnished noparallel, while the Greek of the fourth Gospel is pure, and free fromirregularities; yet after all John the Evangelist also shows thegreatest familiarity with, and the deepest insight into, the Hebrewreligion, and preserves its purest and noblest elements; and his stylehas all the childlike simplicity and sententious brevity of the OldTestament; it is only a Greek body inspired by a Hebrew soul.(22)

In accounting for the difference between the Apocalypse and the otherwritings of John, we must also take into consideration the necessarydifference between prophetic composition under direct inspiration, andhistorical and didactic composition, and the intervening time of abouttwenty years; the Apocalypse being written before the destruction ofJerusalem, the fourth Gospel towards the close of the first century, inextreme old age, when his youth was renewed like the eagle’s, as in thecase of some of the greatest poets, Homer, Sophocles, Milton, andGoethe.

Notes.

I. The Son of Thunder and the Apostle of Love.

I quote some excellent remarks on the character of John from myfriend, Dr. Godet (Com. I. 35, English translation byCrombie and Cusin):

"How are we to explain two features of character apparently soopposite? There exist profound receptive natures which are accustomed toshut up their impressions within themselves, and this all the more thatthese impressions are keen and thrilling. But if it happens that thesepersons once cease to be masters of themselves, their long-restrainedemotions then burst forth in sudden explosions, which fill the personsaround them with amazement. Does not the character of John belong tothis order? And when Jesus gave to him and his brother the surname ofBoanerges, sons of thunder (Mark 3:17), could he have described thembetter? I cannot think that, by that surname, Jesus intended, as all theold writers have believed, to signalize the eloquence whichdistinguished them. Neither can I allow that he desired by that surnameto perpetuate the recollection of their anger in one of the casesindicated. We are led by what precedes to a more natural explanation,and one more worthy of Jesus himself. As electricity is stored up bydegrees in the cloud until it bursts forth suddenly in the lightning andthunderbolt, so in those two loving and passionate natures impressionssilently accumulated till the moment when the heart overflowed, and theytook an unexpected and violent flight. We love to represent St. John toourselves as of a gentle rather than of an energetic nature, tender evento weakness. Do not his writings insist before and above all else uponlove? Were not the last sermons of the old man ’Love one another?’ Thatis true; but we forget other features of a different kind, during thefirst and last periods of his life, which reveal something decisive,sharp, absolute, even violent in his disposition. If we take all thefacts stated into consideration, we shall recognize in him one of thosesensitive, ardent souls, worshippers of an ideal, who attach themselvesat first sight, and without reservation, to that being who seems to themto realize that of which they have dreamt, and whose devotion easilybecomes exclusive and intolerant. They feel themselves repelled byeverything which is not in sympathy with their enthusiasm. They nolonger understand a division of heart which they themselves know not howto practice. All for all! such is their motto. Where that all is not,there is in their eyes nothing. Such affections do not subsist withoutincluding an alloy of impure egoism. A divine work is needed, in orderthat the true devotion, which constitutes the basis of such, may shineforth at the last in all its sublimity. Such was, if we are notdeceived, the inmost history of John." Comp. the third French ed. ofGodet’s Com., I. p. 50.

Dr. Westcott (in his Com., p. xxxiii.): "John knew that tobe with Christ was life, to reject Christ was death; and he did notshrink from expressing the thought in the spirit of the olddispensation. He learned from the Lord, as time went on, a more faithfulpatience, but he did not unlearn the burning devotion which consumedhim. To the last, words of awful warning, like the thunderings about thethrone, reveal the presence of that secret fire. Every page of theApocalypse is inspired with the cry of the souls beneath the altar, ’Howlong’ (Rev. 6:10); and nowhere is error as to the person of Christdenounced more sternly than in his Epistles (2 John 10; 1 John 4:1ff.)."Similar passages in Stanley.

  1. The Mission of John.

Dean Stanley (Sermons and Essays on the Apost. Age, p. 249sq., 3d ed.): "Above all John spoke of the union of the soul with God,but it was by no mere process of oriental contemplation, or mysticabsorption; it was by that word which now for the first time took itsproper place in the order of the world—by Love. It has been reserved forSt. Paul to proclaim that the deepest principle in the heart of man wasFaith; it was reserved for St. John to proclaim that the essentialattribute of God is Love. It had been taught by the Old Testament that’the beginning of wisdom was the fear of God;’ it remained to be taughtby the last apostle of the New Testament that ’the end of wisdom was thelove of God.’ It had been taught of old time by Jew and by heathen, byGreek philosophy and Eastern religion, that the Divinity was wellpleased with the sacrifices, the speculations, the tortures of man; itwas to St. John that it was left to teach in all its fulness that theone sign of God’s children is ’the love of the brethren.’ And as it isLove that pervades our whole conception of his teaching, so also itpervades our whole conception of his character. We see him—it surely isno unwarranted fancy—we see him declining with the declining century;every sense and faculty waxing feebler, but that one divinest faculty ofall burning more and more brightly; we see it breathing through everylook and gesture; the one animating principle of the atmosphere in whichhe lives and moves; earth and heaven, the past, the present, and thefuture alike echoing to him that dying strain of his latest words, ’Welove Him because He loved us.’ And when at last he disappears from ourview in the last pages of the sacred volume, ecclesiastical traditionstill lingers in the close: and in that touching story, not the lessimpressive because so familiar to us, we see the aged apostle borne inthe arms of his disciples into the Ephesian assembly, and thererepeating over and over again the same saying, ’Little children, loveone another;’ till, when asked why he said this and nothing else, hereplied in those well known words, fit indeed to be the farewell speechof the Beloved Disciple, ’Because this is our Lord’s command and if youfulfil this, nothing else is needed.’ "

§ 42. Apostolic Labors of John.

John in the Acts.

In the first stadium of Apostolic Christianity John figures as one ofthe three pillars of the church of the circumcision, together with Peterand James the brother of the Lord; while Paul and Barnabas representedthe Gentile church.(23) This seems to imply that at that time he had notyet risen to the full apprehension of the universalism and freedom ofthe gospel. But he was the most liberal of the three, standing betweenJames and Peter on the one hand, and Paul on the other, and lookingalready towards a reconciliation of Jewish and Gentile Christianity. TheJudaizers never appealed to him as they did to James, or to Peter.(24)There is no trace of a Johannean party, as there is of a Cephas partyand a party of James. He stood above strife and division.

In the earlier chapters of the Acts he appears, next to Peter, as thechief apostle of the new religion; he heals with him the cripple at thegate of the temple; he was brought with him before the Sanhedrin to bearwitness to Christ; he is sent with him by the apostles from Jerusalem toSamaria to confirm the Christian converts by imparting to them the HolySpirit; he returned with him to Jerusalem.(25) But Peter is always namedfirst and takes the lead in word and act; John follows in mysterioussilence and makes the impression of a reserved force which will manifestitself at some future time. He must have been present at the conferenceof the apostles in Jerusalem, a.d. 50, but he made no speech and took noactive part in the great discussion about circumcision and the terms ofchurch membership.(26) All this is in entire keeping with the characterof modest and silent prominence given to him in the Gospels.

After the year 50 he seems to have left Jerusalem. The Acts no moremention him nor Peter. When Paul made his fifth and last visit to theholy City (a.d. 58) he met James, but none of the apostles.(27)

John at Ephesus.

The later and most important labors of John are contained in hiswritings, which we shall fully consider in another chapter. They exhibitto us a history that is almost exclusively inward and spiritual, but ofimmeasurable reach and import. They make no allusion to the time andplace of residence and composition. But the Apocalypse implies that hestood at the head of the churches of Asia Minor.(28) This is confirmedby the unanimous testimony of antiquity which is above all reasonabledoubt, and assigns Ephesus to him as the residence of his latteryears.(29) He died there in extreme old age during the reign of Trajan,which began in 98. His grave also was shown there in the secondcentury.

We do not know when he removed to Asia Minor, but he cannot have doneso before the year 63. For in his valedictory address to the Ephesianelders, and in his Epistles to the Ephesians and Colossians and thesecond to Timothy, Paul makes no allusion to John, and speaks with theauthority of a superintendent of the churches of Asia Minor. It wasprobably the martyrdom of Peter and Paul that induced John to takecharge of the orphan churches, exposed to serious dangers andtrials.(30)

Ephesus, the capital of proconsular Asia, was a centre of Grecianculture, commerce, and religion; famous of old for the songs of Homer,Anacreon, and Mimnermus, the philosophy of Thales, Anaximenes, andAnaximander, the worship and wonderful temple of Diana. There Paul hadlabored three years (54–57) and established an influential church, abeacon-light in the surrounding darkness of heathenism. From there hecould best commune with the numerous churches he had planted in theprovinces. There he experienced peculiar joys and trials, and foresawgreat dangers of heresies that should spring up from within.(31) All theforces of orthodox and heretical Christianity were collected there.Jerusalem was approaching its downfall; Rome was not yet a secondJerusalem. Ephesus, by the labors of Paul and of John, became the chieftheatre of church history in the second half of the first and during thegreater part of the second century. Polycarp, the patriarchal martyr,and Irenaeus, the leading theologian in the conflict with Gnosticism,best represent the spirit of John and bear testimony to his influence.He alone could complete the work of Paul and Peter, and give the churchthat compact unity which she needed for her self-preservation againstpersecution from without and heresy and corruption from within.

If it were not for the writings of John the last thirty years of thefirst century would be almost an entire blank. They resemble thatmysterious period of forty days between the resurrection and theascension, when the Lord hovered, as it were, between heaven and earth,barely touching the earth beneath, and appearing to the disciples like aspirit from the other world. But the theology of the second and thirdcenturies evidently presupposes the writings of John, and starts fromhis Christology rather than from Paul’s anthropology and soteriology,which were almost buried out of sight until Augustin, in Africa, revivedthem.

John at Patmos.

John was banished to the solitary, rocky, and barren island of Patmos(now Patmo or Palmosa), in the Aegean sea, southwest of Ephesus. Thisrests on the testimony of the Apocalypse, 1:9, as usually understood:"I, John, your brother and partaker with you in the tribulation andkingdom and patience in Jesus, was in the isle that is called Patmos,for (on account of) the word of God and the testimony of Jesus."(32)There he received, while "in the spirit, on the Lord’s day," thosewonderful revelations concerning the struggles and victories ofChristianity.

The fact of his banishment to Patmos is confirmed by the unanimoustestimony of antiquity.(33) It is perpetuated in the traditions of theisland, which has no other significance. "John—that is the thought ofPatmos; the island belongs to him; it is his sanctuary. Its stonespreach of him, and in every heart, he lives."(34)

The time of the exile is uncertain, and depends upon the disputedquestion of the date of the Apocalypse. External evidence points to thereign of Domitian, a.d. 95; internal evidence to the reign of Nero, orsoon after his death, a.d. 68.

The prevailing—we may say the only distinct tradition, beginning withso respectable a witness as Irenaeus about 170, assigns the exile to theend of the reign of Domitian, who ruled from 81 to 96.(35) He was thesecond Roman emperor who persecuted Christianity, and banishment was oneof his favorite modes of punishment.(36) Both facts give support to thistradition. After a promising beginning he became as cruel andbloodthirsty as Nero, and surpassed him in hypocrisy and blasphemousself-deification. He began his letters: "Our Lord and God commands," andrequired his subjects to address him so.(37) He ordered gold and silverstatues of himself to be placed in the holiest place of the temples.When he seemed most friendly, he was most dangerous. He spared neithersenators nor consuls when they fell under his dark suspicion, or stoodin the way of his ambition. He searched for the descendants of David andthe kinsmen of Jesus, fearing their aspirations, but found that theywere poor and innocent persons.(38) Many Christians suffered martyrdomunder his reign, on the charge of atheism—among them his own cousin,Flavius Clemens, of consular dignity, who was put to death, and his wifeDomitilla, who was banished to the island of Pandateria, nearNaples.(39) In favor of the traditional date may also be urged anintrinsic propriety that the book which closes the canon, and treats ofthe last things till the final consummation, should have been writtenlast.

Nevertheless, the internal evidence of the Apocalypse itself, and acomparison with the fourth Gospel, favor an earlier date, before thedestruction of Jerusalem, and during the interregnum which followed thedeath of Nero (68), when the beast, that is the Roman empire, waswounded, but was soon to be revived (by the accession of Vespasian). Ifthere is some foundation for the early tradition of the intendedoil-martyrdom of John at Rome, or at Ephesus, it would naturally pointto the Neronian persecution, in which Christians were covered withinflammable material and burned as torches. The unmistakable allusionsto imperial persecutions apply much better to Nero than to Domitian. Thedifference between the Hebrew coloring and fiery vigor of the Apocalypseand the pure Greek and calm repose of the fourth Gospel, to which wehave already alluded, are more easily explained if the former waswritten some twenty years earlier. This view has some slight support inancient tradition,(40) and has been adopted by the majority of moderncritical historians and commentators.(41)

We hold, then, as the most probable view, that John was exiled toPatmos under Nero, wrote the Apocalypse soon after Nero’s death, a.d. 68or 69, returned to Ephesus, completed his Gospel and Epistles several(perhaps twenty) years later, and fell asleep in peace during the yearof Trajan, after a.d. 98.

The faithful record of the historical Christ in the whole fulness ofhis divine-human person, as the embodiment and source of life eternal toall believers, with the accompanying epistle of practical application,was the last message of the Beloved Disciple at the threshold of thesecond century, at the golden sunset of the apostolic age. Therecollections of his youth, ripened by long experience, transfigured bythe Holy Spirit, and radiant with heavenly light of truth and holiness,are the most precious legacy of the last of the apostles to all futuregenerations of the church.

§ 43. Traditions RespectingJohn.(42)

The memory of John sank deep into the heart of the church, and not afew incidents more or less characteristic and probable have beenpreserved by the early fathers.

Clement of Alexandria, towards the close of the second century,represents John as a faithful and devoted pastor when, in his old age,on a tour of visitation, he lovingly pursued one of his former convertswho had become a robber, and reclaimed him to the church.

Irenaeus bears testimony to his character as "the Son of Thunder"when he relates, as from the lips of Polycarp, that, on meeting in apublic bath at Ephesus the Gnostic heretic Cerinthus,(43) who denied theincarnation of our Lord, John refused to remain under the same roof,lest it might fall down. This reminds one of the incident recorded inLuke 9:49, and the apostle’s severe warning in 2 John 10 and 11. Thestory exemplifies the possibility of uniting the deepest love of truthwith the sternest denunciation of error and moral evil.(44)

Jerome pictures him as the disciple of love, who in his extreme oldage was carried to the meeting-place on the arms of his disciples, andrepeated again and again the exhortation, "Little children, love oneanother," adding: "This is the Lord’s command, and if this alone bedone, it is enough." This, of all the traditions of John, is the mostcredible and the most useful.

In the Greek church John bears the epithet "the theologian(θεολόγος), for teaching most clearly the divinity of Christ (τὴνθεότητα τοῦ λόγου). He is also called "the virgin" (παρθένος),(45) forhis chastity and supposed celibacy. Augustin says that the singularchastity of John from his early youth was supposed by some to be theground of his intimacy with Jesus.(46)

The story of John and the huntsman, related by Cassian, a monk of thefifth century, represents him as gently playing with a partridge in hishand, and saying to a huntsman, who was surprised at it: "Let not thisbrief and slight relaxation of my mind offend thee, without which thespirit would flag from over-exertion and not be able to respond to thecall of duty when need required." Childlike simplicity and playfulnessare often combined with true greatness of mind.

Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, at the close of the second century,relates (according to Eusebius) that John introduced in Asia Minor theJewish practice of observing Easter on the 14th of Nisan, irrespectiveof Sunday. This fact entered largely into the paschal controversies ofthe second century, and into the modern controversy about thegenuineness of the Gospel of John.

The same Polycrates of Ephesus describes John as wearing the plate,or diadem of the Jewish high-priest (Ex. 28:36, 37; 39:30, 31). It isprobably a figurative expression of priestly holiness which Johnattaches to all true believers (Comp. Rev. 2:17), but in which heexcelled as the patriarch.(47)

From a misunderstanding of the enigmatical word of Jesus, John 21:22,arose the legend that John was only asleep in his grave, gently movingthe mound as he breathed, and awaiting the final advent of the Lord.According to another form of the legend he died, but was immediatelyraised and translated to heaven, like Elijah, to return with him as theherald of the second advent of Christ.(48)

  22. 格布哈特 (Gebhardt) 的《启示录的教义》(Doctrine ofthe Apocalypse)很好地阐明了这一点；甚至那些否认《启示录》出自约翰（施莱尔马赫学派[Schleiermacher School]），或否认福音书出自约翰（图宾根学派 [TübingenSchool]）的人，实质上也承认这一点。鲍尔 (Baur) 在《教会史》(ChurchHistory，第I卷，第147页) 中说：“Es ist nicht blos eine äussereAnlehnnung an einen vielgefeierten Namen, es fehlt auch nicht an innernBerührungspunkten zwischen dem Evangelium und der Apokalypse, und mankann nur die tiefe Genialität und feine Kunst bewundern, mit welcher derEvangelist die Elemente, welche vom Standpunkt der Apokalypse auf denfreiern und höhern des Evangeliums hinüberleiteten, in sich aufgenommenhat, um die Apokalypse zum Evangelium zu vergeistigen. Nur vomStandpunkt dei Evangeliums aus lässt sich das Verhältniss, in das sichder Verfasser desselben zu der Apokalypse setzte, richtigbegreifen.”（这不只是从外面依附于一个备受颂扬的名字；福音书与《启示录》之间也不乏内在的契合点。福音书作者将那些能从《启示录》的立场引向福音书更自由、更高立场的要素吸收进来，使《启示录》升华为福音书；对此，人们只能赞叹他深邃的天才与精妙的艺术。只有从福音书的立场，才能正确理解其作者使自己与《启示录》所处的关系。）施韦格勒(Schwegler) 和克斯特林 (Köstlin)也作出类似的让步。参我的《使徒教会史》(Hist. of the Apost.Ch.)，第425页。↩︎

  23. 两位杰出的希伯来文学者兼文体鉴赏家所持的相反看法，可以这样调和。勒南(Renan)着眼于表面，论第四福音书说：“约翰的文体毫无希伯来色彩，毫无犹太色彩，毫无《塔木德》色彩。”埃瓦尔德却深入核心，反过来说：“就其真正的精神与灵感而言，没有任何语言比约翰的语言更地道地具有希伯来性质。”戈代赞同埃瓦尔德，说：“只有衣裳是希腊的，身体却是希伯来的。”↩︎

  24. 加2:9，Ἰάκωβος, καὶ Κηφᾶς καὶ Ἰωάννης, οἰ δοκοῦντεςστῦλοι εἷναι ... αὐτοὶ εἰς τὴνπεριτομήν（那被称为柱石的雅各、矶法、约翰……他们往受割礼的人那里去）。这里按他们保守程度的高低依次列名。↩︎

  25. 加2:12，τινὲς ἀπὸἸακώβου（从雅各那里来的人）。林前1:12，ἐγώ εἰμι Κηφᾶ（我是属矶法的）。↩︎

  26. 徒3:1及下文；4:1、13、19、20；5:19、20、41、42；8:14–17、25。↩︎

  27. 他包括在那次聚集于耶路撒冷的“使徒”之中，徒15:6、22、23；保罗在《加拉太书》第二章中明确提到他是三位柱石使徒之一，那里所指的正是同一次会议。↩︎

  28. 徒21:18。不过，约翰可能仍在巴勒斯坦，或许在加利利，在他青年时代生活过的地方。据传统说，他留在耶路撒冷，直到圣母于公元48年左右去世。↩︎

  29. 启1:4、9、11、20；第2、3章。显而易见，只有使徒才能居于这样的地位，而不可能是一个同名而默默无闻的长老，况且此人是否存在，本身就值得怀疑。↩︎

  30. 爱任纽是坡旅甲（约翰的亲传门徒）的弟子，见其《驳异端》(Adv.Haer.) III. 1, 1；3, 4；II. 22, 5等处，以及他致弗洛里努斯(Florinus) 的信（载于优西比乌《教会史》[H. E.] V.20）；亚历山大的革利免，Quis divessalvetur（《谁是得救的富人》），第42章；第二世纪末的阿波罗尼乌斯(Apollonius) 和波利克拉底，见优西比乌《教会史》(H. E.) III.31；V. 18、24；另有俄利根 (Origen)、德尔图良(Tertullian)、优西比乌、哲罗姆等人。被认为在约130年写成《约翰行传》的琉基乌斯(Leucius)，也在察恩 (Zahn)最近刊布的残篇中，见证约翰曾住在以弗所和拔摩，并将他受殉道之刑的地点从罗马移到以弗所。吕策尔贝格尔(Lützelberger)、凯姆 (Keim，《拿撒勒耶稣传》[Leben Jesu v.Nazara]，I. 161及下页)、霍尔茨曼 (Holtzmann)、斯霍尔滕(Scholten)、《超自然宗教》(Supernatural Religion，II. 410)的作者，以及其他反对《约翰福音》的人，竟敢根据《使徒行传》《以弗所书》《歌罗西书》以及帕皮亚(Papias)、伊格那丢 (Ignatius)和坡旅甲的沉默，提出否定性的论据，将约翰排除在小亚细亚之外。这些论据要么全无证明力，要么只能证明约翰在63年以前不在以弗所。然而，不仅埃瓦尔德、格林(Grimm)、施泰茨 (Steitz)、里根巴赫 (Riggenbach)、路塔德(Luthardt)、戈代、魏斯 (Weiss)，甚至图宾根学派的克伦克尔(Krenkel)、希尔根费尔德（《导论》[Einleitung]，第395页及后）和魏茨泽克(Weizsäcker，第498页及后)，都已对这一古老传统作出有力的辩护。↩︎

  31. 戈代 (I. 42)说：“当时，维护福音真理需要强有力的援助。因此，约翰作为使徒中最后几位仍然在世的人之一，感到自己蒙召，要在那些地方接替外邦人使徒的工作，像从前亚波罗在希腊所做的那样，浇灌保罗所栽种的，这就不足为奇了。”普雷桑塞(Pressensé，《使徒时代》[Apost.Era]，第424页)：“若要选择一座城市作为中心，以照管众教会并密切追踪异端的发展，没有比这更合适的了。在以弗所，约翰既处于保罗宣教地区的中心，又离希腊不远。”↩︎

  32. 参他在米利都 (Miletus)的临别赠言，徒20:29、30，以及致提摩太的书信。↩︎

  33. 布莱克 (Bleek) 将 διά理解为表示目的：约翰被带到拔摩（在异象中），为要在那里领受基督的启示。他认为，约翰被放逐到拔摩的整个传统，都源于对这段经文的误解。吕克(Lücke)、德韦特 (De Wette)、罗伊斯 (Reuss) 和迪斯特迪克 (Düsterdieck)也持此说。然而，同一节经文提到 θλίψις、βασιλεία 和 ὑπομονή，加上μαρτυρία的自然含义，以及启6:9和20:4的平行经文，都印证了传统的解释；在这两处经文中，διά同样表示受苦的缘由或原因。↩︎

  34. 爱任纽 (Irenaeus)、亚历山大的革利免 (Clement ofAlexandria)、俄利根 (Origen)、德尔图良 (Tertullian)、优西比乌(Eusebius)、哲罗姆 (Jerome) 等人。↩︎

  35. 蒂申多夫 (Tischendorf)，《东方游记》(Reise in’sMorgenland)，II.257及下页。岛南部一座山丘上的岩洞，至今仍被指认为领受《启示录》异象的地点；山顶则有圣约翰修道院，其图书馆藏有约250部抄本。↩︎

  36. 爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 在《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.)，V.30中说，《启示录》的异象是在 πρὸς τῷ τέλει τῆς Δομετιανοῦἀρχῆς（图密善统治将近结束时）看见的。优西比乌《教会史》(H. E.)III.18、20、33；《编年史》(Chron.)，图密善第14年条；以及哲罗姆《名人传》(Devir.illustr.)，第9章，也持此说。直到不久以前，这种观点一直盛行于释经家和历史学家之间，并得到亨斯滕贝格(Hengstenberg)、兰格 (Lange)、埃布拉德 (Ebrard)的支持（我本人在《使徒教会史》[Hist. of the Ap. Ch.]，§101，第400页及后，也曾支持此说）。爱任纽借着坡旅甲，与约翰所处的时代有直接的联系，要撇开他这明确的见证，确实不易。但我们必须记得，他甚至在更重要的历史问题上也曾出错，例如耶稣的年龄；他援引传统，断言耶稣曾活到五十岁以上。↩︎

  37. 塔西佗 (Tacitus) 庆幸阿格里科拉(Agricola)（《阿格里科拉传》[VitaAgr.]，第44章）没有活着看到这位皇帝治下的“tot consulariumcaedes, tot nobilissimarum feminarum exilia etfugas”（如此多的前执政官遭到杀戮，如此多最高贵的妇女被放逐、被迫流亡）。塔西佗娶了阿格里科拉的女儿；阿格里科拉死于93年，比图密善早两年。↩︎

  38. 苏维托尼乌斯(Suetonius)，《图密善传》(Domit.)，第13章：“Dominus et Deusnoster hoc fieri jubet. Unde institutum posthac, ut ne scripto quidem acsermone cujusquam appellareturaliter.”（我们的主、我们的神命令如此行。从此便立下规矩，任何人在文字或言谈中，都不得用别的称呼称他。）↩︎

  39. 赫格西普 (Hegesippus)，载于优西比乌《教会史》(Hist.Eccl.)，III.19、20。然而，赫格西普对约翰被放逐一事只字未提，布莱克便以这种沉默作为否认此事的论据。↩︎

  40. 狄奥·卡西乌斯 (Dion Cassius)，见克西菲利努斯(Xiphilinus) 的节本，67, 14。↩︎

  41. 《启示录》叙利亚文译本的标题便如此说（不过，这一译本远晚于未收《启示录》的《别西大译本》[Peshitto]）：“Revelatioquam Deus Joanni Evangelistae in Patmo insula dedit, in quam a NeroneCaesare relegatusfuerat.”（上帝在拔摩岛赐给福音书作者约翰的启示；他曾被凯撒尼禄放逐到那里。）亚历山大的革利免（《谁是得救的富人》[Quisdives salv.]，第42章，优西比乌也曾引述，III.23）仅笼统地说，约翰在“暴君”死后（τοῦ τυράννουτελευτήσαντος），从拔摩回到以弗所；这既可指尼禄，也可指图密善。俄利根只提到一位罗马βασιλεύς（皇帝）。德尔图良关于约翰在罗马受油刑殉道的传说，似乎指向尼禄，而非其他皇帝；哲罗姆也是这样理解的（《驳约维尼安》[Adv.Jovin.] I.26），尽管德尔图良并未明说，而且哲罗姆自己又将约翰被放逐及《启示录》的写作归于图密善统治时期（《名人传》[Devir. ill.]，第9章）。埃皮法尼乌斯(Epiphanius)（《驳异端》[Haer.] LI. 33）将此次放逐上推至克劳狄(Claudius) 统治时期（公元41—53年），这显然太早了。↩︎

  42. 尼安德 (Neander)、吉泽勒 (Gieseler)、鲍尔(Baur)、埃瓦尔德 (Ewald)、吕克 (Lücke)、布莱克 (Bleek)、德韦特 (DeWette)、罗伊斯 (Reuss)、迪斯特迪克 (Düsterdieck)、魏斯 (Weiss)、勒南(Renan)、斯坦利 (Stanley)、莱特福特 (Lightfoot)、韦斯科特 (Westcott)。↩︎

  43. 斯坦利座堂主任牧师 (Dean Stanley)在其《使徒时期讲章与论文集》(Sermons and Essays on the Apost.Age)，第266—281页（第3版），以优美的笔调重述了这些传统。参我的《使徒教会史》(Hist.of the Ap. Ch)，第404页及后。↩︎

  44. 据埃皮法尼乌斯(Epiphanius)《驳异端》(Haer.)，xxx. 25，则是伊便 (Ebion)。↩︎

  45. 斯坦利举了一例，说明想象如何夸大事实：杰里米·泰勒(Jeremy Taylor)叙述这个故事时，加上一句：“使徒刚一离开，浴室便倒塌了，将克林妥(Cerinthus) 压死在废墟之中。”（《基督生平》[Life ofChrist]，第xii节，2。）↩︎

  46. παρθένος通常意为童女（太1:23；路1:27；徒21:9；林前7:25、28、34），但也用于从未亲近妇女的男子，见启14:4及教父著作。↩︎

  47. 奥古斯丁 (Augustin)，《约翰福音讲论》(Tract.124 in Joh. Evang.)（《全集》[Opera] III. 1976，米涅[Migne] 编）：“Sunt qui senserint ... a Christo Joannemapostolum propterea plus amatum quod neque uxorem duxerit, et ab ineuntepueritui castissimusvixerit.”（有人认为……使徒约翰更蒙基督所爱，是因为他没有娶妻，并且自幼就过着极其贞洁的生活。）他引用了哲罗姆《驳约维尼安》(Contr.Jovin.)，前引处，但又补充说：“Hoc quidem in Scriptuis nonevidenterapparet.”（不过，这在圣经中并没有明确显明。）据安布罗西亚斯特(Ambrosiaster)《哥林多后书注释》(Ad 2 Cor.)11:2，除约翰和保罗以外，所有使徒都已婚。德尔图良称约翰为 Christispado（基督的阉人）。↩︎

  48. 载于优西比乌《教会史》(H. E.) III. 31, 3；V.24, 3：Ἰωάννης ...ὃς ἐγεννήθη ἱερευς τὸ πέταλον πεφορηκὼς καὶμάρτυς καὶ διδάσκαλος οὗτος ἐν Εφέσω,κεκοίμηται.（约翰……他曾作祭司，佩戴金牌，又是见证人和教师；他已在以弗所长眠。）埃皮法尼乌斯对主的兄弟雅各也有同样的记述（无疑取自赫格西普），并增添了一些禁欲主义的特征。见斯坦利的评论，第276—278页，以及莱特福特《加拉太书注释》(Galat.)，第345页注，和《腓立比书注释》(Philipp.)，第252页。莱特福特说：“无论视为比喻的表达，还是实际的事实，这项记载都表明，圣约翰是一个祭司族系中资深的教师和首要代表。另一方面，波利克拉底(Polycrates)本人赋予这个比喻或事实的，也可能不是这一含义；若是如此，那么在现存基督教著作中，这里或许是最早明确提出圣职之祭司观的段落。”但在《十二使徒遗训》(Didache)（第13章）中，基督徒先知已被称为“大祭司”。↩︎

  49. 奥古斯丁提到这个传说，却予以驳斥，见《约翰福音讲论》(Trad.224 in Ev. Joann.)。↩︎

entry.title: 《基督教会史》第一卷·第六章: 大灾难
entry.content:
Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The ChristianChurch

第六章大灾难（《马太福音》24:21）

目录

§ 37. 罗马大火与尼禄的逼迫。

§ 38. 犹太战争与耶路撒冷的毁灭。公元70年。

§ 39. 耶路撒冷的毁灭对基督教会的影响。

§ 37. 罗马大火与尼禄的逼迫。

“我又看见那女人喝醉了圣徒的血和耶稣殉道者的血。我看见她，就大大地希奇。”——《启示录》17:6。

文献。

I. 塔西佗(Tacitus)：《编年史》(Annales)，第XV卷，第38–44章。

苏维托尼乌斯(Suetonius)：《尼禄传》(Nero)，第16、38章（极简略）。

苏尔皮基乌斯·塞韦鲁斯 (Sulpicius Severus)：《神圣史》(Hist.Sacra)，第II卷，第41章。他将尼禄的逼迫叙述为范围更广泛的事件。

  1. 欧内斯特·勒南 (ErnestRenan)：《敌基督》(L’Antechrist)。巴黎，第2版，1873年。第VI、VIII章，第123页及后。另参其1880年在伦敦所作、论罗马与基督教的《希伯特讲座》(HibbertLectures)。

L. 弗里德兰德 (L. Friedländer)：《罗马风俗史》(SittengeschichteRoms)，I. 6、27；III. 529。

赫尔曼·席勒 (HermannSchiller)：《尼禄统治时期的罗马帝国史》(Geschichte der röm.Kaiserzeit unter der Regierung desNero)。柏林，1872年（第173–179页；第424页及后；第583页及后）。

豪斯拉特 (Hausrath)：《新约时代史》(N. T.licheZeitgeschichte)，III. 第392页及后（第2版，1875年）。

特奥德·凯姆 (Theod. Keim)：《原始基督教论集》(Aus demUrchristenthum)。苏黎世，1878年，第171–181页。《罗马与基督教》(Romu. das Christenthum)，1881年，第132页及后。

卡尔·维泽勒 (Karl Wieseler)：《诸凯撒对基督徒的逼迫》(DieChristenverfolgungen der Cäsaren)。1878年。

G. 乌尔霍恩 (G. Uhlhorn)：《基督教与异教的冲突》(The Conflict ofChristianity with Heathenism)。斯迈思与罗普斯 (Smyth andRopes) 英译，纽约，1879年，第241–250页。

C. F. 阿诺德 (C. F. Arnold)：《尼禄对基督徒的逼迫》(Die Neron.Christenverfolgung)。莱比锡，1888年。

保罗和彼得在罗马的传道，是教会历史上的一个划时代事件。它推动了基督教的发展。他们的殉道最终产生了更大的果效：它巩固了犹太人与外邦归信者之间的联合纽带，并使这座异教大都会的土地成为圣地。耶路撒冷将主钉在十字架上，罗马则将他的两位首要使徒斩首、钉十字架，又使整个罗马教会陷入血的洗礼。无论就善就恶而言，罗马都成了基督教世界的耶路撒冷，梵蒂冈山(Vatican hill) 则成了西方的各各他 (Golgotha)。彼得和保罗如同新的罗慕路斯(Romulus) 与雷穆斯(Remus)，奠定了一个属灵帝国的根基；这帝国比诸凯撒的帝国更广阔，也更长久。十字架取代了刀剑，成为征服与权能的象征。1

但这一转变是以宝贵鲜血的牺牲为代价才实现的。罗马帝国起初凭着其公正的法律，在不知基督教真实性质的情况下，成了它的保护者；又在几次危急关头援救保罗，如在哥林多借着方伯安内乌斯·迦流(Annaeus Gallio)，在耶路撒冷借着千夫长吕西亚(Lysias)，在凯撒利亚借着巡抚非斯都(Festus)。如今，它却与这新宗教展开了殊死冲突，并以偶像崇拜和爱国主义之名，开始了一连串时断时续的逼迫，直到十字架的旗帜在米尔维安桥(Milvian bridge)得胜，这些逼迫才告终结。它从前是一种抑制的力量，曾暂时拦阻敌基督的显露；2如今却挥舞着火与剑，公然显出敌基督的面目。3

尼禄。

这些帝国逼迫中的第一次，发生在尼禄 (Nero)在位第十年，即公元64年；按照教会传统，彼得和保罗的殉道与此次逼迫有关。这场逼迫正是由那位皇帝煽动的，而保罗先前曾以罗马公民的身份，从犹太人的法庭向他上诉。不过，它并不像后来诸皇帝治下的逼迫那样，是严格意义上的宗教逼迫；它起源于一场公共灾难，而无辜的基督徒竟被肆意诬指为这场灾难的祸首。

保罗是人类中最纯洁、最高尚的人物之一，尼禄则是暴君中最卑鄙、最邪恶的人物之一；两者之间的反差，几乎无可比拟。尼禄在塞涅卡(Seneca) 和布鲁斯 (Burrhus)的明智辅导下，在位头五年（54–59年）颇为辉煌，这反而使其余九年（59–68年）显得更加可憎。我们读他的生平，既鄙视他的愚昧，又惊骇于他的邪恶。在他眼中，世界既是一出喜剧，也是一出悲剧，而他要在其中担任主角。他疯狂地渴求民众的喝彩；他弹奏里拉琴，在宴席上吟唱自己的颂诗，在竞技场中驾车，又在舞台上扮演戏子，强迫身份最高贵的人在戏剧或活人画中，表演希腊神话里最淫秽的情节。然而，他作为悲剧制造者的表现，更超过了他作为喜剧演员的表现。他罪上加罪，直到成了恶贯满盈、人人传说的怪物。他先后杀害了弟弟不列塔尼库斯(Britannicus)、母亲阿格里皮娜 (Agrippina)、妻子屋大维娅 (Octavia)和波佩娅(Poppaea)、老师塞涅卡，以及许多显赫的罗马人，最后在三十二岁那年自杀，恰如其分地结束了这一切。尤利乌斯·凯撒(Julius Caesar)的家族随他一同耻辱地灭绝，帝国则成了得势军人和冒险家的争夺品。4

罗马大火。

对于这样一个人形恶魔，杀戮一群无辜的基督徒，不过是取乐的游戏。这场地狱般惨剧的契机，是罗马的一场可怕大火；其破坏之巨、灾祸之重，为历史上前所未有。大火于7月18日至19日之间的夜晚爆发，5起火处是大竞技场 (Great Circus)东南端、帕拉丁山 (Palatine hill) 附近的木造商铺。6火借风势，消防人员和士兵虽竭尽全力，仍无法控制；烈焰肆虐了七夜六日，丝毫不减。7随后，城中另一处、靠近战神广场 (fieldof Mars) 的地方又起大火，再烧了三日，将城内另外两个区化为废墟。8

这场灾难的损失无法估量。全城划分为十四个区，其中只有四区未受损害；三区已成为一片不辨形状的废墟，包括从竞技场到埃斯奎林山(Esquiline hill)之间的整个内城；其余七区也都遭到程度不等的破坏。古老的神庙、王政时期、共和时期和帝国时期的纪念建筑，以及数百年来搜集的希腊艺术最珍贵的杰作，都化作尘土灰烬；人畜葬身火海，这座世界大都会呈现出一片墓地的景象，百万哀恸者在其中痛悼那些无可挽回的珍宝。

圣约翰在《启示录》中写下哀悼帝国罗马倾覆的挽歌时，心中必定浮现着这场可怕的浩劫（《启示录》第18章）。

大火的起因至今仍是一个谜。民间传言将其归咎于尼禄，说他想欣赏特洛伊(Troy)燃烧时那火光冲天的景象，又想满足自己的野心，以更加宏伟的规模重建罗马，并称之为尼禄城(Neropolis)。9火起之时，他正在出生地安提乌姆(Antium)的海滨；直到吞噬一切的烈火烧到自己的宫殿，他才返回，并竭尽全力遏止灾势，随后又以重建来弥补灾难造成的损失。这项工程一直持续到他死后；他也不忘将自己那部分焚毁的临时宫邸（domustransitoria），换成“金宫”（domusaurea），使其成为建筑宏伟奢华的一座长存奇观。

对基督徒的逼迫。

为了转移众人对他纵火的普遍怀疑，同时给他恶魔般的残忍增添新的娱乐，尼禄恶意地将罪责推到备受憎恨的基督徒身上。在此期间，尤其自保罗公开受审并在罗马卓有成效地传道以来，基督徒已逐渐被视为有别于犹太人的“第三类人”（genustertium），或被视为从那个民族分出的最危险的支派。他们确实蔑视罗马诸神，忠于一位比凯撒更高的君王，又被人无端怀疑暗中犯罪。警察和民众因这场可怕灾难而惊恐不安，轻信最恶毒的诽谤，要求有人抵罪。就连塔西佗、苏维托尼乌斯和普林尼(Pliny)这样有教养的罗马人，都把基督教斥为粗鄙而有害的迷信，对无知的群众还能有什么指望呢？在他们看来，基督教甚至比犹太教更坏；犹太教毕竟是一种古老的民族宗教，基督教却是新起的，不依附于任何特定民族，而且以普世统治为目标。一些基督徒被捕，承认了自己的信仰；塔西佗说，他们“与其说是因纵火罪，不如说是因仇恨人类而被定罪”。他们的犹太渊源、他们对政治和公共事务的漠然，以及他们对异教习俗的憎恶，都被解释为“仇恨人类”（“odiumgenerishumani”）；因此，说他们企图毁灭这座城市，便显得足够可信，足以判定他们有罪。暴怒的群众不会停下来讲道理，而且与个人一样容易陷入疯狂。

在这肆意捏造的纵火罪名之下，又加上同样毫无根据的仇视人类与反自然恶行的指控，一场血的狂欢开始了；即使在异教罗马，这也是空前绝后的。10这是地狱的权势对两位首要使徒大有能力的传道所作的回应，因为他们的传道已从根本上震撼了异教。“极多”的基督徒遭到最骇人听闻的杀戮。有些被钉在十字架上，大概是为了嘲弄基督所受的刑罚；11有些被缝在野兽皮里，放到竞技场上任狂犬吞噬。这场撒但般的惨剧，到了夜晚在梵蒂冈山坡上的御苑中达到高潮（据推测，这片御苑包括今天圣彼得广场和教堂的所在地）：基督徒男女被浇上沥青、油或树脂，钉在松木柱上，然后点燃，像火炬一般焚烧，供暴民取乐；尼禄则身着奇装异服，参加赛马，炫耀自己的驭车技艺。活活烧死原是惩治纵火犯的惯常刑罚；但只有这个帝国怪物在魔鬼鼓动下所发挥的残酷巧思，才能发明如此可怕的照明方式。

这就是最伟大的异教历史学家的记述，也是我们所有记述中最详尽的一篇——正如关于耶路撒冷毁灭的最佳叙述，出自那位博学的犹太历史学家之笔一样。这样，仇敌也为基督教的真实性作了见证。塔西佗在这里顺带提到，基督在提庇留(Tiberius) 统治时期，受本丢·彼拉多 (Pontius Pilate)钉十字架。他对基督徒的认识仅来自传闻与阅读，虽以罗马人的傲慢鄙视他们，却仍确信他们并未犯纵火罪；而且，尽管他持守冷漠的斯多葛主义，仍不禁对他们生出怜悯，因为他们遭到牺牲，不是为了公共利益，而是为了满足一个邪恶暴君的凶残欲望。

有些历史学家所怀疑的，并不是这场可怕逼迫的真实性，而是受害者究竟是基督徒而非犹太人，或是否仅有基督徒受害。基督徒无害而和平；同时代的作家塞涅卡、普林尼、卢坎(Lucan)、佩尔西乌斯 (Persius)虽然提及犹太人，却对基督徒只字未提；这样的人竟如此迅速地成为众怒所向，似乎难以理解。因此有人推测，塔西佗和苏维托尼乌斯在事发约五十年后写作时，将基督徒与犹太人混淆了；犹太人素来为罗马人所憎恶，而他们在台伯河彼岸的居住区又免受火灾损害，更使纵火的嫌疑显得有据。12

然而，这一暴行太过公开，不可能留下发生这种误认的余地。塔西佗和苏维托尼乌斯虽对这两个派别都所知甚少，却都将二者区分开来；前者更明确指出，基督徒之名源自这一新宗教的创始者基督。此外，如前所述，尼禄并不反感犹太人；他的第二任妻子波佩娅·萨比娜(PoppaeaSabina)，在大火发生前一年，还曾特别优待约瑟夫斯，并赐给他丰厚的礼物。约瑟夫斯谈到尼禄的罪行，却对自己的同教之人遭受逼迫一事只字未提。13单凭这一点，似乎就足以定论。很有可能，在这一次逼迫中（如同在此前一切逼迫中，以及此后许多次逼迫中一样），狂热的犹太人因基督教迅速发展而愤怒，又急于使自己摆脱嫌疑，便煽动民众攻击那些遭人憎恨的加利利人；而异教的罗马人则加倍凶猛地扑向这些被视为半个犹太人的人，因为连他们自己那些奇特的同胞也不承认他们。14

这场逼迫可能波及的范围

若从异教历史学家的沉默来判断，他们似乎将这场逼迫限于罗马城；但后来的基督教作家则认为它波及各行省。15皇帝在首都树立的榜样，很难不对各行省产生影响，也会为民众仇恨的爆发提供正当理由。如果《启示录》写于尼禄统治时期，或在他死后不久，那么约翰被放逐到拔摩岛(Patmos)，必定与这场逼迫有关。该书提到士每拿 (Smyrna) 的监禁、别迦摩(Pergamus) 的安提帕 (Antipas)殉道，并谈到先知、圣徒和地上一切被杀之人的遇害。16《希伯来书》写于意大利，大概是在64年；其中10:32–34同样提到流血的逼迫，13:23则提到提摩太获释出狱。彼得的第一封书信，也可能写于同一年，即逼迫刚爆发之后、他去世前不久；他在信中告诫小亚细亚的基督徒，将有火炼的试验临到他们，又论及他们已经忍受或将要忍受的苦难，不是因犯了什么罪，而是因“基督徒”的名。17以“巴比伦”18称呼罗马，最容易从写作的时间和处境得到解释。

基督教刚刚达到其创始者在世的年岁，在罗马却似乎已被消灭。随着彼得和保罗的离世，第一代基督徒也一同埋葬了。黑暗必定笼罩着战栗的门徒，他们陷入的沮丧，几乎与三十四年前耶稣被钉十字架那天傍晚一样深重。然而，复活的清晨已经不远；而圣彼得殉道的那块地方，日后竟要成为基督教世界最宏伟教堂的所在地，以及那些被认为是他继承者之人的宫殿式居所。19

《启示录》论尼禄的逼迫

在主要使徒中，除了约翰，没有人留存下来记述这场可怕的屠杀。他或许是在以弗所(Ephesus)听到这件事的；又或许曾陪同彼得来到罗马，并逃过了尼禄御苑中可怕的死亡——如果我们可以相信那古老的传统，即在梵蒂冈山上那场地狱般的照明中，他曾蒙神迹保全，没有与其他基督徒一同被活活烧死。20无论如何，他自己也是因耶稣的名而遭逼迫的人；他被放逐在孤寂的拔摩岛上，在《启示录》的异象中描绘了这场逼迫的恐怖。

这部奥秘的书——无论写于68至69年之间，还是图密善 (Domitian)统治下的95年——无疑既是为那个时代的教会，也是为后世的教会而写；它必定充分切合最初读者的实际处境和周围环境，才能在火炼的试验中给予他们切实的帮助和安慰。由于书中所暗指的事件离他们很近，就实际应用而言，他们对这书的理解，必定比后世读者更加透彻。约翰固然展望最终的成全，却也在开端中看见终局。他立足于自己所生活的古罗马帝国这一历史基础，正如以色列先知的异象，以大卫的王国或被掳巴比伦的时代为出发点。他把当时的异教罗马描绘为“从无底坑里上来的兽”，为“从海中上来的一个兽，有十角七头”（即君王、皇帝），为“坐在众水上的大淫妇”，又为“一个女人骑在朱红色的兽上；那兽有七头十角，遍体有亵渎的名号”，并称之为“大巴比伦，作世上的淫妇和一切可憎之物的母”。21当这位先见称那坐在七座山上的女人“喝醉了圣徒的血和为耶稣作见证之人的血”时，22他心中所指的，必定是有史以来最残酷的尼禄逼迫；他又预言她的倾覆，将成为“圣徒、使徒、先知”欢喜的事。23

近来的注释家甚至发现其中直接暗指尼禄：他的名字用希伯来字母写成（NeronKesar），便表示那奥秘的数目666；他也是兽的七头中的第五头，虽被杀，却要再从无底坑中回来，成为敌基督。然而，这种解释并不确定；无论如何，我们不能认为约翰相信尼禄真的会从死里复活，成为敌基督。他的意思只是说，逼迫基督教会的尼禄（如同安条克·伊皮法尼(Antiochus Epiphanes)一样）是敌基督的先驱，后者将受来自地狱的同一种嗜血之灵驱使。在类似的意义上，罗马是第二个巴比伦，施洗约翰是另一位以利亚。

附注

一、关于尼禄逼迫的记载。

  1. 异教历史学家的记载。

关于第一次由皇帝发动的逼迫，我们主要有两份记载：一份出自塔西佗，他出生于事发前约八年，大概活到了图拉真(Trajan，卒于117年)死后；另一份出自苏维托尼乌斯，他的《十二凯撒传》(XII. Caesares)写得稍晚，约在公元120年。狄奥·卡西乌斯 (Dion Cassius，生于约公元155年)的《罗马史》(History of Rome；ῬωμαικὴἸστορία，现存残篇及修士克西菲利努斯 (Xiphilinus)所作节本)，记述从埃涅阿斯 (Aeneas)到来直至公元229年的历史，其中提到罗马大火，却未提及对基督徒的逼迫。

塔西佗的叙述保持了他简练、含蓄而生动的文风，绝无后人插入的嫌疑，但有些地方含义不明。我们将《编年史》(Annal.)，XV.44全文译录如下：

“然而，无论人们采取怎样的救济措施，皇帝施予怎样的赏赐，或怎样向诸神献祭求恩，都无法使他〔尼禄〕摆脱命人纵火这一传闻所带来的恶名。因此，为了压下谣言，尼禄便将罪名诬加于一些人，以最为惨酷的刑罚折磨他们；这些人因其恶行而遭人憎恨，民众通常称他们为基督徒(subdidit reos, et quaesitissimis poenis affecit, quos per flagitiainvisos vulgus ’Christianos’ appellabat)。这一名称的创始者基督(Christus)，在提庇留统治时期，已被犹太巡抚本丢·彼拉多处死(supplicio affectus erat)；然而，这种一度受到压制的有害迷信(exitiabilis superstitio)，24又重新爆发，不仅遍及这一祸害的发源地犹太，也蔓延到〔罗马〕城；一切凶恶可耻的事物，都从四面八方汇集于此，并受到推崇(quo cuncta undique atrocia aut pudenda confluuntcelebranturque)。于是，起初被捕的，只是那些承认的人。25随后，根据他们提供的消息，极多的人(multitudo ingens) 被定罪，与其说是因纵火罪，不如说是因仇恨人类(odio humani generis)。26他们临死时还成了供人取乐的对象：有的被裹在野兽皮中，让狗撕成碎片；有的被钉在十字架上；有的被点燃，待白日过去，便焚烧他们，作为夜间照明之用(in usum nocturni luminisurerentur)。尼禄把自己〔在梵蒂冈〕的御苑提供出来，供人观看这场奇观，并在此时举行战车竞赛；他时而身穿驭车者的服装，混在群众中，时而亲自执缰驾车。于是，人们对受难者生出了怜悯，尽管他们被认为理当受人憎恶；因为他们看来并非为公共利益而被除灭，倒是成了满足一个人凶残欲望的牺牲品。”

苏维托尼乌斯在《尼禄传》(Nero)第16章中的记载非常简短，不能令人满意：“Afflicti suppliciisChristiani, genus hominum superstitionis novae acmaleficaea.”（“基督徒受到刑罚；这是一群信奉新起而有害之迷信的人。”）他没有将逼迫与大火联系起来，而是将它与治安条例联系起来。

讽刺诗人尤维纳利斯 (Juvenal)提到这场逼迫时，可能是以目击者的身份说话；他同塔西佗一样，对受难的基督徒怀着轻蔑与怜悯交织的感情（《讽刺诗》(Sat.)I. 155）：

“你敢说提盖利努斯 (Tigellinus) 有罪吗？

你也将像我们所见的那些人一样发光，

喉咙被刺穿，立在刑柱旁，

冒着烟，燃烧着。”

  1. 基督徒的记载。

罗马的革利免 (Clement of Rome)在第一世纪末，写到那“极多的选民”因嫉妒而遭受许多凌辱与酷刑，又写到被迫扮演“达那伊得斯”(Danaides) 和“狄耳刻” (Dirces)的基督徒妇女时，所指的必定是尼禄的逼迫，见《致哥林多人书》(AdCorinth.)，第6章。我在正文中没有采用这段文字。勒南将它加以铺陈，织入他对这场逼迫所作的生动叙述之中（《敌基督》(L’Antechrist)，第163页及后；他的《希伯特讲座》(HibbertLectures)几乎逐字重述了这一段）。按传说，狄耳刻被绑在一头狂暴的公牛身上，拖曳至死。那不勒斯(Naples)博物馆中著名的大理石群雕，表现的就是这一场景。但达那伊得斯的故事，却无法提供与基督徒殉道者相切合的类比，除非如勒南所推测的，尼禄曾命人表演塔耳塔罗斯(Tartarus) 中的苦刑。莱特福特采纳华兹华斯 (Wordsworth，注忒奥克里托斯(Theocritus)，XXVI. 1) 的大胆校改，摒弃 Δαναΐδες καὶΔίρκαι（“达那伊得斯与狄耳刻”）这一读法（所有版本，包括格布哈特(Gebhardt) 和哈纳克 (Harnack) 的版本，都保留此读法），以 νεανίδες,παιδίσκαι（“少女、婢女”）取而代之。这样，革利免所说的就是：“妇人(γυναῖκες)、少女、婢女遭受逼迫，忍受残酷而邪恶的凌辱之后，虽身体软弱，却在信心的赛程中安然抵达终点，领受了美好的赏赐。”

德尔图良（卒于约220年）在《致异教徒》(AdNationes)，I，第7章中这样提到尼禄的逼迫：“我们这名称起于奥古斯都(Augustus)统治时期；在提庇留治下，它所代表的教义得到极其清楚而公开的传扬；在尼禄治下，它遭到无情的定罪(sub Nerone damnatioinvaluit)，你们甚至可以从逼迫者其人来衡量它的价值和性质。倘若那位君主是虔诚的人，那么基督徒就是不虔诚的；倘若他公义，倘若他纯洁，那么基督徒就是不义、不洁的；倘若他不是公敌，我们就是国家的仇敌。我们是什么样的人，逼迫我们的人自己就表明了，因为他所惩罚的，自然是那些招致对他本人敌意的东西。如今，虽然尼禄治下存在的其他一切制度都已毁灭，我们的这一制度却仍然坚立——看来，它是公义的，因为它与〔发动逼迫的〕那人截然不同。”

苏尔皮基乌斯·塞韦鲁斯 (Sulpicius Severus)在《编年史》(Chron.)，II.28、29中提供了相当详尽的记载，但大多取自塔西佗。他与奥罗修斯(Orosius，《历史》(Hist.)，VII. 7)最先明确断言，尼禄将逼迫扩展到了各行省。

二、尼禄作为敌基督归来。

尼禄因其年轻、俊美、豪放、挥霍，以及其恶行令人震惊的新奇而在罗马的下层民众中颇受欢迎（塔西佗称他为“incredibiliumcupitor,”，即“追求不可思议之事的人”，《编年史》Ann. XV.42）。因此，在他自杀之后，异教徒中便流传一种谣言，说他其实并未死去，而是逃到了帕提亚人(Parthians) 那里，将率领一支军队返回罗马，摧毁这座城市。在奥托(Otho)、提图斯和图密善 (Domitian)统治期间，先后有三个冒用他名字的人利用这一信念，获得了支持。甚至三十年后，图密善听见尼禄的名字仍会战栗。参见塔西佗，《历史》Hist.I. 2；II. 8、9；苏维托尼乌斯，《尼禄传》Ner. 57；狄奥·卡西乌斯(Dio Cassius)，LXIV. 9；席勒 (Schiller)，前引书，第288页。

在基督徒中，这一传言采取了敌视尼禄的形式。拉克坦提乌斯(Lactantius，《逼迫者之死》De Mort. Persecut.，第2章)提到西比拉 (Sibylline)的预言，说尼禄既是第一个逼迫者，也将成为最后一个逼迫者，并要在敌基督来临之前出现。奥古斯丁（《上帝之城》DeCivil. Dei.，XX.19）提到，他所处的时代，教会中仍流传着关于尼禄的两种意见：有人以为他将从死里复活，成为敌基督；另有人以为他并没有死，只是隐藏起来，并将一直活着，直到显露出来，重掌王权。前者是基督徒的信念，后者是异教徒的信念。奥古斯丁将两者一并否定。苏尔皮基乌斯·塞韦鲁斯(Sulpicius Severus，《编年史》Chron.，II. 29)也提到这种信念（undecreditur，故而人们相信）：尼禄致命的伤已经医好，他将在世界末日归来，成就保罗所预言的那“不法的奥秘”（帖撒罗尼迦后书2:7）。

有些注释家认为，《启示录》应为这荒谬的传言和错误的信念负责；另一些则认为，作者与他同时代的异教徒共有这种信念。他们援引的经文是《启示录》17:8：“那兽先前有，如今没有，将要从无底坑里上来，又要归于沉沦”……“那兽先前有，如今没有，将来要出现”（καὶπάρεσται，而不是 καίπερ ἐστίν，“却仍然存在”；英译本 E. V. 随从公认本文text. ec.作后者）；17:11：“那先前有，如今没有的兽，就是第八位；他也属于那七位，并且要归于沉沦”；以及13:3：“我看见兽的七头中，有一个似乎受了死伤；那死伤却医好了：全地的人都希奇，跟从那兽。”

然而，这些话是指那兽，即罗马帝国；它在全书中始终与那七头，即诸位皇帝，明确区分开来。在《但以理书》中，兽也代表一个整体。此外，必须区分一个统治者（尼禄）的死亡，与这一死亡给兽或帝国所造成的致命创伤；帝国后来却从这创伤中恢复了过来（在韦斯帕芗统治之下）。

§ 38.犹太战争与耶路撒冷的毁灭。公元70年。

“耶稣从殿里出来的时候，有一个门徒对他说：夫子，请看，这是何等的石头，何等的殿宇！耶稣对他说：你看见这大殿宇吗？将来在这里没有一块石头留在石头上，不被拆毁了。”——马可福音13:1、2。

史料。

历史上几乎没有别的时期，像尼禄逼迫与耶路撒冷毁灭之间的六年那样，充满罪恶、腐败和灾难。我们的主对末日所作的预言性描述，在听他说话的那一代人尚未过去之前，就已开始应验，审判之日仿佛近在眼前。基督徒如此相信，而且有充分的理由如此相信。即使在严肃的异教思想家看来，那一时期也黑暗如午夜。我们在别处已经引用过塞涅卡的描绘，说明他的学生兼杀害他的人尼禄统治之下，那种骇人的道德败坏与衰颓。塔西佗叙述尼禄死后罗马历史的著作，以这些话开篇：“我现在着手叙述的这段历史，灾难频仍，充满惨烈的战争、纷争与叛乱，甚至在和平时期也恐怖异常。四位君主〔加尔巴(Galba)、奥托、维特里乌斯(Vitellius)、图密善〕死于刀剑；三场内战，数场对外战争，而且大多同时肆虐。东方有顺利之事〔征服犹太人〕，西方却遭逢不幸。伊利里亚(Illyria) 动荡，高卢 (Gaul) 不安；不列颠 (Britain)被征服后不久又被放弃；萨尔马提亚 (Sarmatia) 和苏维比 (Suevia)的各族起来反抗我们；帕提亚人受一个假尼禄的欺骗而骚动。意大利也被新起或屡次发生的灾祸压得喘不过气来；城市被吞没，或被埋在废墟之下；罗马遭大火蹂躏，古老的庙宇被焚毁，甚至卡庇托尔(Capitol)也被市民纵火焚烧；圣所遭到亵渎；上层社会奸淫横行。海上满是流亡者；岩石岛屿被杀戮玷污。城中的暴虐更为可怕。高贵的出身、财富、显赫的职位，无论辞谢还是担任，都被算作罪行，而美德则注定遭到毁灭。27

迫近的厄运。

那一时期最不幸的地方是巴勒斯坦(Palestine)，一个古老而可敬的民族在那里为自己招来了难以言喻的苦难与毁灭。耶路撒冷的悲剧，以缩影的形式预示了最后的审判；基督从起初就预见了结局，他论末世的讲论正是从这一角度描绘这场悲剧。

上帝对他立约之民的宽容，终于达到了极限；这百姓曾将自己的救主钉在十字架上。凡能循通常途径得救的人，都已蒙拯救。百姓大众却顽固地拒绝一切改进。义人雅各本是最有可能使犹太人与基督教和好的人，却被他那些心硬的同胞用石头打死，而他曾天天在圣殿中为他们代求；随着他的死，耶路撒冷的基督徒群体对那座城也失去了重要意义。“大灾难”与可怕审判的时刻日益迫近。主的预言即将逐字应验：耶路撒冷被夷为平地，圣殿被焚毁，没有一块石头留在石头上。28

犹太战争爆发前不久，也就是耶路撒冷被围攻的七年前（公元63年），一个名叫约书亚(Joshua)，或耶稣 (Jesus)的农夫，在住棚节时来到城中，带着先知狂喜的语调，昼夜在街上的人群中呼喊：“有声音从早晨而来，有声音从晚上而来！有声音从四风而来！有降灾的声音临到耶路撒冷和圣殿！有声音攻击新郎和新妇！有声音攻击全体百姓！耶路撒冷有祸了，有祸了！”官长们被这灾祸的宣告所惊吓，便将这位预告灾难的先知抓起来鞭打。他毫不反抗，仍旧呼喊着“有祸了”。他被带到巡抚阿尔比努斯(Albinus)面前，受鞭打直到骨头显露，却不为自己辩白一句，也不咒诅仇敌；每挨一下，只是悲声呼喊：“耶路撒冷有祸了，有祸了！”巡抚问他是谁，从哪里来，他一概不答。最后，他们把他当作疯子释放了。但他继续如此，长达七年零五个月，直到战争爆发，尤其在三大节期宣告耶路撒冷即将倾覆。围城期间，他最后一次在城墙上吟唱他的哀歌。忽然，他又加上一句：“我也有祸了，有祸了！”——就在这时，罗马人投来的一块石头击中了他的头，使他那先知式的哀号就此终止。29

犹太人的叛乱。

在最后几任总督腓力斯 (Felix)、非斯都 (Festus)、阿尔比努斯和弗洛鲁斯(Florus)治下，道德的腐败与一切社会纽带的瓦解逐年加剧，与此同时，罗马的轭也变得愈加沉重。腓力斯上任后，被称为“短刀党”(Sicarians，源自 sica，意为短刀)的刺客，手持短刀，遍行巴勒斯坦；只要出钱，任何罪行都肯做，危及城乡的安全。此外，犹太人内部的党派之争，以及他们对异教压迫者的仇恨，上升为最肆无忌惮的政治和宗教狂热，又不断受到假先知和假弥赛亚的煽动。例如，据约瑟夫斯记载，其中一人曾吸引三万人跟从他。这样，我们的主所预言的话便应验了：“将有假基督、假先知起来，迷惑许多人。”

终于，在公元66年5月，最后一任巡抚格西乌斯·弗洛鲁斯 (GessiusFlorus，自65年起任职)治下，爆发了一场有组织的反罗马叛乱。此人是个邪恶残暴的暴君，用约瑟夫斯的话说，就是被安置在作恶者之上的刽子手。但与此同时，叛乱者内部的不同派别之间，尤其是奋锐党(Zealots) 与温和派(Moderates)，或激进派与保守派之间，也爆发了可怕的内战。凶悍的奋锐党具有宗教与爱国狂热所能激发的一切热情和力量；有人将他们比作法国大革命中的山岳党(Montagnards)，确是恰当的。他们在战争进程中取得优势，强占了城市与圣殿，实行恐怖统治。他们不断维持百姓对弥赛亚的期待，把每一个走向毁灭的步骤都欢呼为迈向拯救的一步。关于彗星、流星以及各种可怕凶兆和奇事的传闻，都被解释为弥赛亚即将降临并统治外邦人的征兆。罗马人则将韦斯帕芗和提图斯认作弥赛亚。

在那个时代，毫无盟友而挑战罗马，无异于挑战整个武装起来的世界；但马加比家族(Maccabees)英勇功绩的回忆所激发的宗教狂热，蒙蔽了犹太人的眼睛，使他们看不见这场疯狂而绝望的叛乱必然失败的结局。

罗马人的入侵。

尼禄皇帝得知叛乱的消息后，派遣他最负盛名的将领韦斯帕芗，率大军前往巴勒斯坦。韦斯帕芗于67年从叙利亚的港口城市多利买(Ptolemais，即亚柯 Acco)发起战役，率领六万人的军队，冲破顽强抵抗，席卷加利利。但罗马发生的事变阻碍了他完成征服，迫使他返回那里。尼禄已经自杀。加尔巴(Galba)、奥托 (Otho) 和维特里乌斯 (Vitellius)三位皇帝接踵而立。最后一位醉酒时在罗马的狗窝里被人揪出，拖过街头，受辱而死。69年，韦斯帕芗被一致拥戴为皇帝，恢复了秩序与繁荣。

他的儿子提图斯，十年后也成为皇帝，并以温厚仁爱著称，30此时接手继续进行犹太战争，成为上帝手中毁灭圣城与圣殿的工具。他拥有不少于八万名训练有素的士兵，在斯科普斯山(Mount Scopus)及邻近的橄榄山扎营，城与圣殿尽收眼底；从这一高处望去，它们的壮丽景象显露无遗。汲沦谷(Kedron) 将围城者与被围者隔开。

公元70年4月，逾越节刚过，耶路撒冷满是外来客旅，围城便开始了。奋锐党以讥诮而挑衅的态度，拒绝了提图斯一再提出的建议，也拒绝了随军担任翻译与调停人的约瑟夫斯的恳求；凡提议投降的人，都被他们杀死。他们出城突袭，冲下汲沦谷，再攻上山坡，使罗马人蒙受重大损失。困难越多，他们的勇气越大。数以百计的俘虏被钉十字架（一天竟达五百人），只使他们更加愤怒。甚至开始肆虐、每日夺去数千人性命，并迫使一个妇人烤食自己孩子的饥荒，31母亲与婴孩的哀号，以及周围最令人怜悯的种种惨状，也不能打动这些疯狂的狂热者。历史上再没有如此顽强抵抗、如此不顾一切地英勇奋战、蔑视死亡的事例。犹太人不仅为公民自由、生命和祖国而战，也为那构成他们民族的骄傲与荣耀、赋予他们全部历史以意义的事物而战——就是他们的宗教；即便在这种可怕的堕落状态中，这宗教仍赋予他们几乎超人的忍耐力。

城与圣殿的毁灭。

终于，到了7月，安东尼亚堡 (Antonia)在夜间遭突袭而失守。这为圣殿的毁灭开辟了道路，而悲剧也由此达到顶点。7月17日，每日的献祭停止了，因为所有人手都必须用于防守。燔祭坛上最后一次、也是最血腥的祭，便是聚集在祭坛周围的数千犹太人惨遭屠杀。

据约瑟夫斯说，提图斯起初打算保全这座宏伟的建筑，作为胜利的纪念，或许也出于某种迷信的恐惧；当火焰眼看就要烧到至圣所时，他穿过烈火与浓烟，越过死者与垂死者，奋力前去制止大火。32但这场毁灭已由更高的旨意所命定。他手下的士兵被顽强的抵抗激得近乎疯狂，又贪图其中的金银财宝，已无法遏止他们的毁灭行动。起初，圣殿周围的廊屋被点燃。随后，一支火把从金门掷了进去。火焰升起时，犹太人发出可怕的尖叫，竭力扑火；另一些人则以最后一阵痉挛般的力量，紧紧抓住他们对弥赛亚的盼望，深信一个假先知的宣告，说上帝将在圣殿的大火中发出拯救他百姓的信号。各军团争相助长火势，使这些不幸的人尝尽他们肆无忌惮的暴怒。不久，整座宏伟的建筑便陷入火海，映亮天空。圣殿于公元70年8月10日被焚毁；据传统说，这正是第一座圣殿被尼布甲尼撒毁灭的同月同日。约瑟夫斯说：“没有人能够想象，圣殿焚烧时从四面八方响起的尖叫，是何等响亮、何等可怕。军团得胜的呐喊与欢呼，穿过山上和全城那些被烈火与刀剑包围的百姓的哀号。周围群山，甚至远至比利亚(Peraea)（？）的回声，更增添了这震耳欲聋的巨响。然而，惨状本身比这混乱更加可怕。圣殿所在的山丘灼热如沸，仿佛直到山脚都裹在一片烈焰之中。鲜血比烈火更多，被杀者比杀人者更多。地面无处可见，到处都覆盖着尸体；士兵越过这些尸堆，追赶逃亡的人。”33

罗马人在东门对面那不成形状的废墟上竖起鹰旗，向鹰旗献祭，并在极其热烈的欢呼声中，拥戴提图斯为统帅(Imperator)。这样，关于“那行毁坏可憎的站在圣地”的预言便应验了。34

耶路撒冷被夷为平地；只留下希律王宫的三座塔楼——希庇库斯(Hippicus，至今仍存)、法赛尔 (Phasael) 和马利亚姆尼(Mariamne)——以及西城墙的一部分，作为这座被征服之城昔日坚固的见证；这里曾是犹太神权政治的中心，也是基督教会的摇篮。

据传，连异教徒提图斯也曾公开宣称，上帝以特别的护理帮助罗马人，将犹太人逐出他们坚不可摧的堡垒。35约瑟夫斯亲历了这场战争的始末，起初是加利利的总督和犹太军队的将领，后来成为韦斯帕芗的俘虏，最后又随侍提图斯，作罗马人与犹太人之间的调停者。他在这场悲剧中看见了上帝的审判；对于那些堕落的同胞，尽管他在其他方面对他们仍怀着真挚的感情，却也承认：“我不愿迟疑不说，虽然说出来使我痛心：我相信，倘若罗马人迟迟不惩罚这些恶徒，这城也必被大地吞没，或被洪水淹没，或像所多玛一样，被天火烧灭。因为住在其中的这一代，比从前遭受这些惩罚的人更加不敬虔。整个民族因他们的疯狂而归于毁灭。”36

因此，罗马最优秀的皇帝之一，竟必须执行上帝早已警告的审判，而当时最博学的犹太人则必须将它记述下来；他们由此在无意也不知情之中，为预言的真实和耶稣基督使命的神圣作了见证。这个背道的民族正因弃绝了他，才招致这一切以及后来接踵而来的灾祸。

耶路撒冷的毁灭，足以成为一位基督徒荷马 (Homer)施展天才的题材。它被称为“整个古代史中最震撼心灵的斗争”。37然而，当时没有耶利米来为大卫与所罗门之城吟唱挽歌。《启示录》早已写成，并且预言外邦人“要践踏圣城四十二个月”。38近代绘画大师之一考尔巴赫(Kaulbach)，以此为题材创作了他最伟大的画作之一，收藏于柏林博物馆。画中呈现的是焚烧中的圣殿：前景中，大祭司将剑刺入自己的胸膛；他周围是令人心碎的苦难景象；上方，古代的先知们正在观看他们预言的应验；在他们下方，提图斯与罗马军队成了不自知的神怒执行者；左下方是中世纪传说中流浪的犹太人亚哈随鲁(Ahasuerus)，被复仇女神驱赶着，走向永不终结的未来；右边则是一群基督徒，平静地离开这毁灭的现场，还有犹太儿童恳求他们的保护。

幸存者的命运与罗马的凯旋。

经过五个月的围攻，全城落入胜利者手中。据约瑟夫斯所报，围城期间丧生的犹太人，包括从乡间涌入城中的所有人，多达一百一十万；这个数字大得惊人，很可能有所夸张。围城结束后不久，又有一万一千人饿死。九万七千人被掳，被卖为奴，或送往矿场，或在凯撒利亚(Caesarea)、贝里图斯(Berytus)、安提阿及其他城市的角斗表演中被杀。最强壮俊美的男子被挑选出来，参加罗马的凯旋游行；其中包括主要的守城将领和叛乱首领西门·巴尔－乔拉(Simon Bar-Giora) 与吉斯卡拉的约翰 (John of Gischala)。39

韦斯帕芗与提图斯共同庆祝了这场付出惨重代价的胜利（71年）。这场盛典不惜任何费用。两位征服者头戴桂冠，身披紫袍，分乘战车缓缓前行；图密善(Domitian)则骑着一匹骏马，在民众与贵族的欢呼声中，一同前往卡庇托山朱庇特神庙(JupiterCapitolinus)。身着节庆服装的士兵和七百名犹太俘虏走在他们前面。诸神的像，以及圣殿的圣器——陈设饼的桌子、七枝灯台、宣告禧年的号角、香器和律法书卷——都在行列中被抬着前行，随后存放于新建的和平神庙(Temple of Peace)；40惟有律法书卷与圣所的紫色幔子，由韦斯帕芗留在自己的宫中。西门·巴尔－乔拉被从塔尔佩亚岩(Tarpeian Rock)上扔下；吉斯卡拉的约翰被判终身监禁。所铸钱币刻有铭文：Judaea capta,Judaeadevicta（犹太被掳，犹太被征服）。但韦斯帕芗与提图斯都没有采用“犹太征服者”(Judaeus) 这一胜利称号；他们鄙视一个已经丧失祖国的民族。

约瑟夫斯目睹了这场铺张的盛典，看着自己的民族受辱、仿佛全族被钉十字架，却不带一滴眼泪地将它记述下来。41提图斯凯旋门至今仍矗立于罗马斗兽场与广场之间；深思的基督徒望着门上犹太俘虏抬着圣殿器具的浮雕，面对神圣预言的应验，心中满了敬畏。

巴勒斯坦的征服，也意味着犹太国家的毁灭。韦斯帕芗将土地留作私产，或分配给麾下的老兵。五年的战争使百姓陷入极端贫困，没有官长（按犹太人的意义而言），没有圣殿，也没有国家。在假弥赛亚巴尔－科赫巴(Bar-Cocheba) 领导下再度爆发的叛乱，只导致哈德良 (Hadrian)的军队更彻底地摧毁耶路撒冷、蹂躏巴勒斯坦（132—135年）。然而，犹太人仍保有律法、先知书和神圣的传统；直到今日，他们仍以不可摧折的坚韧持守这些，并盼望一个伟大的未来。他们散居全地，处处为家，又处处无家；拒绝与任何其他种族通婚，聚居于各自的社群，面容的每一特征、宗教的每一礼仪，都标明他们是一个独特的民族；他们忍耐、节制、勤勉，凡所经营多有成就，虽受压迫仍然兴旺，受人嘲笑却又令人畏惧，遭人抢夺却仍富有，屡遭屠杀却又重新兴起。他们历经数世纪的逼迫而存留下来，而且很可能继续生存，直到时间的尽头：成为世人鄙视、钦佩与惊奇交织的对象。

§ 39.耶路撒冷的毁灭对基督教会的影响。

耶路撒冷的基督徒记得主的劝诫，及时离开了这座注定毁灭的城，逃往约旦河外、比利亚(Peraea) 北部低加坡里 (Decapolis) 的佩拉 (Pella)城；保罗曾在其面前受审的希律·亚基帕二世 (Herod Agrippa II)王，在那里为他们提供了安全的避难所。一个古老的传统说，有神圣的声音或天使向他们的领袖启示了逃离的责任。42在那里，在以外邦人为主的居民中，受割礼者的教会重新建立起来。可惜，我们对它的历史一无所知。但它再也没有恢复先前的重要地位。耶路撒冷重建为基督教城市后，其主教被擢升为东方四位牧首之一；然而，这只是享有荣誉、而无实权的牧首之位，在穆罕默德教徒入侵以后，更沦为徒具虚名的影子。

犹太神权政体毁灭的可怕浩劫，必定在基督徒中引起了极其深刻的震动；如今，由于缺乏有关此事的一切具体记载，我们几乎无法真切地想象当时的情形。43这是犹太教最大的灾难，却给基督教带来了极大的益处；它驳倒了前者，却使后者得到昭雪与解放。它不仅极大地激发了信心，同时也在这两个宗教群体的关系史上划出了一个真正的时代界限。它使两者永远分离。诚然，使徒保罗早已借着其整个教义体系所具有的基督教普世性，在内在原则上完成了这种分离；但在外在行为上，他曾以种种方式迁就犹太教，并且不止一次虔诚地前往圣殿。他不愿以革命者的姿态出现，也不愿抢在历史的自然进程、上帝护理的道路之前。44然而，如今全能上帝的雷霆一击，也使这决裂在外在形式上彻底完成。上帝亲自毁掉了他迄今所居住、耶稣曾教训人、使徒曾祷告的殿；他弃绝了自己特选的子民，因为他们顽梗地弃绝了弥赛亚；他拆毁了摩西神权政体的整个架构，其敬拜制度在本质上原先专与会幕、后来专与圣殿相联系。然而，他这样做，也割断了那些迄今一直束缚着幼年教会的绳索；按照有机发展的规律，这些绳索必然使教会与旧约的外在体制及其中心耶路撒冷相联。从此，异教徒再不能把基督教仅仅看作犹太教的一个宗派，而必须将它视为一个新的、独特的宗教来对待。因此，耶路撒冷的毁灭，标志着那一重大的转折：基督教会作为一个整体，永远破开犹太教的蛹壳，意识到自己已经成熟，并立即在治理与敬拜上，以独立的姿态立于世人面前。45

然而，这种与顽梗的犹太教及其宗教形式的决裂，并不意味着背离旧约启示的精神。相反，教会承受了以色列的产业。基督徒显明为真正的犹太人，亚伯拉罕属灵的子孙；他们顺着摩西宗教的内在潮流，寻见了那位成全律法和先知者；他是旧约完美的果实，也是新约活的胚芽；是新的道德创造的开端与本原。

如今剩下的工作，只是在这改变了的局势中，完成教会的巩固；将各种前提汇合为其应有的结果；把分别体现于犹太基督徒教会和外邦基督徒教会中的彼得的保守倾向与保罗的进取倾向接纳进来，融合为第三种更高的倾向，形成一个持久的有机体；既阐明新旧两约在差异中的统一，也阐明它们在统一中的差异；并以这种方式，完成使徒教会的历史。

这就是使一切臻于完成的使徒约翰的工作。
